title: People stand behind owner of La Galette bakery being detained by ICE - KAKE
description: The owner of La Galette French Bakery in Wichita was detained by ICE and faces possible deportation to Lebanon. He has been in the U.S. since 1993 and has past convictions that affected his legal status. Attorneys are seeking a stay of deportation while employees strive to keep the bakery running.
text:
WICHITA, Kan. (KAKE) - The owner of a La Galette French Bakery was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and may be deported to Lebanon.
Attorneys for the restaurant owner, Rob Attar, hope to get a “stay-in-place.”
Employees at La Galette say ICE took him into custody while he was doing his regular annual immigration check-in.
“The phone rang, and it was him from the facility saying that he was arrested,” Maria Esparza, an employee at La Galette, said. “They said that he has nothing to withhold, and he doesn’t know what else is going to happen, so he just wants to let us know to do whatever we can and try to keep the business going.”
He’s accused of being in the U.S. illegally.
Esparza says she and other employees are stepping up to keep Attar’s 40-year-old restaurant open.
“I mean, we have to relearn from scratch,” Esparza said. “We try to do our best, and as I said, it’s not just for him; it’s for us, for the family, and for the economy.”
Immigration Attorney Abdul Arif represents Attar. Attar has been in the U.S. since 1993, and in 2000, Arif says police arrested Attar on federal weapons and other charges. He says Attar served six years in prison, completed his probation, and hasn’t been in trouble with the law since. He also says Attar married an American woman, but he couldn’t get his green card because of his conviction.
“I don’t want to get too technical with it, but we are exploring a possibility that his conviction can somehow be waived because it’s 20 years old and he has not reoffended, and he is a model citizen by all accounts,” Arif said. “We have filed an emergency motion with ICE to stay his deportation.”
La Galette customers are doing all they can to support Attar.
“It’s a disgrace,” Pat Lehman said. “It’s like we know what it was like to live in Nazi Germany, because that’s exactly what’s happening to people in our country today, and it’s a disgrace. He’s been a member of our community for years and years, and to have someone just snatched away like that, I can’t imagine.”
A spokesperson with the Department of Homeland Security says Attar was convicted of smuggling marijuana and selling cocaine, as well as multiple weapon offenses. The spokesperson said Attar lost his legal status in 2004 because of his convictions.
Attar’s attorney says Attar’s was driving to Kansas City to meet with ICE in hopes of getting a stay in the case. The attorney says that will give him more time to research the case and move forward.

title: Trump deportees to Sierra Leone risk being forced home, rights group says - Internazionale
description:
DAKAR, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Amnesty International on Friday urged Sierra Leone to halt the expected repatriation of three people deported from the United States, saying they could face serious human rights violations if returned to their home countries elsewhere in West Africa.
• The rights group said Abalo Agba of Togo, Alfred Kamara of Liberia and Fatou Traore of Ivory Coast had each lived in the United States for more than 20 years when they were removed by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement to Sierra Leone on October 12, and that they all have children under 18 still in the US • They had previously secured a form of protection in the US known as withholding of removal, meaning a US immigration judge found they were more likely than not to face torture or other abuses if forced home • Since taking office in January last year, the Trump administration has struck several deals with African governments that have agreed to accept migrants from other countries.
• Sierra Leone reached an agreement with Washington to accept up to 300 West African third-country nationals annually • Amnesty said on Friday that migrants previously deported under the deal had been quickly repatriated, and it criticised what it described as a “revolving door” policy of forcing people home • A Sierra Leone government spokesperson and the US State Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment (Writing by Ayen Deng Bior; Editing by Robbie Corey-Boulet and Ros Russell)

DAKAR, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Amnesty International on Friday urged Sierra Leone to halt the expected repatriation of three people deported from the United States, saying they could face serious human rights violations if returned to their home countries elsewhere in West Africa.

• The rights group said Abalo Agba of Togo, Alfred Kamara of Liberia and Fatou Traore of Ivory Coast had each lived in the United States for more than 20 years when they were removed by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement to Sierra Leone on October 12, and that they all have children under 18 still in the US

• They had previously secured a form of protection in the US known as withholding of removal, meaning a US immigration judge found they were more likely than not to face torture or other abuses if forced home

• Since taking office in January last year, the Trump administration has struck several deals with African governments that have agreed to accept migrants from other countries.

• Sierra Leone reached an agreement with Washington to accept up to 300 West African third-country nationals annually

• Amnesty said on Friday that migrants previously deported under the deal had been quickly repatriated, and it criticised what it described as a “revolving door” policy of forcing people home

• A Sierra Leone government spokesperson and the US State Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment

(Writing by Ayen Deng Bior; Editing by Robbie Corey-Boulet and Ros Russell)

text:
Two deportation flights are expected to carry critically ill ICE detainees from south Florida to the Central African Republic — and possibly Burundi — by Friday, according to immigration advocates who learned of the planned operations only after detainees inside two South Florida facilities were called in for interviews with removal officers. The flights would push the limits of a third-country deportation policy the Supreme Court reactivated less than a month ago, sending people with serious medical conditions on journeys of more than 20 hours to nations where no reception plan, no medical arrangement, and no diplomatic acknowledgment appears to be waiting.

Families and Advocates Sound the Alarm

Detainees inside Krome North Processing Center in Miami and the Broward Transitional Center in Pompano Beach were recently summoned to meet with deportation officers — a step immigration advocates consistently read as a signal of imminent removal. Both facilities are run by private contractors under ICE agreements and sit in neighboring Miami-Dade and Broward counties.

The advocacy organization Workers Circle, which has maintained contact with detainees at both sites, flagged the situation to families and media after learning of the officer interviews. Immigration attorney Shalyn Fluharty, working from information the detainees themselves relayed, told The Guardian that two flights were anticipated — one Thursday, one Friday — headed to the Central African Republic, with Burundi named as another possible destination. She stressed that long-haul deportation flights carry particular risk for anyone managing diabetes, heart conditions, or stroke vulnerability, given the combination of prolonged restraint, disrupted meal schedules, and severely limited access to medical intervention mid-flight.

Workers Circle Director of Social Justice Noelle Damico did not mince her words at a press conference this week: "It's abhorrent. This is profoundly inhumane."

The Cuban Man at the Center of the Story

The case drawing the most public attention involves Noslén Sendra, a 41-year-old Cuban who has been in ICE custody since November 2025. He spent his first months detained at the remote Everglades facility known as "Alligator Alcatraz," which ceased operations in June 2026, before being transferred to Krome North in April. His wife, Anisley Cortés, has told multiple outlets that Sendra — who has type 2 diabetes and has been hospitalized three times with acute pancreatitis — lost more than 50 pounds in custody and remains medically fragile.

ICE informed Sendra, according to his wife, that Cuba would not accept him as a deportee and that Mexico had similarly declined, citing his health needs. Africa, he was told, would be the destination. No confirmed flight manifest has placed Sendra on either of this week's planned operations, and the Department of Homeland Security did not respond substantively to The Guardian after receiving his personal details. In a broader denial, a DHS spokesperson insisted that no sick detainees are being sent anywhere, that all deportees undergo medical clearance before boarding, and that they travel with any required medications in hand. Cortés said she has no idea where her husband might land — or whether the family will ever be reunited.

Attorney Fluharty questioned how ICE could realistically certify as fit for travel a person with Sendra's documented medical history, given the agency's own standards requiring a fitness-to-fly assessment before any deportation.

Krome's Collapsing Medical Infrastructure

The government's own auditors had already sounded alarms about Krome North's capacity to manage detainees with complex health needs before this week's reports surfaced. A Department of Homeland Security Inspector General report released September 11, 2026 — based on an unannounced inspection from May 2025 — counted 1,102 detainees at a facility built for a maximum of 882, putting occupancy 25 percent above its authorized limit. The same report documented 15 vacant medical positions covering behavioral health, psychology, nursing support, and administration, alongside active food-safety violations that included raw poultry stored improperly and detainees sleeping on temporary cots or the floor.

At least 27 people died in ICE custody in 2026 through September, according to data tracked by civil liberties organizations — a tally they describe as an undercount, in part because ICE rescinded a rule requiring disclosure of deaths within 30 days of release from custody. That death toll accumulated as the detention system held more than 68,000 people as of February, a roughly 70 percent increase over pre-second-term levels. Workers Circle immigrant rights organizer Arianne Betancourt told Axios that detainees with serious conditions routinely arrive in third countries only to find no medical support on the other side.

A Policy Cleared by the High Court

These flights flow directly from a September 29 Supreme Court order that handed the administration a broad interim victory. The court stayed a ruling by Boston federal district judge Brian Murphy — upheld in most of its key provisions by the First Circuit Court of Appeals on September 18 — that had required the government to give migrants meaningful written notice and a realistic opportunity to raise objections before removal to a country not listed in their deportation orders. Full oral arguments on the policy's legality are set for the December session; in the meantime, every legal obstacle to carrying out such removals was removed.

In filings submitted ahead of the ruling, Solicitor General John Sauer described third-country removals as "an essential tool to remove certain aliens." The United States has now reached removal agreements with more than three dozen countries, the majority in Africa, using the program to move tens of thousands of individuals whose home nations decline to take them back. In a 10-day span in late August alone, ICE sent more than 100 immigrants on three flights to eight African nations, according to internal government documents obtained by CBS News. A Human Rights Watch report released October 8 — titled "To Scare People" — tallied 536 third-country removals to Africa between January 2025 and early August 2026, none of them to the deportees' country of citizenship, a number that will have grown significantly before December's arguments reach the court.

No Safety Net at the Destination

The personal toll of this policy is already on the record. Arístides Fernández García, a 37-year-old Cuban, was removed to the Central African Republic at the end of July and spent nearly three months stranded in Bangui — the capital of a country the U.S. State Department rates a Level 4 "Do Not Travel" zone due to armed conflict, kidnapping, landmine risk, and health dangers — before finally managing to leave this week for Bolivia. A separate West Africa-bound deportation flight was canceled in 2021 following brutality allegations, with Cameroonian detainees submitting sworn affidavits describing coerced fingerprinting and physical abuse by ICE officers during the boarding process.

DHS pushed back forcefully against the entire premise of this week's reports. A department spokesperson stated that no medically ill individuals are being deported, that all travelers have completed a fitness-for-travel assessment and carry required medications, and that each receiving country has provided diplomatic assurances of safety for incoming deportees. As of Friday morning, no federal court had issued an emergency order blocking either of the reported flights. Neither the Central African Republic nor Burundi has publicly acknowledged that it was expecting incoming transfers from the United States this week.

text:
The right to vote on the leadership and legislation of America belongs only to American citizens

WASHINGTON – The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released the following statement after a joint investigation by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) led to the arrest of TEN non-citizens, including an illegal alien, for illegally voting in several U.S. elections in North Carolina.

On October 14 and 15, ICE, HSI, and the FBI arrested the following aliens, including nine Lawful Permanent Residents (LPRs) and one illegal alien, after they were charged with voting by alien in a federal election for illegally voting in several U.S. elections:

Edduard Omar Majano-Sosa, an illegal alien from El Salvador, charged with false claim to citizenship for illegally registering to vote in 2024 and voting by an alien. He illegally voted in the 2024 general election. He illegally entered the United States in July 2022 near El Paso, Texas, and was RELEASED into the country by the Biden Administration. He was arrested by HSI on October 15, 2026. He is facing an additional charge of prohibited person with a firearm for a pistol that was found in his vehicle during the arrest.

Karl Paul Fout, an alien from Germany, charged with false claim to citizenship for illegally registering to vote in 2008 and voting by an alien. He illegally voted in SEVEN general elections from 2008 to 2024. Fout’s criminal history includes prior convictions for TWO counts of possession of marijuana and cocaine with intent to sell and deliver and possession of cocaine. He was arrested by HSI Cary on October 15, 2026. He was lawfully admitted to the United States in February 1960.

Lawton Caswell Broomfield E McKenzie, an alien from Jamaica, charged with false claim to citizenship for registering to vote in 2007 and 2012 and voting by an alien. He illegally voted in THREE general elections between 2012 and 2024. McKenzie’s criminal history also includes convictions for manufacturing, possession, or distribution of controlled substances and arrests for disorderly conduct while intoxicated by alcohol or drugs, battery, disturbing the peace, trespassing, communicating threats, assault, and driving while impaired. He was arrested by ICE on October 15, 2026. He was lawfully admitted to the United States in November 1986.

Lionel Paul, an alien from Haiti, charged with false claim to citizenship for registering to vote in 2024 and voting by an alien. He illegally voted in the 2024 general election. He was arrested by HSI Cary on October 15, 2026. Paul’s criminal history also includes arrests for fleeing/eluding arrest with a motor vehicle and assault. He became an LPR in October 2018.

James Edward Herrmann, an alien from Germany, charged with false claim to citizenship for registering to vote in 2018 and voting by an alien. He illegally voted in TWO general elections between 2018 and 2024. Herrmann’s criminal history also includes a conviction for larceny. He was arrested by the FBI on October 14, 2026. He was lawfully admitted to the United States in December 1983.

Ramona Abreu-Exia, an alien from Germany, charged with false claim to citizenship for illegally registering to vote in 2004 and voting by an alien. She illegally voted in EIGHT general elections from 2004 to 2024, as well as in the 2008 primary election. She was arrested by the FBI on October 14, 2026. She was lawfully admitted to the United States in October 1977.

Mervin Sylvester Bogle, an alien from Jamaica, charged with falsely claiming citizenship to vote. He illegally registered to vote in 2024, and illegally voted in THREE general elections between 2008 and 2024. He was arrested by the FBI on October 15, 2026. He was lawfully admitted to the United States in February 1981.

Robert Harold Corbett, an alien from Canada, charged with false claim to citizenship for registering to vote in 1998 and voting by an alien. He illegally voted in SIX general elections between 1998 and 2024. He was arrested by the FBI on October 14, 2026. He was lawfully admitted to the United States in December 1963.

Ludgardys Olena Matthews, an alien from Panama, charged with false claim to citizenship for registering to vote in 2009 and voting by an alien. She illegally voted in THREE general elections between 2018 and 2024, as well as in the 2020 primary election. She was arrested by HSI Cary on October 15, 2026. She was lawfully admitted to the United States in October 1986 and was granted LPR status in September 2015 under the Obama Administration.

Gjina Gojcaj McDonald, an alien from Montenegro, charged with false claim to citizenship for illegally registering to vote in 2008 and voting by an alien. She illegally voted in SEVEN general elections from 2008 to 2024, as well as in the 2012 primary election and the 2019 special election. She was arrested by the FBI on October 14, 2026. She was lawfully admitted to the United States in February 1969.

“These aliens have been arrested and charged with illegally voting in multiple elections,” said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “They knowingly violated our laws. Now, thanks to the devoted patriots of HSI and our partners at the Department of Justice, these aliens will have to answer for violating the sacred right of Americans to elect their own leadership. Let this be a message to any non-citizens out there who are thinking about voting in our elections: If you illegally vote, we will arrest you and you will be charged. Only American citizens should be electing American leaders.”

"The right to vote is one of American citizens' most fundamental rights, and protecting our elections' integrity is a responsibility we take seriously," said Acting ICE Director David J. Venturella. "When people illegally cast ballots, they undermine the law and the trust Americans place in our democratic process. These arrests send the message that election laws are not optional, and those who violate them will be held accountable. Working alongside our federal and state partners, we will continue to investigate election fraud and hold offenders accountable."

“There is no more important right a citizen possesses above the right to vote. All other rights flow from this Constitutional principle when We the People select our government. Every non-citizen who chooses to illegally vote subverts our constitutional republic, actively canceling out the vote of a law-abiding citizen,” said Ellis Boyle, U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of North Carolina. “This is not a victimless crime – quite the opposite. Every voting citizen is a victim every time. These indictments should serve as a stark warning to anyone contemplating voting illegally in our 2026 election: we are watching, we will find you if you do it, and we will prosecute you.”

“The integrity of federal elections is essential to the health of our democracy,” said Reid Davis, FBI Special Agent in Charge in North Carolina. “Every FBI field office assigns dedicated election‑crimes coordinators because protecting the election process is core to our mission. When questions about voter eligibility arise, we work closely with our state and federal partners to review records, confirm the facts, and ensure election laws are honored. Any violation erodes public trust and dilutes valid votes. When any aspect of our democratic process is threatened, the FBI will act decisively to defend it.”

This is part of the Trump Administration’s broader focus on stopping non-citizens from voting in American elections. Recent examples include:

In October, HSI arrested Lizbeth Almonte-Rosa, a naturalized U.S. citizen from the Dominican Republic, for registering to vote and then illegally voting in 2022 in New Jersey prior to her naturalization.

In October, HSI arrested Andres Garcia, an alien from Cuba, who registered to vote and then illegally voted in 2022 and 2024 in Missouri.

In October, HSI arrested Paulo Jorge Silva, an alien from Portugal, who registered to vote and then illegally voted in 2024 in Pennsylvania.

In September, Secretary Mullin and Attorney General Todd Blanche held a press conference announcing federal indictments against ten non-citizens for illegally voting in Minnesota.

In September, HSI arrested Mukeshkumar Somabhai Chaudhari, a non-citizen from India, for knowingly making a false claim of U.S. citizenship to vote in the 2024 election in Minnesota.

In September, HSI and the FBI arrested Sanata Coulibaly, an alien from Senegal, who admitted to voting in 2020 and 2024 in New Jersey.

In September, an HSI investigation led to the conviction of Evelyn Novelles Miller, an alien from the Philippines, who illegally voted in the 2024 election in Pennsylvania.

In September, HSI arrested Ludwig Uriel Espejo-Carrillo, an alien from Mexico, and charged him with unlawful voting and false claim to U.S. citizenship after illegally voting in American elections in 2015.

In September, ICE arrested Anthony Tyrone Higgs, an alien from the Bahamas who had illegally voted in the 2020 election, and whose criminal history includes convictions for TWO counts of possession of a weapon during a violent crime, TWO counts of grand larceny, armed robbery with a deadly weapon, criminal domestic violence, assault on a police officer, and resisting arrest.

In September, ICE arrested Mariana Alexandra Dewey, an alien from Peru, for illegally misrepresenting herself as a U.S. citizen to vote in the 2024 election in Kansas.

In August, Carlos Felipe Jaramillo-Grajales, a criminal illegal alien from Colombia, was sentenced to three years in prison after an ICE investigation led to him pleading guilty to committing identity theft to illegally vote in elections for more than 20 years.

In July, HSI arrested Marian Charitun, an alien from Slovakia who had illegally voted in the 2022 election in New Jersey.

In July, an HSI investigation led to the arrest of Denise Nataly Migliore, an alien from Australia who illegally voted in the 2022 and 2024 elections in Louisiana.

In May, DHS and the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced charges against four non-citizens in New Jersey who illegally voted in federal elections and made false statements while applying for U.S. citizenship.

In April, Jose Ceballos, an alien from Mexico, pleaded guilty to THREE counts of disorderly election conduct after illegally voting multiple times and falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen in Kansas.

In March, ICE arrested Mahady Sacko, a criminal illegal alien from Mauritania who had been illegally voting in the United States since 2008.

In recent months, DHS has taken additional steps to safeguard the integrity and security of American elections. These measures include:

In September, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) released its 2026 Election Infrastructure Security Plan: Securing the Next 250.

In July, Secretary Mullin sent letters to secretaries of state in several states across the country warning that tens of thousands of non-citizens are registered to vote.

In July, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) announced that grant recipients will be required to take several key actions on election integrity.

In June, DHS directed ICE to enforce stricter penalties for non-citizens who illegally vote in American elections, including deportation.

text:
FOLKSTON, GA – Today, American Oversight, Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, and Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta launched an investigation into Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE’s) response to the ongoing hunger strike led by people detained at the Folkston ICE Processing Center in Georgia.

The groups filed two Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests seeking the expedited release of significant incident reports, hunger-strike-related monitoring data, and communications with ICE’s Atlanta Field Office about the hunger strike. These records could provide critical information about how facility officials have responded to the protest, including the retaliatory use of solitary confinement, transfers or deportations, and any other measures taken against people participating in the strike.

“The conditions inside the Folkston facility are so dire that human beings detained there have been forced to starve themselves as a cry for help,” said Chioma Chukwu, Executive Director of American Oversight. “ICE created this situation, and its continued failure to address even the most basic human needs, including access to food and safe drinking water, is a choice. Lives are at stake, and every day of inaction puts people at greater risk. The public needs to know whether ICE has retaliated against those participating in the strike and what it is doing to end the deplorable conditions in Folkston. ICE must act immediately to protect the people in its custody and be held accountable for its choices that put their lives in danger.”

“These men are putting their own bodies and lives on the line because they feel they have no other way to be heard. That should tell all of us just how desperate and intolerable conditions inside Folkston have become,” said Evan Benz, Managing Attorney at the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights. “Hunger strikes require extraordinary courage. No one stops eating for days or weeks at a time lightly. ICE owes them, their families, and the public answers about how it has responded to this protest and what it is doing to address their demands for better conditions at Folkston.”

“It has been nearly 20 days since the brave men detained at Folkston collectively reclaimed their power from a system built to convince them they have none. The hunger strikers and the public deserve to know the full extent of ICE’s efforts to suppress their resistance. ICE must be held accountable for its actions, and transparency is the bare minimum,” said Samantha C. Hamilton, Senior Litigation Staff Attorney at Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta. “This FOIA request is a demand for accountability. No system that enables such cruelty and profits from human suffering can be reformed from within. The inhumane conditions at Folkston reflect the fundamental cruelty of an immigration detention system that treats human lives as commodities. Advancing Justice-Atlanta demands the closure of Folkston and every immigration detention facility, and calls for ICE to be abolished once and for all. No one should profit from the suffering of our communities.”

The requests come amid serious concerns about retaliation against the hunger strikers and the health and safety of people who have gone without food for prolonged periods. The advocates and watchdog are also seeking information that could shed light on whether ICE has considered or used forced feeding or other medical interventions in response to the strike.

On Oct. 4, men detained at Folkston released a video calling public attention to their prolonged detention in ICE custody. The men featured in the video were asylum seekers, many of whom had reportedly been detained for two years or longer. Two days later, people detained at Folkston began a hunger strike protesting their prolonged detention and the conditions inside the facility, including moldy food, insects in drinking water, unsanitary conditions, lack of adequate medical treatment, and abuse by staff.

text:
Oregon is dropping its lawsuit to halt construction of an immigrant detention center in Newport, after the U.S. Department of Homeland Security confirmed it’s no longer pursuing the project.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials’ effort to build a detention center at the Newport Airport first came to light a year ago, after the agency relocated a Coast Guard rescue helicopter that had been based there since 1987. That prompted a series of lawsuits from the city, the state and community members — some aimed at preserving rescue helicopter access for coastal tourists and the local fishing fleet, others at keeping ICE from setting up a jail.

On Friday, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, confirmed in federal court filings that it has abandoned plans to build a detention center in Newport and that it presently has no plans to build anywhere in Oregon. DHS also agreed to give Newport leaders at least 30 days’ notice if it resumes efforts to build a detention center there, through Aug. 1 of next year.

Officials in Newport, which joined Oregon in the lawsuit to keep ICE out, applauded the news.

“Our responsibility is to stand up for our residents, protect our community’s future and ensure that decisions affecting Newport are made with the transparency and accountability our community deserves,” Mayor Jan Kapla said.

DHS officials did not respond to an emailed request for a comment. In earlier court disclosures, the agency revealed that it had started working to bring a detention center to Newport by fall 2025, moving the Coast Guard helicopter to make room for that project, and originally expected to house detainees there as early as the start of 2026.

The helicopter has been back since December, after a judge ordered its return in a separate lawsuit that is still under way.

State Attorney General Dan Rayfield said Oregon will continue to fight to keep the rescue helicopter in Newport, and celebrated the end of the lawsuit over the planned detention center.

text:
96

WASHINGTON (OSV News) — A divided D.C. Circuit panel Oct. 20 reversed a lower court ruling and allowed a multifaith coalition to continue its challenge to a Trump administration policy reducing restrictions on U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement actions at what are seen as sensitive locations, including houses of worship.

In 2025, a coalition of more than two dozen religious organizations filed a lawsuit to challenge a Trump administration policy that rescinded long-standing restrictions on arrests at sensitive locations, also including schools and hospitals, with exceptions for public safety or national security threats.

In its ruling, the panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit overturned an April 2025 decision by the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia that the multifaith coalition lacked standing to challenge the Trump administration’s rescission of “sensitive locations” protection.

Kelsi Brown Corkran, the Supreme Court director for the Institute for Constitutional Advocacy and Protection at Georgetown Law and the lead counsel for plaintiffs, said in a written statement shared with OSV News, “The D.C. Circuit’s decision recognizes the real harm that DHS inflicted on religious communities when it rescinded the sensitive locations policy that had protected places of worship from immigration enforcement activity for over three decades.”

Victory for millions of people of faith represented by coalition

“It is an important victory for the millions of people of faith represented by the 27 Jewish and Christian denominations and organizations that came together to file this suit in defense of their right to worship and serve their communities without fear of intrusion by ICE officers,” Brown Corkran said.

The Rev. Carlos L. Malave, president of Latino Christian National Network, an organization among the plaintiffs in the lawsuit, said in a statement, “Our faith calls us to persevere in doing good.”

“The Latino Christian National Network celebrates the D.C. Court’s decision regarding our case to protect ‘sensitive locations,'” he said. “Houses of worship and sacred spaces must be respected, and the constitutional right of all church members to worship freely and without fear must be safeguarded.”

The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops was not a plaintiff in the lawsuit but filed an amicus brief in support of the plaintiffs.

Trump policy change creates ‘an untenable position’

That brief argued that the “rescission of the Sensitive Locations Policy at issue here,” which the brief noted was in effect for over three decades, “has had the predictable, deleterious effect of forcing Plaintiffs into an untenable position: they either increase the risk to their congregants of harmful enforcement action by maintaining the obligation to attend weekly services, or limit the provision of in-person religious services to their congregants in response to the imminent threat of an enforcement action, and their congregants’ well-founded fears thereof.”

They said either scenario presents “severe and concrete” injury that “the courts are ill-suited to dismiss as speculative.”

The Trump administration rescinded the long-standing ICE policy — which prohibits immigration enforcement arrests at certain locations, as well as other sensitive events like weddings and funerals without approval from supervisors — shortly after he returned to the White House in 2025. The previous policy had exceptions for public safety or national security threats.

In a separate lawsuit, a federal judge previously blocked immigration agents from conducting enforcement operations in houses of worship for Quakers and a handful of other religious groups limited to those who filed that suit.

text:
Immigration lawyers in Whatcom and Skagit counties are bracing for an onslaught of new cases as deportation efforts ramp up at the Canadian border.

The federal government appears to be using Washington voter rolls to facilitate deportations as the Trump administration cracks down on illegal voting ahead of the midterm elections. The new trend is likely to jam immigration courts creating a backlog and burdening the area’s immigration lawyers who say they already are stretched thin.

In the crossfire are U.S. permanent residents. One woman, a 61-year-old Canadian citizen and U.S. permanent resident, was held and questioned by U.S. border agents for six hours in September about whether or not she had ever voted in a U.S. election. (Paige Adamson, who — fearing deportation, declined to seek medical care in Bellingham — died Oct. 18 in Point Roberts.) Attorneys have heard from others, including a disabled truck driver who has lived in Washington alongside his American spouse for decades, and a Filipino woman with a green card in Point Roberts who now worries about being effectively trapped in the exclave.

“There aren’t a lot of lawyers in Whatcom County that do deportation,” Blaine-based immigration lawyer Len Saunders said. “A lot of these lawyers who take the cases, I’ve been told, are overwhelmed by what’s already in the pipeline for immigration courts.”

A spokesperson for the Washington state Attorney General’s Office said the state is tracking reports of incidents similar to the Canadian woman’s experience at the border but declined to discuss specific cases or comment on the number of cases the office has recorded.

More than a numbers game

Data from the Washington State Bar Association show about 35 immigration and naturalization attorneys in Whatcom County and five in Skagit. Across the state, there are nearly 1,200.

But the number of immigration lawyers alone doesn’t tell the whole story. The majority of immigration attorneys in Whatcom County, for example, focus on employment- and family-based immigration law, said Hannah Stone, a Bellingham City Council member and immigration attorney.

“Many of those attorneys have never stepped foot inside an immigration courtroom, yet their clients could ultimately receive notices to appear,” Stone wrote in an email. “I can say unequivocally there are not enough local immigration lawyers practicing removal defense.”

Nick Berning, a Bellingham attorney who works on U.S. and Canadian citizenship cases, stressed that experience within another area of immigration law doesn’t directly translate to deportation defense.

“Of immigration law, which is in itself highly specialized, removal defense is more complicated than everything else by a wide margin,” Berning said. “And of course, there’s still tons of demand in all aspects of immigration law. … We’re all very, very busy, and we don’t have time to learn this new, incredibly complicated, incredibly nuanced field of immigration law.”

Bellingham-based lawyer Gabe Harrison is one of those few attorneys who specialize in deportation defense. Although he’s only seen a handful of cases involving voting records so far, he expects there to be more.

He said the question of whether or not the area has enough immigration attorneys to meet demand predates the new trend at the border but will be exacerbated by the development.

“We are definitely overwhelmed as an office,” he said. “Certainly, adding a whole other segment is going to be difficult for us to absorb, but we will do it to the best of our ability, and we really don’t want to say no to people.”

Berning said that removal defense has historically been one of the largest areas of unmet need in immigration law, partially because many people often don’t have the resources to pay for such drawn-out, complicated cases.

In fact, the Washington Immigrant Solidarity Network (WAISN) requested $5 million from the state Legislature earlier this year to continue running its deportation defense hotline amid a surge in demand. Unlike in criminal and civil courts, respondents in immigration court do not have the right to legal counsel paid by the federal government.

A shift in priorities

The new focus on voter rolls for deportation efforts, lawyers say, represents a broader change.

U.S. permanent residents cannot legally vote in federal elections and most local elections. But Saunders said it wasn’t previously a big hurdle for immigrants to remedy the situation if they had unknowingly registered to vote (such as automatic registration through driver license registration) and voted without knowing they weren’t supposed to.

“A lot of these people unknowingly either registered to vote or thought that they could vote. So they’re naive, and I don’t think that should make them deportable,” he said. “In the past, it was kind of overlooked as long as the person had cured whatever the problem was.”

Now, however, there seems to be no discretion, lawyers say. For Harrison, it’s a poor allocation of resources.

A case focusing on a permanent resident who registered to vote, for example, could drag out for about four years, with several hearings during that period and hours of work done by both federal immigration lawyers and attorneys like Harrison. The end result, he added, could be the individual successfully defends themselves and keeps his or her green card — or in other words, the legal standing would stay the same regardless of the output of both the immigrant’s personal resources as well as taxpayers’.

“We’re spending all this money and government resources and enforcement and removal operations and online security resources to put people into proceedings that take all this time that clog the courts, create backlogs, and then years later, the people are still here,” he said. “It’s just not what we should be focusing on, in my opinion.”

Sydnee Chapman is an award-winning reporter whose work has appeared in news outlets across the western U.S. When not reporting, Sydnee enjoys traveling in her camper van, knitting, hiking and climbing.

text:
From La Prensa San Diego / Oct. 22, 2026

The Pentagon has authorized the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to test a military-grade weapon known as a “heat ray” for potential use along the U.S.-Mexico border, prompting concerns from border-community advocates about the expansion of military technology in immigration enforcement.

The weapon, officially known as the Active Denial System and deployed atop an eight-wheels armored vehicle, emits an invisible beam of electromagnetic energy that heats the surface of the skin, causing an intense burning sensation intended to make people move away from the beam.

CNN reported Oct. 21 that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth approved a seven-month loan of the system to DHS for testing and the development of tactics for possible border operations. The authorization does not mean the weapon has been approved for operational deployment.

The Southern Border Communities Coalition (SBCC), a network of organizations advocating for border communities, condemned the decision, calling it another step toward increased militarization of the region.

According to the U.S. military, the beam can reach more than half a mile. Officials have described the resulting sensation as intense but temporary, although advocates have raised concerns about potential injuries and other health effects.

The technology was considered for possible use at the southern border during the first Trump administration and was also discussed as a potential response to protests in 2020. Those proposals did not result in its use in those situations.

“Customs and Border Protection is already infamous for abuse and violence,” said Ricky Garza, SBCC’s border policy counsel. “The last thing they need is more untested dangerous military equipment.”

Pedro Rios, director of the American Friends Service Committee’s U.S.-Mexico Border Program, said the decision risks normalizing the use of painful force against migrants and border residents.

“The United States has an obligation to welcome people with dignity, but instead, it’s choosing to inflict pain with untested military weapons,” Rios said.

Jovanny Sebastian Hernandez, SBCC co-chair and campaign manager for the New Mexico Dream Team, also criticized the authorization, arguing that border security should address the needs of communities on both sides of the border rather than rely on additional military equipment.

“My home is not a war zone,” Hernandez said.

SBCC also cited concerns raised by Physicians for Human Rights about the potential short- and long-term medical effects of weapons designed to cause intense physical discomfort.

The federal government, meanwhile, has defended its broader evaluation of new enforcement technology. U.S. Customs and Border Protection told CNN that it continually evaluates technologies intended to improve operational effectiveness and strengthen its capabilities. The agency’s statement did not address the specific health concerns raised by advocates.

The testing authorization comes amid broader disputes over the expanding military role in border enforcement. Advocates argue that border communities should not become testing grounds for military equipment and that enforcement policies must respect the safety and rights of migrants and residents.

The Pentagon’s authorization permits DHS to test the system and develop possible tactics. Whether the department ultimately seeks to deploy the weapon along the border remains an open question.

Oscar David Hernandez-Gonzalez aka Juan Higera-Medrano was arrested after he allegedly jumped out of a rail car during a Customs and Border Protection inspection on a train at the BNSF railyard in El Paso. Gonzalez-Sanchez was transferred to ICE custody on Oct. 17. He has four prior convictions for illegal re-entry and now faces the same charge for the fifth time. Ruben Salazar-Lopez, an illegal alien from Mexico, was arrested by U.S. Border Patrol agents on Oct. 17, near Eagle Pass. title: Immigrants in ICE custody don't have right to bond, court rules - The Texas Tribune
authors: Uriel J. García, Alexandra Glorioso, Jeremy Schwartz, Misty Harris, Zach Despart, The Texas Tribune, Jess Huff, Eleanor Klibanoff, graphics  Apurva Mahajan, Dang Le
description:
Immigrants who entered the country illegally don’t have a right to seek bond while they’re in custody and going through deportation proceedings, even if they’ve set roots in the U.S., a federal appeals court ruled Friday.
The Trump administration appealed, arguing that federal immigration law says undocumented immigrants should be held until deportation without bond hearings — a policy it put in place in July 2025.
Friday’s ruling is welcome news for the Trump administration, which has prioritized immigration enforcement as part of its mass deportation efforts.
Since January 2025, immigrants have filed more than 89,000 petitions against the Trump administration, seeking their release.
The Trump administration appealed some of the cases to higher courts, leading to conflicting rulings.
text:
Immigrants who entered the country illegally don’t have a right to seek bond while they’re in custody and going through deportation proceedings, even if they’ve set roots in the U.S., a federal appeals court ruled Friday.

In a 10-7 ruling, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans ruled that current immigration laws allow the federal government to hold detained immigrants until they’re deported — regardless of whether they have made a life in the U.S. and lack a criminal history.

Trump-appointed Judge Cory Wilson wrote in the court’s ruling that if undocumented immigrants have not been legally admitted to the U.S., they are only entitled to whatever rights Congress has spelled out in immigration laws. He added that if undocumented immigrants in custody want to be free from detention, “they can do so at any moment by agreeing to leave the country.”

In a concurring opinion, Judge Andrew Oldham agreed.

“Because such aliens remain legally unadmitted, they receive exactly the same due process rights that they would have if they had come through a legal port of entry — which are whatever rights Congress chooses to give them,” Oldham wrote.

Judge Leslie Southwick, a George W. Bush appointee, wrote in his dissent that the ruling has created an “impenetrable wall between the Constitution and these long-term residents.”

Rebecca Cassler, senior litigation attorney at the American Immigration Council, who argued the case before the 5th Circuit, said the court’s ruling is an attack on constitutional due process rights, which have been guaranteed to anyone living in the U.S., regardless of immigration status.

“The right to due process is a fundamental constitutional protection, and it is meant to protect every person in this country. Because of today’s decision, that right is hollow for immigrants in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi,” she said. “But the logic of the 5th Circuit’s decision threatens everyone in this country: When courts degrade the meaning of liberty for some, we all suffer the consequences.”

Mass deportation efforts

The case stems from the arrest of three men in Texas by state troopers between November 2025 and February 2026 during routine traffic stops. All three have lived in the country for at least 14 years, worked during that time and have children who are American citizens. The troopers turned the men over to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who held them in detention without allowing them to see a judge.

Ignacio Sosnava Rodriguez, Miguel Angel Gomez Alvarado and Alejandro Villegas Angel were eventually released from ICE custody after federal judges found that holding them without a chance for a bond hearing violated the men’s due process rights. The Trump administration appealed, arguing that federal immigration law says undocumented immigrants should be held until deportation without bond hearings — a policy it put in place in July 2025.

Friday’s ruling is welcome news for the Trump administration, which has prioritized immigration enforcement as part of its mass deportation efforts.

“Big win in the Fifth Circuit on mandatory detention for illegal aliens, a principle codified in 1996 legislation but ignored by the deep state for decades,” James Percival, a lawyer in the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, said on social media, referring to Clinton administration immigration law that expanded the list of immigrants who can be more easily deported.

“Rejecting due process”

Gracie Willis, an attorney with the National Immigration Project, which is representing the three Texas men, said the general public should be concerned that a federal court believes the government can hold people indefinitely without justification.

“We look at this case as an affront to due process, as the 5th Circuit rejecting due process,” Willis said. “It’s really a shocking extension of this attempt to criminalize immigrants and to hold immigrants in detention without any opportunity for them to be released, thereby creating an environment of fear.”

Willis said her organization is still assessing what legal action to take and has not decided if it plans to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.

She said immigration lawyers are anticipating how district courts are going to react to this ruling. Many district judges have ruled that immigrants being held in detention centers have a right to bond as long as they are not a flight risk or a danger to the community.

Even though Friday’s ruling is limited to the 5th Circuit, which includes Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, the Trump administration has transferred many immigrants from other states to detention centers in Texas.

A policy change by the Trump administration

Under federal immigration laws, the government can quickly deport undocumented immigrants who recently crossed the U.S.-Mexico border without giving them a chance for a bond hearing. But for those who have lived in the U.S. for months or years before being detained, the law gave them the right to challenge their detention.

In July 2025, the Trump administration announced a policy change, saying that anyone who has been arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents — regardless of how long they’ve been in the country — doesn’t have a right to bond.

Earlier this month, the U.S. Supreme Court agreed to hear a separate but similar case that directly challenges the Trump administration’s mandatory detention policy.

According to ProPublica, immigrants filed more habeas corpus petitions — a legal procedure that allows a person detained by the government to challenge their imprisonment — in the first 13 months of the second Trump administration than in the past three administrations combined.

Since January 2025, immigrants have filed more than 89,000 petitions against the Trump administration, seeking their release.

Friday’s ruling doesn’t prohibit other detainees from filing habeas corpus petitions if they entered the country legally.

Politico found that more than 400 federal judges — appointed by presidents of both major political parties — have ruled in favor of immigrants’ right to due process in more than 5,000 cases since the Trump administration’s policy change last year.

In comparison, 41 judges have sided with the administration’s interpretation of the law in 250 cases, according to a Politico analysis of federal government data.

The Trump administration appealed some of the cases to higher courts, leading to conflicting rulings.

text:
LAKEWOOD – Congresswoman Brittany Pettersen (CO-07) and Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi (IL-08) today led an effort demanding answers from the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) following reports the agency has used local police to gain backdoor access to a nationwide license plate surveillance network, allowing the federal government to track private citizens’ movements. In the Members’ letter to Acting Director David Venturella, which was signed by 33 other Democrats, the Members press ICE to disclose whose movements it is tracking, what legal authority it relies on, and what safeguards protect the public from abuse.

“Reports that ICE is using local police as a backdoor to track people’s movements is terrifying and should alarm every single one of us. Especially during the Trump administration, which is looking for every opportunity to track and deport even law-abiding people,” said Congresswoman Pettersen. “I’m demanding answers about who ICE is tracking, how this information is being used, and what is stopping agents from abusing it. ICE does not get a blank check to spy on families and communities.”

“ICE’s use of local police as a backdoor to access Flock’s license plate cameras and secretly track Americans’ movements is an outrageous abuse of power,” saidCongressman Raja Krishnamoorthi. “The Trump administration cannot use local law enforcement to circumvent the Fourth Amendment and evade accountability. We are demanding answers about who ICE has been tracking, how this information has been used, and whether anyone has been detained or arrested as a result of this surveillance.”

A recent investigation uncovered more than 4,000 searches of Flock Safety camera data by state and local law enforcement conducted for federal authorities or with a potential immigration focus. The reporting described how ICE obtained access through local law enforcement despite having no formal contract with Flock governing that access.

Flock’s automatic license plate readers capture vehicle information and locations, allowing law enforcement to search records across camera networks. Access to those records can reveal incredibly personal details about people’s daily routines and whereabouts, raising concerns about privacy and the potential misuse of information collected in communities across the country.

“Such chilling, unrestrained surveillance obtained without judicial authorization, contractual safeguards, or public transparency, represents far more than a procedural lapse—it represents the quiet expansion of a federal surveillance system operating out of sight and beyond any meaningful public oversight,” the Members write in the letter.

The letter requests answers by November 20, 2026, including:

How often ICE has accessed Flock camera data, directly or through state and local partners and for what purposes.

How many people have been detained, arrested, or subjected to other enforcement actions as a result.

What legal authority and internal policies govern ICE’s access to and use of this information.

Whether ICE has reviewed these practices for compliance with federal privacy protections, the Fourth Amendment, and Department of Homeland Security policy.

Whether ICE intends to establish a formal agreement with Flock safety or another license plate reader vendor .

Congresswoman Brittany Pettersen has consistently fought back against the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement overreach and defended due process. In the Colorado legislature, she helped pass legislation ensuring local law enforcement agencies do not serve as an extension of ICE. In Congress, she voted against legislation that would force Washington, D.C. police to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement and condemned ICE operations in schools, churches, and hospitals. This letter builds on her work to protect immigrant communities and demand accountability for federal enforcement practices that threaten people’s rights.

The full text of the letter can be found HERE and below.

Dear Acting Director Venturella:

We write with serious concern regarding reports that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has been accessing data from Flock Safety automatic license‑plate‑reader (ALPR) cameras, an AI‑powered surveillance system, with no formal contract or governing agreement in place, creating serious concerns around data privacy and overreach. According to recent reporting, ICE has used state and local law‑enforcement agencies to conduct more than 4,000 searches of Flock camera data on its behalf, enabling ICE personnel to obtain personally identifiable information without a criminal warrant.

Not only is this protocol potentially illegal, exploiting this information side-door allows ICE personnel to query ALPR cameras deployed across multiple states – in effect granting federal agents access to a nationwide, continuously updated surveillance grid capable of tracking the movements of millions of people in real time. Such chilling, unrestrained surveillance obtained without judicial authorization, contractual safeguards, or public transparency, represents far more than a procedural lapse — it represents the quiet expansion of a federal surveillance system operating out of sight and beyond any meaningful public oversight.This is a serious breach of privacy and a clear departure from federal law and agency policy. The ability of federal agents to access vast quantities of location‑tracking data, without judicial authorization and without public disclosure, constitutes an unprecedented intrusion into the privacy of the general public, and must be explained immediately.

Please provide a response to the following no later than November 20, 2026:

How many times has an ICE agent obtained data from Flock Cameras, whether directly or through state or local law‑enforcement partners?

For what purpose is ICE accessing and obtaining data from Flock Cameras?

Have any individuals been detained, arrested, or otherwise subjected to enforcement actions as a result of information obtained from Flock Cameras? If yes, please provide that number.

What authority or legal statute is ICE purporting to operate under when accessing Flock Camera data? Please provide that authority or legal statute.

Does ICE maintain any internal policy governing the use of ALPR data obtained through third‑party or indirect means? If so, please provide that policy.

Has ICE conducted any legal review regarding whether accessing ALPR data through state or local partners complies with federal privacy protections, the Fourth Amendment, or DHS policy? If so, please provide that review. If not, please indicate whether the agency plans to do so.

Does ICE intend to formalize a contract or memorandum of understanding with Flock Safety or any other ALPR vendor?

We look forward to your prompt response.

text:
The full Fifth Circuit upheld the Trump administration’s policy of mandatory detention for noncitizens, saying in a split decision Friday that constitutional due process protections didn’t entitle three migrant men to bond hearings in immigration court.

While the petitioners have Fifth Amendment rights, they haven’t been admitted to the US and so aren’t entitled to procedures beyond what’s spelled out in immigration statutes, wrote Trump-appointed Judge Cory Wilson in an opinion joined by eight of his colleagues. A ninth, Judge Priscilla Richman, concurred with the result of the majority opinion.

Echoing a point frequently made by Trump administration officials, Wilson wrote that noncitizens can be released from detention “at any moment by agreeing to leave the country.”

Furthermore, the length of their stay in immigration detention “presented no constitutional issues” warranting their release, Wilson wrote.

Seven judges, all appointed by Democrats or Republican President George W. Bush, dissented, with Judge Leslie Southwick saying the majority built “an impenetrable wall between the Constitution and these long-term residents.”

The decision marks another significant Fifth Circuit win for the Trump administration, which has used the detention policy as a legal cornerstone of its mass-deportation efforts. Thousands of immigrants are detained in Fifth Circuit states, particularly Texas and Louisiana, and the court is an outlier among appellate circuits in upholding the policy.

Only one other circuit has blessed the policy, while nine have ruled against it.

The Supreme Court has agreed to consider whether Trump’s mandatory detention scheme correctly interprets the statute, a separate legal question than the Fifth Circuit considered in Friday’s decision.

Attorneys for the noncitizen petitioners castigated the decision in a statement Friday.

“At a time when conditions in immigration detention are increasingly dangerous, this ruling opens the door to more people being locked up for no reason, with devastating consequences for them, their loved ones, and their community,” said Ellie Norton of the National Immigration Project.

The Fifth Circuit previously found there’s no statutory right to a bond hearing in such cases. Congress has significant power over immigration issues and is free to make rules for noncitizens that wouldn’t be acceptable for citizens, Wilson wrote.

“Controlling illegal immigration is, no doubt, an important and controversial issue of public policy. But the Constitution entrusts broad authority to delineate immigration policy, and to design proceedings to effectuate those policy choices, to Congress — not courts,” Wilson said. “Neither we nor the district courts are free to ignore that bedrock principle and rewrite the immigration policy Congress has enacted.”

Last year, in a departure from nearly three decades of practice, the Trump administration began to classify noncitizens who have long lived within US borders as “seeking admission,” the same as noncitizens who’d just entered the country — a legal interpretation that denied them bond hearings.

That helped spark a flood of immigrant habeas corpus petitions in which noncitizens argued they were being illegally detained.

In a concurrence, Judge James Ho wrote that courts, unlike Congress, shouldn’t have a say over immigration policies.

“These habeas petitions, far from affirming American liberty, are profoundly un-American — because they send the message that the only people who are above the law in our country are the ones who violated our laws to get in,” said Ho, a Trump appointee.

Judge Andrew Oldham, another Trump appointee, wrote a lengthy response to Judge Dana Douglas’ assertion that the majority opinion relies on “sham history.”

The writ of habeas corpus doesn’t define “the strike zone,” which is left up to “Congress, and Congress alone,” he said. “Congress can expand it or contract it, as it has over time. But what Congress says goes, and the Constitution does nothing to change what counts as a ball or a strike.”

In dissent, Southwick said that while detention can be a valid part of deportation proceedings, there’s no support for the idea that a noncitizen can be locked up for as long as they’re pending, “however delayed,” with no option for possible release. Southwick was joined by Douglas and Judges Carl Stewart, James Graves Jr., Stephen Higginson, Irma Carillo Ramirez.

Under longstanding Supreme Court precedent, Southwick wrote, a noncitizen’s “presence and residence” in the country — not their technical “admission” to it — entitles them to due process.

Judge Catharina Haynes said she agreed with Southwick’s “basic points” but stressed that his logic should apply only to residents like the petitioners, who’ve been in the country for more than a decade, have no criminal history, and have US citizen relatives.

Douglas also wrote a separate dissent, joined by Stewart, Graves, Higginson, and Ramirez. The majority opinion “detonates the core of the Due Process Clause,” she wrote.

“A country where a roaming police force must seek out millions of noncitizens for mandatory detention without meaningful process or recourse to even a rudimentary hearing is a less decent place for people like Petitioners who have led law-abiding lives, committed no crimes, and raised United States citizens,” she wrote.

Higginson wrote separately, joined by five fellow dissenters, to say that the court was wrong in the first place when it upheld the Trump detention policy on statutory grounds. The en banc court should have revisited the statutory question and interpreted the law in a way that doesn’t raise such significant constitutional concerns, he said.

Ho’s concurrence in particular “implies that any judicial inquiry into the constitutionality of executive immigration detention impermissibly injures Congress,” Higginson wrote. “That proposition cannot be true.”

The due process question came to the court after district court judges began granting noncitizen habeas claims even after the Fifth Circuit panel upheld the Trump policy on statutory grounds.

When the government challenged those grants at the Fifth Circuit, a panel agreed that due process required bond hearings. But the en banc court threw out that decision and agreed to hear the due process arguments as a full court.

Noncitizen petitioners are also represented by American Immigration Council and Garza & Narvaez PLLC.

text:
A federal appeals court has revived a lawsuit filed by FaithWorks and more than two dozen other religious organizations to prevent immigration enforcement actions in houses of worship and other sensitive locations.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia released a divided opinion Oct. 20 concluding plaintiffs offered sufficient proof their congregations and ministries faced imminent threats from immigration agents and therefore could move ahead with Mennonite Church USA, et al. v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

The action stems from the Trump administration’s January 2025 decision to roll back a decades-old sensitive locations policy directing immigration agents as much as possible from operating on the properties of schools, places of worship and hospitals. The revised policy removes those limits and simply asks agents to “use their discretion along with a healthy dose of common sense” when operating at or near sensitive locations like churches.

The lawsuit contends the new approach violates the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, the First Amendment’s guarantee of freedom of religion and the Administrative Procedures Act which governs the federal government’s rule-making processes.

In April, U.S. District Judge Dabney Friedrich denied the preliminary injunction sought by the faith-based groups, concluding they lacked standing to bring the lawsuit and the negative consequences anticipated from the updated policy had occurred in insufficient numbers.

But judges Florence Pan and Robert Wilkins ruled the plaintiffs have standing to proceed by representing “millions of worshippers, including Baptists, Brethren, Catholics, Conservative Jews, Episcopalians, Evangelicals, Mennonites, Quakers, Pentecostals, Presbyterians, Reconstructionist Jews, Reform Jews, Unitarian Universalists, United Methodists, and Zion Methodists.”

In addition to concerns about disruptions and fears caused by immigration raids, the litigants also demonstrated harms to ministries nationwide, the majority wrote. “In their complaint, every plaintiff alleges that at least one of its member congregations provides support to undocumented immigrants — some of whom are members of the congregations, and others of whom benefit from their charitable work.”

The 2-1 ruling also took into account incidents of federal agents spying on congregations and other controversial enforcement actions that have occurred since the lawsuit was filed in February.

“Given the ‘credible threat’ of impending enforcement activity at or near plaintiffs’ members’ premises, plaintiffs ‘should not be required to await and undergo (further enforcement) as the sole means of seeking relief,’” the majority wrote, citing relevant case law.

“Plaintiffs’ members likely face imminent harm from increased enforcement at their houses of worship; that harm is traceable to the new enforcement policy; and the relief requested will likely redress their injury, at least in part.”

But in her dissent, Judge Neomi Rao argued that even restoring the policy to its previous form would not redress plaintiffs’ alleged harms: “The memo simply discouraged immigration enforcement in protected areas but imposed no actual restriction on enforcement authority or discretion. Enforcement priorities and policies are the exclusive purview of the executive branch, and supervising these choices is beyond the judicial province.”

The appellate decision reversed Friedrich’s ruling and remands the case back to the district court where plaintiffs can again seek a temporary restraining order while the litigation continues.

Stephen Reeves, executive director of FaithWorks (formerly Fellowship Southwest), expressed gratitude for the ruling and said the ministry will continue to defend the right for people to serve their neighbors without fear from Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“We hope this decision will result in an injunction so that our immigrant neighbors will know their faith community is free from the threat of ICE enforcement and that our partner churches can continue exercising their faith by serving neighbors regardless of immigration status,” he said. “While this injunction would not prevent enforcement in most places, it would guarantee that houses of worship are truly sanctuaries. It’s the very least we can offer them: a refuge in times of trouble.”

Nothing less than freedom of religion is at stake in the case, said Bishop Thomas Bickerton, leader of the New York and New England conferences of the United Methodist Church.

“It’s inherent in our Wesleyan DNA to fight for justice for those that are marginalized and those that are oppressed, and this is an accentuated case,” he said.

Bickerton also cited the long history of New York’s Methodist congregations welcoming immigrants into membership. “They are our people, and we’re standing with them at all costs.”

The Unitarian Universalist Association, also a plaintiff, said faith groups have to be diligence given the Trump administration’s disregard for individual rights and sacred spaces.

“As the threats to our sanctuaries — including documented instances of surveillance of UU congregations — and religious practices intensify, we will continue our practice of faithful dissent against such oppression, and we look forward to being a part of the next step of the legal process.”

The Mennonite Church USA cautioned members that the ruling is not victory in the lawsuit itself, but an important moment in the struggle for the right to serve those targeted by the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign.

“We’re asking the government to not interfere with our right to practice our faith freely, which is protected by the Constitution,” said Michael Danner, associate executive director for church vitality in Mennonite Church USA and executive director for the Mennonite Education Agency. The lawsuits asks the federal government “to enforce laws in ways that don’t stop us from following Jesus’ command to love our neighbors.”

Mennonite Church v. DHS is one of multiple lawsuits filed against the administration’s focus on houses of worship for immigration enforcement raids.

In August, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit upheld a lower court’s injunction blocking DHS operations on the sites of Cooperative Baptist Fellowship and other plaintiffs’ properties in Philadelphia Yearly Meeting of the Religious Society of Friends v. DHS. A district court in Massachusetts issued a preliminary injunction in February for American Baptist Churches USA, the Alliance of Baptists and other faith groups in New England Synod, Evangelical Lutheran Church in America v. DHS.

However, the decisions, which apply only to the groups that filed the lawsuits, have not discouraged DHS and ICE from conducting immigration operations near and on plaintiffs’ church properties. In August, University Baptist Church in Minneapolis learned that ICE agents had entered its facilities at least four times, including in May, to secretly record conversations between worshipers. The congregation is affiliated with the Alliance and ABCUSA, both plaintiffs in New England Synod.

The intrusions possibly violated the restraining order in that case and a contempt-of-court motion was filed in response to complaints of “egregious violations of the preliminary injunction, including deploying an undercover ICE agent into one of plaintiffs’ protected churches to surveil and record people inside.”

The spying at UBC and other churches was part of DHS efforts to crack down on activists and demonstrators opposed to ICE operations in Minnesota.
