text:
A US judge has ordered President Donald Trump to answer questions under oath in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by 11 December.

Trump is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.

Charles Tobin, a lawyer representing the BBC, said in court that "we still haven't been able to depose the plaintiff" with two months left in the discovery period, during which both sides are legally required to exchange information with each other on their case.

Trump cancelled a previous deposition on 16 October, citing "matters of national importance" while he was campaigning in Georgia.

In US law, a deposition is an out-of-court statement made under oath in response to questions, which is recorded for use in later proceedings.

The judge in the case, US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett, said that Trump must sit for the deposition by 11 December, unless the discovery period is extended.

Last week, attorneys asked that Lett compel Trump to face deposition after the last scheduled meeting did not take place.

On that day, Trump attended a midterms campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia and a fundraiser at his property in Mar-a-Lago in Florida.

In a separate filing on Wednesday, Trump's lawyers said that the president could appear for the interview between 11 and 22 January next year, and claimed that the BBC was "wrong to claim that President Trump is avoiding his deposition in this action."

Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.

The BBC apologised for the error and said that the broadcast gave "the mistaken impression that President Trump made a direct call for violent action".

The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US.

In July, Trump's lawyers conceded that they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service - as they originally claimed - or on the BBC's website, BBC select or through US broadcasters.

Trump ultimately agreed to drop the lawsuit against BBC Studios, its commercial arm, after the BBC argued that it had "no role in creating or producing the documentary".

Typically, depositions take place in a lawyer's office - rather than a courtroom - without a judge physically present.

Depositions, however, carry legal weight and take place under oath. They are recorded verbatim by a court reporter, and the transcripts can later be used as evidence during trials.

name: Policy
title: The midterm effect: What the 2026 election could mean for public policy | Brookings
authors: Ted Piccone, Diana Paz García, Bruce Jones, Valerie Wirtschafter, Emily Markovich Morris, William A. Galston, Ashley Jochim, Lesley Lavery
description:
Given the parties’ divergent views on health care, major changes are unlikely while President Trump remains in office.
Bipartisan legislation remains possible, as it was on housing this year, even though President Trump withheld his signature.
In fact, it was through executive orders that President Trump expanded the reach of ICE on the first day of his second term.
In a few states, a swing to unified Democratic control could lead to much stronger climate policies along with regulations against fossil fuels.
What began as neighborhood concerns about local environmental and utility issues grew into a fight over AI power.
text:
On Nov. 3, voters will cast ballots that decide the balance of power in Congress and set the stage for what legislation, investigations, and rulemaking could be possible for years to come.

If the blue wave that polls predict materializes, efforts to enact and change the policy agenda will play out against a backdrop of government divided along political fault lines—with the 2028 presidential contest looming.

In this collection of essays, Brookings experts examine the implications of the upcoming election on the most significant issues facing the nation.

Loren Adler and Matthew Fiedler

Democrats’ health care agenda may matter even if it stalls

The most consequential health care legislation from the next Congress may be bills that have almost no chance of becoming law.

If Democrats capture one or both chambers, health care will likely be high on their agenda. Given the parties’ divergent views on health care, major changes are unlikely while President Trump remains in office. Yet recent history shows that Democratic efforts could still shape future legislation.

House Democrats passed bills authorizing Medicare drug price negotiation in 2019 and expanding Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplace subsidies in 2020, despite little prospect of enactment under President Trump. Versions of both policies became law during the Biden administration. Similarly, House Republicans passed a debt ceiling bill that included Medicaid work requirements in 2023, despite President Biden’s opposition. Similar requirements became law under unified Republican control in 2025.

A Democratic agenda would likely start with reversing cuts to Medicaid and the Marketplaces enacted in 2025 and restoring enhanced Marketplace premium subsidies. But it might also include other efforts to expand or improve insurance coverage, and the appropriate scope of these efforts may spur intense intraparty debate.

Democrats may also explore cost-cutting measures, both as a way of directly lowering costs for consumers and of generating federal savings to help finance coverage improvements. This could include steps to lower hospital or drug prices or to reduce payments to Medicare Advantage plans.

Even if nothing becomes law, effort spent developing and socializing proposals might leave Democrats better positioned to enact reforms when political conditions change.

Scott R. Anderson

The challenges of reining in the Iran war, and prospects for broader reform

If Democrats take control of one or both chambers of the 120th Congress, they are likely to feel immense pressure to rein in the Iran war, among other controversial aspects of the Trump administration’s foreign policy. But this will be easier said than done. Trump’s continued pursuit of the war is premised on broad claims of inherent constitutional authority. Even a new majority is unlikely to have the two-thirds support necessary to override a presidential veto in order to install new legislative restrictions. Nor is cutting off funding always a politically viable alternative.

For this reason, if controlled at least in part by Democrats, the 120th Congress is likely to see more of the innovative methods the current minority has used to pressure the Trump administration into winding down the Iran war, including by withholding funding, rehabilitating dormant expedited procedures, enacting nonlegislative measures opposed to administration policies, and even exploring new litigation options. By combining these measures with newly available oversight tools and the sorts of small-bore legislative solutions (including funding limitations) that can be more readily incorporated into annual “must-pass” defense and appropriations legislation—making them difficult for the president to veto—the new majority will be able to put substantial new pressure on the Trump administration. But harder and more forward-looking limits on presidential authority will likely have to wait at least until a change in the presidency in 2029.

At that point, if Democrats secure control of both Congress and the White House—and particularly if restraint-oriented Republicans in Congress are willing to collaborate—there could be a window for foreign relations law reform not seen since the post-Vietnam era. The question will then be whether Democrats will be willing to use their undoubtedly limited time in power to engage in reforms instead of advancing their substantive policy agenda. In 2021, Democratic leaders chose to focus on the latter. But the experiences of the past few years may have changed the calculus the next time around.

Bill Baer

Democrats are poised to investigate antitrust enforcement

If the Democrats win control of one or both chambers of Congress, expect considerable focus on antitrust. Why? First, there are serious allegations that the Trump White House worked with favored lobbyists to dictate nonmerits-based resolution of investigations and litigation over the vigorous objections of both political and career staff at the Antitrust Division of the Department of Justice (DOJ). Roger Alford, a Trump appointee who served as the division’s second-ranking official until he was fired in July 2025, laid out those allegations before the House Judiciary Subcommittee on the Administrative State, Regulatory Reform, and Antitrust. A full Democrat-chaired committee will likely want to uncover the backstories behind actions at both the DOJ and Federal Trade Commission, where the courts have questioned investigations into disfavored news organizations like Media Matters.

In addition, hearings on antitrust legislation will likely be in the offing. There is growing sentiment that antitrust enforcement against tech platforms takes too long and provides little disincentive for dominant firms to stop exploiting their gatekeeper status. That worry carries over into agentic AI. While some AI firms are seeking antitrust immunity to coordinate efforts to address rogue behavior—something they likely can do now under current antitrust law—Democrats and at least some Republicans will probably want to ensure our antitrust laws are updated to prevent a handful of AI firms from dominating this powerful new technology and foreclosing meaningful rivalry. And, if the Democrats control both the Senate and the House, there could even be AI legislation sent to Trump to face an inevitable veto.

Sarah A. Binder

Numerous barriers will limit what the next Congress can do

With divided party government likely, a lame duck president evincing little interest in Congress, and the 2028 presidential election already underway, prospects for major legislative change in the new 120th Congress seem slim.

Plenty of issues will be ripe in the new Congress. First in line? Any of the measures that Congress and the president fail to resolve in the upcoming lame duck session. Few expect much of the lame duck, especially if Democrats’ electoral dividends lead them to withhold support until they take the reins of one or both chambers next year. Still, other lawmakers suggest that Democrats might prefer to clear some decks before the new Congress convenes

What’s at stake for next year if not finished by year-end? Full-year funding for nearly every government agency, bipartisan permitting reform and multiyear farm bills, reauthorizing Pentagon programs (plus Trump’s demand for large increases in defense funding), and increasing the government’s borrowing limit.

Divided governments do not always stalemate. Crisis can compel politicians to act, as they did in spades in response to the 2020 global pandemic. That Congress also rewrote NAFTA and enacted several measures targeting China.

But the 120th Congress will face several barriers.

First, lawmakers will need supermajorities to overcome potential Senate filibusters. True, it’s technically possible to attempt a filibuster-proof “reconciliation” bill (like the One Big Beautiful Bill Act), but it’s been nearly two decades since Congress pursued one during divided government. Intense partisan team play and onerous federal debt will complicate negotiations. Second, whether in control of one or both chambers, Democrats will likely devote the lion’s share of their attention to investigating the conduct of the Trump administration. With little prospect of cooperation by the administration, “messaging” oversight will be the name of the game.

Finally, the 2028 race for the White House will loom large. Will legislators prefer policy accomplishments to herald on the campaign trail in 2028? Or will each party prefer to run on stalemate, blaming the other party for failure to address voters’ concerns. Either way, the road ahead will be challenging for Congress, let alone for voters demanding change.

William A. Galston

A Democratic Congress could curb executive power

During his second term, President Trump has expanded the scope of executive power, often with the support of the Supreme Court and even when some members of the majority have expressed doubts about his approach. Other than the One Big Beautiful Bill, Congress has enacted little significant legislation, and the president has operated mostly through executive fiat.

Would Democratic victories in the forthcoming midterm elections alter this pattern? Democrats are already debating whether they should use expanded executive power for their own purposes if they regain the presidency in 2029 or instead push for a rebalancing that restores the constitutional role of Congress as a coequal branch of government.

In the short term, it is very likely that when Democrats take control of the House, they will use their powers of oversight and investigation to hold the president accountable for his policies. Administration officials will be required to testify, and some will be cited for contempt if they refuse. In addition, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), the Democratic leader who will almost certainly become speaker if Democrats regain the majority, plans to bring to the floor a series of bills that will spell out his party’s policy priorities and underscore the differences between the parties. If Democrats win a majority in the Senate, President Trump may have a hard time getting Cabinet nominees confirmed, confirmation of lower-court judges would slow, and it would be nearly impossible to replace a retiring Supreme Court justice from the conservative bloc with a like-minded appointee.

But even more important, a Democratic-controlled Congress could challenge the president’s actions at every turn, slowing and perhaps halting the steady expansion of executive power since the beginning of President Trump’s second term and making it more difficult for a subsequent president of either party to follow in Trump’s footsteps.

Ryan Hass

Trump may favor trade battles over military confrontation

On the foreign policy front, President Donald Trump’s response to a turnover in congressional power will differ between trade and national security. On trade, I expect he will show unrelenting activism, testing the outer limits of his authority as he looks for leverage to bend other countries to his will. He will probably not shy away from congressional criticism or legal battles over his trade activism, viewing them as the price of expanding his presidential power. He also will likely view these battles as a way to shift the narrative away from congressional investigations into his actions, those of his family, and his administration. He may see value in casting himself as fighting for American workers and against entrenched interests.

On national security, Trump will likely draw down U.S. troop numbers in the Middle East and Europe, citing a reduced tempo of military operations against Iran and the results of a posture review in Europe as rationales for his decisions. Bringing troops home stands to be broadly popular with the American public, even as such decisions will likely invite scrutiny from the national security establishment. Trump is poised to shield himself against accusations of retreat and isolationism by exercising toothy power projection in Latin America under the guise of stopping narcotics trafficking and stemming immigrant flows. He will likely throw punches in directions where he does not fear counterpunches while avoiding direct confrontation with other major powers, notably China and Russia, in his final two years in office.

Elaine Kamarck

Weighing the pursuit of presidential or cabinet officer impeachment

As the norm-breaking first half of the second Trump administration unfolded, several Democratic members of Congress introduced legislation calling for the president’s impeachment. Trump himself raised the specter of impeachment, saying at a Republican retreat, “If we don’t win the midterms … they’ll find a reason to impeach me. I’ll get impeached.”

Yet, as the midterm elections approach and Democratic prospects for significant electoral gains improve, impeachment remains largely absent from the party leadership’s public agenda. The biggest reason is that while impeachment requires only a majority vote, conviction requires a two-thirds vote in the Senate. Even with control of the Senate in sight, Democrats are extremely unlikely to win the two-thirds needed to convict. In addition, Trump’s declining public approval may give Democrats another reason to avoid impeachment. With the 2028 presidential election in mind, Democrats may calculate that keeping an unpopular Trump in office would be more advantageous than elevating a younger JD Vance to the presidency, which would give him an opportunity to establish his own political identity and distance himself from the administration’s record.

But that need not be the end of impeachment. Cabinet secretaries can be impeached in the same way that presidents can. Six articles of impeachment have already been filed against Defense Secretary Hegseth and one against Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. In addition, Hegseth could face legal scrutiny for U.S. military strikes against alleged drug traffickers in Latin American waters, which critics argue may constitute unlawful extrajudicial killings. He is also politically vulnerable for the ongoing Iran war. Kennedy has undertaken sweeping changes that have weakened America’s public health infrastructure, and the results are apparent with the worst outbreak of measles in decades.

Odds are that if impeachment of a Cabinet officer proceeds to a trial in the Senate and picks up even a small amount of Republican support, the Cabinet officer will be forced to resign. For those who want to unseat Trump, this scenario would weaken his ability to implement what many think are impeachable policies without actually impeaching him. But perhaps most importantly, the impeachment of Cabinet officers would be a warning to Democratic and Republican presidential candidates that there is another tool that can be used to hold presidents accountable.

Aaron Klein and Anisha Singhal

Financial regulation could supersede presidential action in new Congress

In financial regulation, personnel is policy. The midterms leave Democrats facing two problems. The first is the Supreme Court, which stripped most financial regulators of their political independence, so these agencies now report to the White House. The second is that Donald Trump, unlike Joe Biden, quickly put his people in place, meaning a Democratic Senate has limited leverage on personnel unless someone leaves. Expect President Trump’s team to continue promoting crypto and rolling back bank regulation with little Congress can do to stop it. Going forward, Democrats face a choice: They can defend institutions like the Federal Reserve and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) even as their leaders take policy positions at odds with Democratic priorities, or they can acknowledge the court’s restructuring of government has made financial regulation an express policy lever of the White House.

Progressive Democratic chairs could force Republicans to vote on populist ideas President Trump has endorsed, such as capping credit card interest at 10%. This would put Republicans on record either against the president or against their own deregulatory philosophies. Bipartisan legislation remains possible, as it was on housing this year, even though President Trump withheld his signature. Democrats can investigate conflicts of interest around Trump’s personal crypto profits. Investigations tend to increase partisanship. Future deals will depend on whether President Trump views his legacy as being burnished by bipartisan laws or enhanced by unilateral executive action coupled with growing vitriol toward Congress.

Michael O'Hanlon

Defense budgets, not war powers, are where Democrats can act

If the Democrats control one or both houses of Congress starting in January 2027, I expect some significant changes in national security policymaking, perhaps most notably on the defense budget and related matters.

But first, some areas where I doubt change would be significant: war powers, military reorganization, and decisions on the use of force. In each of these areas, presidents, including Trump, have generally decided that they can avert, outflank, or run over Congress. Even in the case of a modest Democratic advantage, President Trump could likely count on enough Republican support to sustain his vetoes on key issues. For example, if Congress tried to reform or rewrite the 1973 War Powers Resolution, Trump could veto such a bill—and I doubt the next Congress would do what the Senate and House did back in 1973 when they overrode President Nixon’s veto with a two-thirds majority in each chamber.

By contrast, on the core matter of defense budgeting, I expect change if the Democrats gain control (of either one or both houses). President Trump’s efforts to gain $350 billion in “mandatory” funding for the fiscal year 2027 budget, already delayed by the current Congress, would stand virtually no chance, as Congress would insist on the normal budget process and oversight (with annual “discretionary” funding that it helped manage). The Golden Dome missile defense system and Golden Battleship would get no big chunks of financial support absent detailed plans and substantial debate. Trump would probably not be able to tell the Navy how to reposition its aircraft carrier control towers and how to change the technology for its catapults. That is because, knowing of Trump’s personal and even idiosyncratic interests in these matters, Congress could insist as a condition for funding future ships that best technological and scientific practices govern how the ships are designed and built. These demands could be written into defense authorization and appropriations bills, making them binding.

This may not seem like a big deal, but normalcy, and checks and balances, need to start somewhere!

Gabriel R. Sanchez

A blue wave election is not likely to create a major shift in ICE activities

As indicators of a potential blue wave begin to take shape across the political landscape, there is growing optimism that Democratic control of the House will lead to notable shifts in policy outcomes across several domestic policy domains, including immigration. Unfortunately, there might not be much change in one of the more controversial and high-profile aspects of the Trump administration’s priorities: the enforcement of deportation policy through ICE. The executive branch has a lot of power independent of Congress to enforce immigration. In fact, it was through executive orders that President Trump expanded the reach of ICE on the first day of his second term. Even if Democrats win the House, they will not be able to do much to overcome the executive power to continue ICE operations.

The main power for Congress in this area is their oversight of the federal budget, which would ordinarily allow the House to curtail operations by cutting off funds. However, Congress has used the reconciliation process in both 2025 and 2026 to appropriate nearly $240 billion for immigration purposes. This is more than enough funds to allow the Trump administration to continue their operations without much resistance from the legislative branch. One of the few prospects for Democrats eager to show voters that they are doing all they can to reform deportation policy would be clawing back unspent funds or restricting how those funds could be leveraged. Whether the new Congress will have the votes to make this happen will depend largely on how big the forecasted blue wave is in November. This is not good news for the immigrant community and the many mixed-status families living through a constant state of fear that they or their loved ones may be deported. They may have to wait until after the 2028 election to see any major changes in immigration policy.

Nicol Turner Lee

A new Congress should address the impacts of redistricting and racial gerrymandering

The GOP’s efforts to redistrict ahead of the 2026 midterm elections will further disenfranchise Black voters, particularly in the wake of the Supreme Court’s April Louisiana v. Callais decision that delivered another blow to the already weakened Voting Rights Act (VRA). In addition to the ongoing efforts by the Trump administration to impose more stringent voter identification requirements, redistricting, which mirrors the historical process and goals of racial gerrymandering, is disproportionately impacting majority-Black and plurality-Black districts that leaned heavily Democrat in prior elections. Newly redrawn maps are taking away incumbent seats held by Black legislators, while establishing new Republican seats and thus diminishing Black political power. If Democrats can shift control in the midterms, one of their first priorities should be to enact legislation that limits, bans, or institutes objective oversight of the process.

Six states—Texas, Florida, Louisiana, Alabama, Tennessee, and North Carolina—have already split up majority- and plurality-Black districts. Nine additional states have initiated mid-decade restricting efforts. This has forced some incumbent Black legislators to run in majority-white, heavily Republican districts. Leading up to the midterms, it will be critical to thwart these increasing acts of voter suppression through more robust voter education, stronger oversight of AI’s role in enabling mis- and disinformation, and an increased number of poll watchers on Election Day, among other protections.

However, efforts to dilute the Black vote could also backfire for the GOP as Democrat and Republican voters share similar concerns regarding the economy and cost of living. Additionally, a transfer of control to Democrats could revive debates over electoral reform. Congress could pass anti-gerrymandering legislation to avoid future partisan takeovers or require independent, bipartisan commissions as proposed in the Redistricting Reform Act of 2025. Efforts could even be bipartisan as some Republicans have called for outright bans on mid-decade changes to electoral maps. Several states have also instituted their own provisions to stop gerrymandering, and installed state-level, independent commissions that are separate from legislatures to make the process less vulnerable to partisanship. Although not currently active, Michigan has an independent citizens’ redistricting commission to review congressional and state maps.

Congressional and state oversight alone will not fully address the damage done to the Voting Rights Act, which has been pillaged and weakened by a series of Supreme Court decisions that have enabled loopholes for misinterpretation and misuse. The new Congress should make time to address these vulnerabilities in the VRA to eliminate the growing partisan influence that keeps trying to alter who gets to vote, where, and for whom, going forward.

Jon Valant

A Democratic Congress would have limited effects on K-12 education

Even if Democrats take the House and Senate, I expect the immediate effects on K-12 education to be modest. There are a few reasons for that. First, the federal government isn’t the main stage for education policymaking; state and local governments matter more. Second, Democrats almost certainly won’t win large enough majorities to override a presidential veto, which limits what they can change from Washington. Third, it’s not all that clear what Democrats want. The party has seemed directionless on K-12 education for some time, and even the DSA platform says little about it.

Still, there would be some impacts. Congressional Democrats would throw sand in the gears of GOP policymaking. That wouldn’t necessarily stop the president’s executive actions, but it’d likely prevent another budget reconciliation package with K-12 policies that Democrats dislike. Democrats also could more forcefully resist the administration’s efforts to dismantle the Department of Education (ED)—with oversight hearings and some concrete actions. For example, they could include language in a funding bill to prohibit the interagency agreements being used to offload ED’s responsibilities to other agencies.

Perhaps the most interesting move would be Democrats passing a bill to signal their future K-12 plans should they retake the White House. One notable development is Rep. Suzanne Bonamici declaring for the race to be the top Democrat on the House Education and Workforce Committee—weeks after introducing a bill with a sprawling set of K-12 proposals. Perhaps that bill is foreshadowing Democrats’ education policy agenda for 2028.

David G. Victor

Midterms may reshape energy policy despite little talk of it

Looking at physical reality, you’d think that 2026 would be a banner year for political attention to climate change and energy. Extreme weather, wildfires, and other perils that voters often associate with climate change are constantly in the news. Two wars entangling supplies from major oil and gas producers have sent energy prices soaring. Electricity bills are rising nearly everywhere.

Yet almost none of the midterm races will turn on energy or climate. Climate change is strikingly absent. Even Democrats inclined to support climate policy are wary of becoming too visible on a topic that voters generally don’t prioritize—despite the fact that many voters want them to say more. Despite energy being a key driver of inflation that worries voters, energy itself mostly isn’t a top campaign issue. Of the eight top issues that the Pew Center tracks for political attention, voters put energy nearly last.

Although climate and energy aren’t directly driving the upcoming elections, electoral sweeps by Democrats could have huge implications for policy. In a few states, a swing to unified Democratic control could lead to much stronger climate policies along with regulations against fossil fuels. Democrats leading one or both chambers on Capitol Hill will likely lead to investigations, retaliations, and chaos in Washington, D.C.—hardly the stuff of the stable policy signals needed on energy and climate. That looming gridlock may put a spotlight on the brief lame duck period when more bipartisan legislation might get through Congress and even be signed by the president—for energy mavens, top of that list is a new bill that would help streamline permitting and make it easier to build. With the cost of oil and refined products, such as diesel fuel, you might think that Democrats would pivot toward policies that emphasize all forms of energy, including more oil. But there is little reliable support for oil and gas expansion in the Democratic base; more likely will be investigations about the Trump administration’s diesel fuel deal with Russia and a lot more emphasis on electric vehicles, biofuels, and efficiency—all policies that are unlikely to get consent from the White House, as needed for new legislation.

One of the hottest issues this election cycle is data centers, thanks to a litany of fears that include voter worries that data center power needs will jack up prices for everyone else. Unlike practically everything else in American politics, however, data centers don’t yet have ideological fault lines. Democrats and Republicans alike are scrambling to look decisive on the matter—mainly by supporting bans. No matter who wins federal and local elections, politicians know who they should abhor. Look for more symbolic political pressure on data centers. Beyond symbolism, with D.C. locked in political gridlock, the bulk of legislative efforts may, mostly, offer a sandbox for elaborating concepts that eventually could be adopted by future governments when officeholders shuffle again after the 2028 elections.

Darrell M. West

Congress should act on AI safety before states fill the gap

One of the big challenges facing policymakers after the midterms will be addressing public concerns about AI. Polls show large majorities expressing worries about AI safety and security. With a number of news stories detailing AI agents going rogue and engaging in unauthorized or prohibited activities, there is a need for members of Congress to address these problems.

There are steps legislators can take. First is mandatory reporting of rogue actions by AI agents from large tech firms. Their tools reach millions of people and therefore are capable of harming a substantial number of individuals. Mandatory reporting would improve transparency about the scope of the problem and the types of intrusions that are most problematic.

In addition, legislators can improve legal liability for AI agents that inflict harm on consumers, businesses, or government agencies. Right now, accountability for unauthorized behavior is murky, and it’s unclear to what extent existing laws on consumer protection or business practices apply to digital tools. Clarifying liability rules would improve accountability and give tech companies clear incentives to make sure large language models are not engaging in harmful behavior.

If Congress does not move, state legislatures will act. Several states have already passed AI safety bills, and that trend will likely accelerate in the coming months. A patchwork of state rules poses an enormous challenge for tech companies, which would have a difficult time developing different models for California or New York versus Texas or Florida. It makes sense for representatives and senators to enact meaningful safeguards before conflicting policy rules proliferate at the state level.

Russell Wheeler

Senate control will decide Trump’s final judicial legacy

Among presidents’ major accomplishments are significant changes in the federal judiciary’s composition. President Trump’s 231 first-term lower court judicial appointments were fewer than President Carter’s and, by a slim margin, President Biden’s.

If Republicans retain the Senate, Trump, with 308 projected appointments so far (assuming post-election confirmation of pending and announced nominees) may get the roughly 70 appointments he needs to match Presidents Reagan and President Clinton’s eight-year totals. The 22 current and announced vacancies without nominations are—at the moment—mainly in Democratic-senator states, but home-state senators’ “blue-slip” veto over district court nominees may not survive a change in Judiciary Committee leadership. And it’s anyone’s guess how many of the 55 Republican-appointed district judges and 23 circuit judges who will be eligible to retire on salary by late 2028 will do so; judges during Trump’s second term have been more reluctant than under recent predecessors to create vacancies.

A Democratic Senate, however, may be in payback mode. In their final two years, the four two-term presidents before Trump all faced opposition-controlled Senates. Until Obama, final two-year confirmations represented about 20% of total confirmations. Of Reagan’s 379 total confirmations, 84 (22%) came during his final two years. Clinton and Bush had similar percentages.

But Republicans took control of the Senate in 2015 and basically shut down judicial confirmations, resulting in only 22 confirmations—7% of all Obama confirmations.

What about the Supreme Court? If the Senate stays Republican even with a slimmer majority, look for Justice Alito to retire. If Democrats take the Senate, any vacancies will be health related, with ferocious battles over Trump’s proposed replacements either way.

Tom Wheeler

Midterm winners will face pressure to rein in AI power

The backlash over data centers necessary for artificial intelligence (AI) became a major campaign topic involving everyone from local candidates to the president of the United States. What began as neighborhood concerns about local environmental and utility issues grew into a fight over AI power.

Data centers were the first place voters could clearly see the costs and risks of AI being shifted to them. The backlash exposed the corporate power dilemma of AI: that a handful of executives are making unsupervised decisions that affect everyone.

Zoning boards and state utility commissions can decide where a data center is located and who pays for its power. Some states are trying to address how AI companies behave. But only Congress can establish uniform national rules.

The challenge for the new Congress is to turn public concern into enforceable oversight of AI. The test will be whether legislators take symbolic but limited action or step up with meaningful requirements supervised by an agency with technical expertise to oversee safety evaluations, mandatory incident reporting, and protections against the abuse of market power.

The data center backlash brought the power of AI into public debate. Elected leaders must now decide whether public interest oversight or private interests will shape that power.

Authors

The Brookings Institution is committed to quality, independence, and impact.

We are supported by a diverse array of funders. In line with our values and policies, each Brookings publication represents the sole views of its author(s).

text:
On Oct. 21, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California granted our motion for a preliminary injunction. The court held that DHS’s efforts to investigate in the final weeks before Election Day, based on records known to be inaccurate and to misidentify U.S. citizens as noncitizens, is voter intimidation.

The order bars the Department of Homeland Security from conducting field operations related to individuals known or suspected to be citizens, and from conducting operations based solely on the flawed data sources without further investigation. The order applies in the nine states known to be involved in HSI’s preelection field operations surge: California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington, and Wisconsin.

Beau Tremitiere, Counsel at Protect Democracy, said:

“Today, the courts affirmed a vital principle of our democracy: Voting is a fundamental right that citizens – whether born here or naturalized – should be able to exercise without armed government agents harassing them.

“It was clear from the start that DHS built its lists on bad data, never checked how often it was wrong, and recklessly sent agents to people’s homes weeks before an election. Today’s ruling should remind us that American citizens hold the ultimate power in our democracy, not the government–no matter what the administration says otherwise.”

The plaintiffs are the California Nurses Association, National Nurses United, the Voto Latino Foundation, the City and County of San Francisco, and Santa Clara County. Protect Democracy and the National Immigration Law Center represent the unions and Voto Latino, and the municipalities represent themselves. The suit was filed on Sept. 21, 2026, and the claims rest on the Voting Rights Act, the Administrative Procedure Act, and the U.S. Constitution.

title: Deportations climb under Trump but fall short of White House target, a new report finds
description:
The report by the Migration Policy Institute shows deportations increased from 620,000 during the first year of Trump’s second administration.
Trump, a Republican, returned to power last year promising to stanch crossings at the southern border and crack down on immigration.
More people being deported, but not at all-time highs The analysis found that the Department of Homeland Security carried out 980,000 deportations during the first 18 months of the second Trump administration.
Despite the surging arrests, the report details some of the challenges to the Trump administration reaching its deportation targets.
Figures the Trump administration has released are inconsistent and unverifiable.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump’s administration is on track to deport about 660,000 people over the past year, a new report released Thursday shows, as arrests ramp up across the country fueled by billions of dollars meant to supercharge his immigration agenda.

The report by the Migration Policy Institute shows deportations increased from 620,000 during the first year of Trump’s second administration. The numbers fall short of previous highs in the early 2000s and fail to meet the Trump administration’s promise, made when it received the billions from Congress, that the money would allow for 1 million deportations annually.

The report, based on publicly available data obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests, comes after the Trump administration in January 2025 stopped publicly releasing similar figures compiled by the Department of Homeland Security.

Trump, a Republican, returned to power last year promising to stanch crossings at the southern border and crack down on immigration. His administration has pushed through restrictions on both legal and illegal immigration and launched high-profile arrest operations in its bid to force migrants out.

More people being deported, but not at all-time highs

The analysis found that the Department of Homeland Security carried out 980,000 deportations during the first 18 months of the second Trump administration.

During the last fiscal year — when the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement mechanisms were shifting into high gear — an estimated 660,000 people were deported.

According to MPI’s analysis, that’s a 26% increase from the yearly average from 2021 to 2024 during the administration of President Joe Biden, a Democrat, but well below the 1.86 million deportations recorded in 2000, under President Bill Clinton, another Democrat.

Despite the surging arrests, the report details some of the challenges to the Trump administration reaching its deportation targets.

Historically, many immigrants living in the U.S. without authorization were from Mexico and didn’t often seek asylum. But in recent years, migrants have come to the U.S. from a wide range of countries, which can make it more complicated to deport them. And immigration courts, which ultimately decide whether someone can be removed from the country, face more significant case backlogs.

Voluntary departures are increasing as are interior arrests

The report said voluntary departures — when people give up their cases in immigration court and agree to leave the country — were at an “all-time high,” with 170,000 choosing to do so since Trump returned to office in January 2025. People who choose voluntary departure could one day return to the U.S. But some immigrant advocates and lawyers say that people give up their court fight and agree to leave simply to get out of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, detention.

The Trump administration was also increasingly deporting people it arrested in the country’s interior, the report said, reflecting how it was stepping up enforcement against migrants who have been in the country for a long time. In 2025, about 28% of the people deported were arrested inside the country, but by July of this year that had risen to 39%.

Migrants arrested at the southern border still make up a large number of deportations, the report said — 69% of all deportations between Jan. 20, 2025, and July 31, 2026, were of people initially intercepted at the border.

People in the country longer may have more opportunities to contest their removal while the government typically has greater authority to fast-track deportations for people arrested at the border.

The analysis said most people deported have never been convicted of a crime, despite the Trump administration claiming to be targeting the “worst of the worst.” Previous data has showed the same.

In response to the MPI report, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said: “President Trump has delivered the largest reduction in illegal immigration in modern history.”

Trump administration no longer regularly releases immigration data

Homeland Security stopped releasing similar data when Trump took office, making it difficult to track one of his key campaign promises. Figures the Trump administration has released are inconsistent and unverifiable.

The administration says it is transparent. On Tuesday, it released some of its own figures as part of a document boasting of its achievements on immigration, including that 1.2 million migrants have been deported or removed during Trump’s second term. The discrepancy could not immediately be reconciled.

In the absence of regular data, analysts and activists interested in immigration trends have relied on information obtained through lawsuits or limited and sporadic information released by federal agencies to track deportation data.

title: Trump's America: Immigration for me, not for thee - Courier-Herald
description:
Let us consider the hypocrisy surrounding Trump’s and the administration’s immigration rhetoric.
Donald Trump’s mother was born in Scotland, his paternal grandparents emigrated from Germany, and two of his three wives were born abroad.
Melania’s parents became U.S. citizens by taking advantage of chain migration; the very program Trump threatens to discontinue.
Stephen Miller, also not a veteran, is the architect of many of Trump’s hardcore restrictive immigration policies, also has immigrant ancestry.
Military service is not a prerequisite for public office, but officials enforcing immigration laws should understand the difference between protecting America and humiliating its citizens.
text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

Two 17-year-old Hispanic American citizens in Alamo, Texas, reportedly were on their way to deliver paperwork related to joining the U.S. Marine Corps when they were encountered by “the worst of the worse” ICE agents. Video of the Sept. 11 confrontation appears to show an agent repeatedly striking one teenager; the other said he was pepper-sprayed while his hands remained on the car’s steering wheel. Their ordeal reportedly left both reconsidering their plans to enlist in the military.

Let us consider the hypocrisy surrounding Trump’s and the administration’s immigration rhetoric. Donald Trump’s mother was born in Scotland, his paternal grandparents emigrated from Germany, and two of his three wives were born abroad. Melania’s parents became U.S. citizens by taking advantage of chain migration; the very program Trump threatens to discontinue. In 2019, Trump infamously told four congresswomen of color to go back to the countries from which they came—even though three were born in the United States.

Trump received draft deferments during the Vietnam War, and neither he nor his children have served in the military. Trump, a felon and a notorious tax cheat, was convicted in New York in 2024 of falsifying business records.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a former member of Congress, also has no reported military service.

Stephen Miller, also not a veteran, is the architect of many of Trump’s hardcore restrictive immigration policies, also has immigrant ancestry. His maternal grandparents came to America from Russia and Belarus. Miller’s family members have publicly criticized his views and it has been said that his family has disowned him. Is it any wonder why?

Military service is not a prerequisite for public office, but officials enforcing immigration laws should understand the difference between protecting America and humiliating its citizens.

Trump rails against communism while fawning over and rolling out the red carpet for authoritarian leaders like Putin, Xi Jinping, and Kim Jong Un—a glaring hypocrisy that exposes how his supposed defense of freedom takes a back seat to his personal admiration for dictators. What does Putin have on fanboy Trump anyway?

Here is the fundamental question: If ancestry determines who belongs in America, why should Trump, Miller or their families be exempt from the same standard they apply to others? Why shouldn’t we tell them to go back where their ancestors came from?

Of course not. That is precisely the point. America is not the exclusive property of people whose ancestors arrived earliest. And one’s citizenship is not a condition of ethnicity or political loyalty.

Those two bullied and abused teenagers deserve an impartial investigation into their treatment, accountability for any unjustified misuse and abuse of force, and the freedom to decide whether they still wish to become Marines. Their country should encourage their aspirations to serve—not leave them wondering whether their own government regards them as outsiders.

Patriotism should be measured by respect for the Constitution and equal treatment under the law, not by xenophobia and the ancestry of the people Trump chooses to target.

Stanley McKie

title: Inside Trump's DOJ, The Scary Part Was Following Court Orders Too Fast - Above the Law
description:
On her first day in office, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi made declining to sign a brief a fireable offense.
The Office of Immigration Litigation, which had more than 300 attorneys when Trump took office, has lost at least 100 of them.
For those who don’t practice in the federal government, telling your client how to comply with a court order is… kind of the whole job.
Reuveni’s complaint was explicit that the department “consistently advises its clients of their obligation to follow court orders, not to ignore them.” That was the baseline.
It feels like it’s going to take generations.” It’s chilling stuff from inside the DOJ.
text:
It’s been a rough couple of years at the Justice Department. On her first day in office, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi made declining to sign a brief a fireable offense. Later, rather than stop asking her lawyers to do things that could get them disciplined, she tried to take over bar discipline herself. The Office of Immigration Litigation, which had more than 300 attorneys when Trump took office, has lost at least 100 of them. The department is recruiting prosecutors over Twitter. And judges across the country have all but declared the presumption of regularity dead on arrival.

The rot set in early. Back in April 2025, Erez Reuveni, then acting deputy director of the Office of Immigration Litigation, told U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis that Kilmar Abrego Garcia should not have been removed, and added: “I am also frustrated that I also have no answers for you on a lot of these questions.” He was placed on leave the next day and fired within the week, with Bondi explaining that every DOJ attorney is required to zealously advocate. He later alleged in a whistleblower complaint that then–Principal Associate Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove floated telling the courts “fuck you” and ignoring any order that got in the way of the deportation flights.

That’s the view from the outside: the filings, the whistleblower complaints, the exit numbers. Bloomberg Law’s UnCommon Law podcast has someone who lived through it.

Sarah Wilson, the former Acting Deputy Assistant Attorney General overseeing DOJ’s Office of Immigration Litigation and now a partner at Colombo & Hurd, spent 14 years defending immigration policy for Democratic and Republican administrations alike. She tells host Matthew S. Schwartz that within weeks of Donald Trump’s return to the White House, the job changed, and that Reuveni’s firing was when the office knew it:

I think that was maybe the first moment at our office where we realized that something really different was going on here. Prior to this administration, people were wrongfully removed. Contrary to court order, there was a standard protocol within our office for how you might go about addressing that issue, how you would alert the court and just the tone that you would take in those filings, which would generally be fairly contrite.

We approached this case like we had hundreds of other wrongful removal cases in the past and marched into court and said all the same things that we would have said under other circumstances. And the reaction to that resulted in a firestorm.

Owning up to a judge after deporting someone in violation of her order used to be standard operating procedure. Under this DOJ, it got you fired.

It didn’t stop there. According to Wilson, in some of the highest-profile cases, career lawyers were told they could no longer advise the agencies they represented on how to comply with court orders. Those calls would be made further up the chain.

For those who don’t practice in the federal government, telling your client how to comply with a court order is… kind of the whole job. Reuveni’s complaint was explicit that the department “consistently advises its clients of their obligation to follow court orders, not to ignore them.” That was the baseline. Now the lawyer who has to stand in front of the judge and answer for whether the government complied has been walled off from the conversation about whether it will comply.

Wilson describes what that did to the people still in the building:

It was a scary time. It was a scary time to be at the department.

People started to wonder, can I do this without having someone be upset with me? Can I actually direct that this person be released? Or is there going to be a higher level call? Am I going to be called to explain why it is we complied with this order so quickly?

There’s a lot of that that I still wonder about today. There’s several things that happened that I thought like, why didn’t I just walk out the door then? Why wasn’t that a clear enough sign that I didn’t need to be here anymore?

Wilson describes the decision to leave the DOJ as “heartbreaking,” and emphasizes the importance of getting the DOJ back to how it operated under every other administration. But is that even possible? Wilson says, “that’s going to take a long time to undo. It feels like it’s going to take generations.”

It’s chilling stuff from inside the DOJ. You can listen to the full episode below.

RICHMOND, Va. – Attorney General Jay Jones, as part of a coalition of 21 attorneys general, filed an amicus brief in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in support of litigation challenging the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) policy and practice of conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests.

Under federal law, immigration officers conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests must have probable cause to believe that an individual is unlawfully present in the United States and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained.

“The Trump Administration is creating and stoking fear in our communities through these unlawful arrests that aim to make a political statement and sow mistrust between law enforcement and the communities they serve,” said Attorney General Jones. “Threats to our neighbors, friends, teachers, and families have resulted in widespread fear. President Trump’s DHS continues to strip people of their humanity and dignity, and it continues to exacerbate mistrust when we should be strengthening relationships and transparency between law enforcement and communities. My office will keep using every legal power and tool at our disposal to stand up for our communities and Virginians.”

The brief was filed in Escobar-Molina v. DHS, a case challenging DHS’s policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests in the District of Columbia. On December 2, 2025, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted in part a motion for a preliminary injunction.

In filing the brief, Attorney General Jones joins the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, and Washington.

text:
The Trump administration was on track to complete about 660,000 deportations last fiscal year, far lower than the goal of 1 million, according to a nonpartisan analysis.

Immigration officials are deporting more people who were initially arrested in the interior parts of the country, and those who have been in the US for years, the think tank Migration Policy Institute said in the report released Thursday. Still, the largest share of those deported were arrested at the border, according to the analysis.

The report is one of the first holistic views of how the Trump administration’s deportation strategy is unfolding.

Congress mandated in 2019 that Immigration and Customs Enforcement release data that includes how many people have been deported. However, the agency hasn’t updated its removal and deportation dashboard since January 2025 despite noting that the pages will be updated quarterly. Data and immigration advocates said the gaps in data decrease transparency and hinder the ability to track the administration’s progress and claims.

“We’re releasing many fewer numbers than the department has historically released,” Marc Rosenblum, visiting senior fellow at the Migration Policy Institute, told reporters during a call this week. Rosenblum was, until July of this year, leading the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Homeland Security Statistics. “Even with this fact sheet, we still know much less about the results of the department’s actions than we have historically known.”

DHS didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the missing data and updated deportation figures.

The report from MPI estimates that ICE has deported just under 1 million people since the start of the administration, with about 69% of those deportations being of people arrested at the border. Although the number of interior arrests are trending up, they’re not at the same level as the peak numbers under the George W. Bush or Obama administrations, Rosenblum said. DHS had 235,000 removals in 2008 and 238,000 in 2009, according to the report. The Trump administration was on track to come just shy of that with 230,000 interior deportations in 2026.

Counting Self-Deportations

The data also highlights a “major break from the longstanding DHS effort to reduce returns” and focus on formal removals, which could bar someone from returning to the US, Rosenblum said. And no previous administration, he said, had asked for the agency to keep track of estimated “self departures,” which are people who leave on their own.

While a “return” is considered a type of deportation, immigrants who are returned are not subject to penalties connected with removals, such as waiting years for the opportunity to try to reenter legally. One form of return is voluntary departure, which an immigrant can use to opt against fighting their case in the immigration court system.

“What we’re seeing in the current period is a major expansion of the use of voluntary departure to deport migrants arrested or detained within the United States,” he said, noting that between January 2025 and July 2026 ICE granted about 170,000 requests for voluntary departure. “That’s about a tenfold increase over any number that we’ve seen in the historic data.”

He also noted that the app promoted by DHS to track so-called “self deportations” may also be counting legal immigrants and US citizens.

title: Deportations climb under Trump but fall short of White House target, a new report finds
description:
The report by the Migration Policy Institute shows deportations increased from 620,000 during the first year of Trump’s second administration.
Trump, a Republican, returned to power last year promising to stanch crossings at the southern border and crack down on immigration.
More people being deported, but not at all-time highs The analysis found that the Department of Homeland Security carried out 980,000 deportations during the first 18 months of the second Trump administration.
Despite the surging arrests, the report details some of the challenges to the Trump administration reaching its deportation targets.
Figures the Trump administration has released are inconsistent and unverifiable.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump’s administration is on track to deport about 660,000 people over the past year, a new report released Thursday shows, as arrests ramp up across the country fueled by billions of dollars meant to supercharge his immigration agenda.

The report by the Migration Policy Institute shows deportations increased from 620,000 during the first year of Trump’s second administration. The numbers fall short of previous highs in the early 2000s and fail to meet the Trump administration’s promise, made when it received the billions from Congress, that the money would allow for 1 million deportations annually.

The report, based on publicly available data obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests, comes after the Trump administration in January 2025 stopped publicly releasing similar figures compiled by the Department of Homeland Security.

Trump, a Republican, returned to power last year promising to stanch crossings at the southern border and crack down on immigration. His administration has pushed through restrictions on both legal and illegal immigration and launched high-profile arrest operations in its bid to force migrants out.

More people being deported, but not at all-time highs

The analysis found that the Department of Homeland Security carried out 980,000 deportations during the first 18 months of the second Trump administration.

During the last fiscal year — when the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement mechanisms were shifting into high gear — an estimated 660,000 people were deported.

According to MPI’s analysis, that’s a 26% increase from the yearly average from 2021 to 2024 during the administration of President Joe Biden, a Democrat, but well below the 1.86 million deportations recorded in 2000, under President Bill Clinton, another Democrat.

Despite the surging arrests, the report details some of the challenges to the Trump administration reaching its deportation targets.

Historically, many immigrants living in the U.S. without authorization were from Mexico and didn’t often seek asylum. But in recent years, migrants have come to the U.S. from a wide range of countries, which can make it more complicated to deport them. And immigration courts, which ultimately decide whether someone can be removed from the country, face more significant case backlogs.

Voluntary departures are increasing as are interior arrests

The report said voluntary departures — when people give up their cases in immigration court and agree to leave the country — were at an “all-time high,” with 170,000 choosing to do so since Trump returned to office in January 2025. People who choose voluntary departure could one day return to the U.S. But some immigrant advocates and lawyers say that people give up their court fight and agree to leave simply to get out of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, detention.

The Trump administration was also increasingly deporting people it arrested in the country’s interior, the report said, reflecting how it was stepping up enforcement against migrants who have been in the country for a long time. In 2025, about 28% of the people deported were arrested inside the country, but by July of this year that had risen to 39%.

Migrants arrested at the southern border still make up a large number of deportations, the report said — 69% of all deportations between Jan. 20, 2025, and July 31, 2026, were of people initially intercepted at the border.

People in the country longer may have more opportunities to contest their removal while the government typically has greater authority to fast-track deportations for people arrested at the border.

The analysis said most people deported have never been convicted of a crime, despite the Trump administration claiming to be targeting the “worst of the worst.” Previous data has showed the same.

In response to the MPI report, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said: “President Trump has delivered the largest reduction in illegal immigration in modern history.”

Trump administration no longer regularly releases immigration data

Homeland Security stopped releasing similar data when Trump took office, making it difficult to track one of his key campaign promises. Figures the Trump administration has released are inconsistent and unverifiable.

The administration says it is transparent. On Tuesday, it released some of its own figures as part of a document boasting of its achievements on immigration, including that 1.2 million migrants have been deported or removed during Trump’s second term. The discrepancy could not immediately be reconciled.

In the absence of regular data, analysts and activists interested in immigration trends have relied on information obtained through lawsuits or limited and sporadic information released by federal agencies to track deportation data.

text:
Two U.S. Border Patrol vehicles parked outside Leon County's busiest early voting site in Tallahassee, Florida, on the first day of voting, prompting the county's elections supervisor to file a formal FBI complaint over possible voter intimidation just two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections.

Leon County Supervisor of Elections Mark Earley said the vehicles arrived outside the Northeast Branch Library around 10:15 a.m. on October 19, 2026, and remained for approximately 10 minutes before leaving. The incident came after Earley had received assurances from federal and state law enforcement agencies that immigration agents would stay away from polling places during the election.

Earley confirmed the FBI complaint on October 21, saying the bureau was taking the matter seriously. His office received no complaints from voters about the incident, although he expressed concern about the effect of federal immigration enforcement vehicles appearing outside an active voting location.

"I will do everything in my power to ensure that our voters can vote in a fair election free from intimidation or implied threats," Earley said.

The stop occurred two months after Earley publicly assured residents that federal immigration agents would be absent from polling locations. In an August interview with the Tallahassee Democrat, he said the Department of Homeland Security, FBI, and Florida Department of Law Enforcement had repeatedly told him that officers would stay away from voting sites.

"I've been reassured by DHS themselves that they understand that federal laws explicitly prohibit that kind of a presence at the polls, as do state laws," Earley said at the time.

His earlier assurances followed inquiries from Leon County residents worried about encountering immigration officers while voting. Earley said his office had received roughly a dozen calls expressing those fears, including one from a Latina voter who was concerned about being detained at a polling location.

Federal law makes it a crime to intimidate, threaten or coerce someone for the purpose of interfering with their right to vote in a federal election. Under 18 U.S.C. § 594, violations can carry fines and imprisonment of up to one year. Prosecutors pursuing charges must establish the prohibited conduct and the required intent, making the circumstances of the Border Patrol stop central to any potential criminal case.

The incident follows a September 10 federal lawsuit filed by the city of Denver and several voting rights organizations seeking to block the Trump administration from deploying armed immigration officers to polling places. The lawsuit challenges a federal policy allowing Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to enter voting sites to serve warrants or conduct other enforcement operations.

The plaintiffs argue that the policy violates a longstanding federal prohibition on sending armed personnel to election locations, except under narrowly defined circumstances. Homeland Security officials have maintained that immigration officers may carry out authorized enforcement duties, while the lawsuit seeks restrictions on those operations at polling places.

On October 7, the plaintiffs expanded their challenge to include Hennepin County, Minnesota, and added a claim under the Voting Rights Act alleging that the federal policy could intimidate or discourage eligible voters. The case remains pending in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.

The dispute centers partly on 18 U.S.C. § 592, which restricts federal officials from sending armed personnel to places where elections are held. That statute is separate from the voter intimidation provision and carries different legal requirements. Its application to immigration enforcement officers is among the issues raised in the litigation.

In Tallahassee, the Border Patrol vehicles' purpose remains unconfirmed, including whether agents conducted any enforcement activity or interacted with people at the library. Earley said he was coordinating with local, state, and federal law enforcement officials following the incident.

text:
A federal appeals court has rejected the Trump administration's argument that it can restart a six-month detention clock when immigrants are detained again after being released.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit ruled Wednesday in the case of Kavah Abedi, an Iranian national who was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in June 2025, more than two decades after he was released from immigration custody.

The court found that the government could not treat the first six months of Abedi's re-detention as presumptively reasonable under a Supreme Court ruling governing prolonged detention while the government seek to remove a person from the United States.

Read More on News

The appeals court also ruled that immigration officials violated federal regulations by failing to provide Abedi with a prompt interview after revoking his release, denying him an opportunity to challenge the basis for his detention.

The decision reverses parts of a lower court ruling and sends the case back for further proceedings.

Why Does This Matter?

The ruling addresses the limits of the federal government's authority to detain immigrants who have final orders of removal but cannot be deported in the reasonably foreseeable future.

In its 2001 decision in Zadvydas v. Davis, the Supreme Court established a six-month period of presumptively reasonable detention following the removal period.

After that, if a detainee provides good reason to believe there is no significant likelihood of removal in the reasonably foreseeable future, the government must respond with evidence sufficient to rebut that showing.

The Trump administration argued that the six-month presumption should restart when a person is released from immigration detention and later detained again.

The Tenth Circuit rejected that interpretation, concluding that the six-month presumption applies only to the first six months after the removal period begins and should not be applied again to Abedi's re-detention.

The court sent the case back to the district court to reconsider his detention claim without applying that presumption.

The ruling does not automatically require the release of all immigrants who are detained again. Instead, it establishes how the six-month presumption must be applied when courts assess the legality of detention in circumstances like Abedi's.

What Happened To Kaveh Abedi?

Abedi was 10 when his family fled Iran and entered the United States in 1991, where they were granted asylum, according to the court's opinion.

After he was convicted of a drug possession offense in California, he was placed in removal proceedings.

In September 2002, an immigration judge granted Abedi deferral of removal under the Convention Against Torture.

He was later released under an order of supervision because his removal was not considered reasonably foreseeable.

Over the following two decades, Abedi complied with the conditions imposed by immigration officials, including attending required check-ins and seeking permission before traveling outside his state of residence, the court said.

Abedi married a U.S. citizen in 2016 and had been his wife's primary provider and caretaker since 2020, as her chronic health conditions prevented her from continuing to work as a chef.

In 2025, the couple moved from California to Kansas for financial reasons after receiving approval from ICE.

On June 23, 2025, ICE officers detained Abedi outside his home while one told his wife that he was being deported to Iran, according to the court's account.

Abedi had previously been granted protection under the Convention Against Torture, which had resulted in the deferral of his removal.

While in detention, he received a notice stating that his release had been revoked because "removal to a country other than Iran is now a possibility". The notice also said he would "promptly be afforded an informal interview" at which he could respond to the reasons for the decision.

However, the government did not dispute that Abedi had not received the promised interview by the time the case was briefed on appeal.

The court noted that documents from a following case suggested an interview may eventually have taken place in January 2026, more than six months after his re-detention.

Abedi filed a habeas corpus petition in July 2025, challenging the legality of his detention, but a district court denied his petition that October.

In January 2026, he filed a second petition arguing that his detention had exceeded six months and that there was no real likelihood of his removal in the reasonably foreseeable future.

The district court granted that petition in February and he was released under an order of supervision on February 25, but the government then argued that his release meant the original appeal should be dismissed.

The Tenth Circuit rejected that argument, finding that the dispute could recur and evade judicial review.

What The Court Decided

The appeals court found that the district court had made legal errors in assessing Abedi's claims on two central issues.

First, it ruled that the government had violated its own regulations by failing to provide the required prompt interview after revoking his release.

The court said the interview requirement was designed to allow a detained person to challenge the reasons for their detention, but it rejected the government’s position that it should not be held to a particular time frame for providing that process.

The court said that accepting that argument would make the promptness requirement meaningless and effectively insulate administrative decisions from judicial review.

The government had not explained why it could not have interviewed Abedi within the four weeks before he filed his first habeas petition or the three months before the district court ruled on it.

The appeals court also rejected the lower court's conclusion that Abedi had not demonstrated sufficient prejudice from the failure to provide the interview.

It found that the regulatory safeguards protected fundamental due process rights and that the government's failure to follow them warranted relief.

Second, the court found that the district court had applied the wrong legal standard to Abedi’s claim under Zadvydas v. Davis by treating the first six months of his re-detention as presumptively reasonable.

The Supreme Court’s decision limits post-removal-period detention to a period reasonably necessary to secure a person’s removal, while its six-month presumption is intended to help courts assess when continued detention may no longer be lawful.

The Tenth Circuit also rejected the government’s interpretation that the presumption could begin again following re-detention.

The appeals court’s decision does not itself establish that every instance of re-detention is unlawful, instead it requires courts to assess the legality of detention without automatically treating the first six months after re-detention as presumptively reasonable.

The case will now return to the district court for further proceedings.

double quotation markMaanvi: Donald Trump ran on immigration as a top issue – but since taking office, voter support for his immigration crackdown has flagged. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on 21 September found that only 36% of voters approved of Trump’s handling of immigration. According to Pew research, half of Americans see the administration’s immigration tactics as too aggressive. Voters who self-identify as “Maga” still seem to strongly support Trump’s immigration policies, but fissures have appeared among Republican voters overall. This is especially clear in Republican districts that Trump easily carried during the presidential election. In deep-red Texas, for example, a poll by the New York Times and Siena University found voters there evenly split on which Senate candidate they trusted more to handle immigration – a striking shift in a state that hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in almost 40 years. Republican candidates are now trying to distance themselves from the most extreme parts of the administration’s crackdown. Republican senator Roger Marshall – who had once vehemently backed Trump’s immigration agenda – recently softened his hardline rhetoric, saying ICE should coordinate with local law enforcement. We’ve already mentioned here how this is playing out with Latino Republicans in Florida. Overall, an October NBC News/Telemundo poll of registered Latino voters found that two-thirds believe his enforcement policies have gone “too far”.
