title: DOD Memo Greenlights DHS Use of Military 'Heat Ray' at US-Mexico Border
description:
CNN published additional details Tuesday, reporting that internal discussions have centered on using the system to disperse crowds at the southern border.
When contacted for comment by Military.com, a Pentagon spokesperson deferred comment to DHS.
A former DHS official told the network the proposal raised concerns about treating immigrants and American citizens like enemy combatants.
Border Patrol's El Centro sector in California evaluated the system several years ago under Rodney Scott, who now leads CBP.
Officials previously raised sovereign concerns about a beam that can reach across the border into Mexico, according to CNN.
text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has reportedly loaned the military's so-called "heat ray" to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), handing civilian law enforcement a crowd-control weapon the Pentagon developed two decades ago.

The memo, signed by Hegseth last month and obtained by CNN, authorized a "temporary loan" of one Active Denial System for seven months starting in September. The system was originally sent to Afghanistan and brought home without ever being used in combat.

The memo says the system "shall not be operated by DoW (Department of War) personnel," leaving DHS solely responsible for employing the weapon and for developing the tactics, techniques and procedures governing its use.

DHS can ask to keep the system longer when the loan ends.

Former CNN correspondent Jim Acosta first reported the leaked memo Oct. 8 on his independent platform. CNN published additional details Tuesday, reporting that internal discussions have centered on using the system to disperse crowds at the southern border.

When contacted for comment by Military.com, a Pentagon spokesperson deferred comment to DHS.

A U.S. Customs and Border Protection spokesperson told Military.com the following: “CBP is continually evaluating new technology, especially technology that can save lives while simultaneously enhancing national security effectiveness.”

A Weapon the Military Shelved Without Firing

Built around an invisible beam of 95 GHz millimeter-wave energy, the Active Denial System has a range of more than half a mile, according to the military's descriptions of the weapon.

The beam heats the surface of the skin, producing a burning sensation Pentagon officials have compared to opening a hot oven, along with an effect officials say lasts 10 to 15 minutes and creates a strong urge to move away.

During testing in 2007, an airman with the 820th Security Forces Group at Moody Air Force Base in Georgia suffered second-degree burns and was treated at a hospital, according to the Valdosta Daily Times.

The military later deployed the system to Afghanistan but brought it home in 2010 without using it in combat, according to the BBC at the time. Officials considered it for crowd control at overseas detention facilities without employing it there.

It surfaced again in 2020. NPR reported that the Pentagon's lead military police officer for the National Capital Region emailed the District of Columbia National Guard asking whether it had an Active Denial System available before federal forces cleared protesters near Lafayette Square.

A Guard major later told Congress the Guard had no such system.

DHS Asked Before and its Own Secretary Said No

CBP officials weighed using the system against migrants in 2018, but then-DHS Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen rejected the idea, according to CNN.

A former DHS official told the network the proposal raised concerns about treating immigrants and American citizens like enemy combatants.

Border Patrol's El Centro sector in California evaluated the system several years ago under Rodney Scott, who now leads CBP. Those discussions focused on deterring river crossings or pushing people out of the water, according to CNN, and a former CBP official warned of drowning risks if people were driven toward the water.

Some Border Patrol agents doubt they need the tool at all, another former CBP official told CNN, with illegal crossings at low levels and staffing up.

A CBP spokesperson said the agency continually evaluates new technologies, especially those that improve operational effectiveness.

The memo does not say where or how the system would be tested or used, and the weapon has never been operationally deployed anywhere.

Federal law allows the defense secretary to make military equipment available to civilian law enforcement, and the memo's bar on military operators tracks the laws that keep troops out of direct domestic enforcement.

The loan language does not, however, guarantee how the weapon could lawfully be used against people.

DHS regulations require officers to use the objectively reasonable level of force necessary based on the totality of the circumstances. Officials previously raised sovereign concerns about a beam that can reach across the border into Mexico, according to CNN.

The loan runs into next spring, with an extension available on request. No document made public so far explains where the system is, who would fire it, or under what rules of engagement it would be utilized.

text:
A new “war on narco-terrorism” is fuelling unlawful killings and other grave human rights violations, United Nations experts warned the Third Committee (Social, Humanitarian and Cultural) today, as they sounded the alarm over mass displacement, the separation of migrant children from their families and mounting attacks on judicial independence.

‘Serial Extrajudicial Killings’ Amount to Crimes against Humanity

“In the past year, the United States has unlawfully killed at least 239 people in 71 military attacks on civilian vessels at sea”, declared Ben Saul, Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms while countering terrorism.

“These serial extrajudicial killings gravely violate the right to life and are a systematic attack on civilians amounting to crimes against humanity”, he said, calling for perpetrators to be held accountable.

Warning against conflating terrorism with organized crime, he reported that at least 15 countries, mostly in the Americas, have recently designated 39 criminal groups as terrorist organizations, expanding the use of exceptional security measures.

While organized crime is primarily profit-driven, terrorism involves political or ideological violence, he explained. A new “war on narco-terrorism” has led to grave human rights violations, including unlawful killings, torture and enforced disappearances. Conflating criminal and terrorist groups could also trigger travel bans, asset freezes and refoulement, he added.

He also criticized military aggression in Venezuela and Ecuador's authorization of a “shoot to kill” approach against criminal groups designated as terrorist.

“This new war on ‘narco-terrorism’ is not effective in reducing drugs or violence, and can make both worse”, he warned, noting that decades of militarized responses to drug cartels have failed to curb trafficking. Rather than pursuing “kinetic suppression of drugs”, States should invest in poverty reduction, public services, development and evidence-based prevention, he urged.

Turning to wider conflicts, he recalled earlier warnings against illegal wars justified by counter-terrorism. “Venezuela was invaded. Aggression against Iran has killed innocents and destabilized the Middle East, and energy shocks have impoverished the vulnerable worldwide”, he said. He also warned that peace in Gaza remains elusive without self-determination and justice.

Reconstruction Must Break Cycles of Displacement, Not Deepen Them

“Imagine returning home, only to find that home no longer exists”, said Paula Gaviria Betancur, Special Rapporteur on the human rights of internally displaced persons.

“For millions of internally displaced persons affected by mass devastation, this is not imagination. It is the reality awaiting them, if they can return at all”, she said, reporting that more than 82 million people are internally displaced worldwide by conflict, violence and disasters — the second-highest number ever recorded.

Reconstruction needs exceed $71 billion in Gaza, $11 billion in Lebanon, $216 billion in Syria and $588 billion in Ukraine, she reported. “The decisions taken in the first months of reconstruction will determine whether people can rebuild their lives in dignity or face new cycles of exclusion and displacement”, she warned.

Poorly designed rebuilding efforts can reward those who profit from destruction, trigger forced evictions and deepen land disputes. Yet, reconstruction also offers “a rare opportunity to confront the causes of displacement and break cycles of exclusion”.

Those who have lost everything need not only housing, but also recognition and justice, she emphasized, noting: “Reconstruction must reckon with what cannot be rebuilt with bricks and mortar: the missing whose fate is unknown, the process of mourning, the places of memory, the social bonds that held communities together.”

Delegates Clash over Gaza Reconstruction, Displacement

During the ensuing interactive dialogue, Malaysia’s representative condemned the repeated displacement of Palestinians in Gaza, accusing Israel of obstructing reconstruction by restricting building materials and equipment.

“Calling our security measures an obstruction is a moral failure”, Israel’s delegate responded, pointing to Hamas’ use of human shields. She also urged recognition of tens of thousands of Israelis displaced by attacks from Hamas, Hizbullah and Iran.

Iran’s representative rejected allegations that his country targets civilians, accusing Israel of “systematic targeting of Palestinian civilians and civilian objects” and of attacking civilian areas in his country.

Yemen’s delegate blamed Houthi militias for forcing millions from their homes, reporting that over 217,000 people had been internally displaced since September. Sudan’s representative similarly highlighted “lengthy waves” of displacement caused by conflict and militia violence, including sexual violence.

Turning to reconstruction, Azerbaijan’s delegate reported that over $16 billion had been allocated to rebuild conflict-affected towns, enabling over 100,000 people to return to newly constructed areas.

Syria's representative said Government policies had facilitated the return of approximately 2 million displaced people since the fall of the Assad regime, highlighting plans to close displacement camps through reconstruction.

‘Fossil Fuel Companies Systematically Manufacture Doubts’

Margaret Satterthwaite, Special Rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers, warned that justice systems seeking to enforce climate commitments face intimidation, political interference and powerful economic opposition.

“Fossil fuel companies systematically manufacture doubts about climate science, target their critics and wage war on effective climate action”, she declared.

Judges and prosecutors frequently lack adequate training in environmental law and climate science, while lawyers struggle to obtain evidence from companies refusing access to sites or environmental impact studies.

“Such restrictions undermine equality of arms and the right to a fair trial”, she warned, potentially preventing communities from challenging destructive projects before irreversible damage occurs.

The most entrenched obstacle is “hostility from powerful political and economic forces”, she said, warning that the climate crisis is unfolding alongside a global wave of “autocratization” and rising inequality.

‘Immigration Detention of Children Is Never in Their Best Interests’

Gehad Madi, Special Rapporteur on the human rights of migrants, warned that detention, deportation and restrictive border policies continue to tear migrant families apart. “Family unity saves lives and serves as an essential protective factor for children in situations of migration”, he stressed.

“Immigration detention of children is never in their best interests”, he underlined, warning of serious consequences for children's mental health and development.

Voicing further concern over “migration externalization”, he stressed that transferring migrants to third countries increases their chances of separation and protection failures. “Outsourcing migration governance does not diminish States’ obligations”, he said.

Calling for stronger family reunification measures and regular migration pathways, he urged Governments to prohibit immigration detention of children and families. “Migration status must never determine whether a child can enjoy family life”, he added.

Also briefing the Committee today were Prasad Kariyawasam, Chair of the Committee on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families, and Morris Tidball-Binz, Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions.

The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to allow it to resume plans to build a border wall through the Big Bend region of West Texas, as part of its anti-immigration policy to strengthen security on the border with Mexico.

The Justice Department filed an emergency request on Wednesday asking the court to lift a federal judge’s injunction in a lower court that has halted construction while a lawsuit against the project, brought by an environmental group and other challengers, plays out.

The Department of Homeland Security plans include vehicle barriers, patrol roads, lighting and detection technology in and around Big Bend National Park.

Landscape, historic church

The lawsuit, filed by plaintiffs including the Center for Biological Diversity and a Big Bend-area river guide, seeks to preserve the landscape, protect a historic church, and challenge the federal government’s waivers of environmental and historical laws to fast-track the $1.7bn project.

Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and current Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who issued the waivers between February and July, found the region to be an “area of high illegal entry”, requiring additional barriers to control the border.

US District Judge Kathleen Cardone issued an injunction in El Paso on October 2 halting work “until and unless Defendants comply with all applicable laws,” she wrote in her order.

In a later opinion, the judge found that the waivers exceeded the authority of Noem and Mullin.

The Justice Department in its request urged the Supreme Court to pause or overturn Cardone’s injunction.

The Supreme Court has not yet responded to this appeal.

“Even assuming that the secretary’s waiver authority implicates a question of ‘vast economic and political significance,’ Congress did clearly authorize the secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction,” the Justice Department wrote.

In August, the administration paused construction in Big Bend after the project drew bipartisan criticism over its potential impact on the park’s landscape and wildlife.

text:
In response to surging immigration operations across California in the final weeks before the midterm elections, community leaders and elected officials said the heightened raids are meant to keep voters from the polls.

They encouraged Angelenos to be vigilant and exercise their right to vote and to vote before Nov. 3.

Angelica Salas, executive director of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights (CHIRLA), recommended that eligible voters mail in their ballots early or use an official drop box. Those who want to vote in person can opt to visit an early voting center. Taking advantage of these early options avoids any concern about encountering the possibility of voter suppression at the polls on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3.

Salas said multiple organizations across the state are working together in a coalition called Can’t Stop California to train individuals to be observers at polling places “when people are casting their [ballots], to protect their [vote] at the ballot box.”

“We’re protecting our people [and] we’re also protecting our people’s ability to participate in the elections,” said Salas.

As immigration raids continue expanding ahead of the election, so do community concerns, said Los Angeles City Councilmember Imelda Padilla, who represents the Northeast San Fernando Valley, speaking at CHIRLA’s LA headquarters.

“These so-called agents have been using … aggressive tactics, like crashing into cars, blocking roads and causing chaos,” said Padilla, adding that her district “has been hit the hardest.”

Videos of agents pursuing and detaining people in various areas of the valley have been widely distributed, “showcasing the madness … of what this is doing to our communities,” she said.

“Parents shouldn’t have to be afraid to take their children to school, and workers shouldn’t be afraid to show up to their jobs. … It’s all tied to making sure that we stay home and don’t vote,” said Padilla. “To those of you who can [vote] … please do not cave in to the fear. We need you to listen to our main message today, which is preparation, not panic, and solidarity, not isolation.”

Jeannette Zanipatin, policy director for CHIRLA, said people from LA to Northern California are reporting more Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) activity, which she described as a “coordinated effort to spread fear in our communities” and attempt to intimidate voters.

The escalating sweeps are a direct result of the Trump administration’s 45-day ICE enforcement crackdown throughout California known as Operation Safe California, which began in early October. The ICE surge has impacted both metropolitan areas and agricultural regions.

“The timing of these actions, just weeks before the midterm elections, is no accident,” said Zanipatin, adding that the dual goal is to sow division and “suppress civic participation.” She urged people to document suspected ICE activity they witness when it is safe to do so; report incidents to trusted community networks, such as the LA Rapid Response Network (LARRN); support families impacted by detention or deportation; and “vote your values,” said Zanipatin.

“To those seeking to frighten our communities into silence, you will not succeed,” she said. “California immigrant communities are strong, organized and resilient. We will protect one another, defend our rights and show up at the ballot box.”

LA Mayor Karen Bass, who is running for reelection, said President Donald Trump is “putting immigrant communities at risk” in an effort to “scare people away from voting.” But despite Trump’s fearmongering tactics, added Bass, “the election is [already] going on right now.”

Be Prepared and “Stay Calm”

As ICE activity increases, families continue to be separated and traumatized. Jennifer Baltazar, a county social worker, shared her own family’s experience. Her father, who she described as “everything” to her and her brothers, was picked up by ICE last week and remains in detention.

“ICE took him from us,” said Baltazar, while holding back tears. “ICE and this administration don’t view people like my father as human [beings], don’t consider their contributions, don’t care to see what people like my father mean to [their] communities and to [their] families.”

She vowed to keep advocating for her father and others who are unjustly detained, and stressed the importance of being prepared in case a loved one is picked up, detained or deported.

“My message to other vulnerable families: create a plan of action,” continued Baltazar. “Get educated. Connect with resources that are already in place for the community.”

“And if you are stopped, do not run. Remain as calm as you possibly can,” said Salas. “Your ability to stay calm allows you to protect your rights … [including the] right to remain silent. … And by remaining calm and not running, you can also protect your life.”

She pointed out that ICE tactics have changed since the summer of 2025, resulting in more detentions. Previously, agents routinely conducted operations in the middle of the day, and the “inhumanity” was on full display. While that sometimes still happens, they are increasingly conducting raids early in the morning, so that it “happens in the shadows,” she said.

“They will wait for … people [to be] leaving for work, at 5 o’clock in the morning, 6 o’clock in the morning, so it’s really a grab and snatch. They do it as quickly as possible – get them in the car, have them disappear,” described Salas. “That is why all of us being vigilant is so important.”

“Elections have consequences. Look at the consequences we’re living with because certain people stayed home,” said Salas. “That is what we need everybody to be aware of: how crucial it is for everybody to vote.”

To reach the hotline for the Los Angeles Rapid Response Network (LARRN), call 1-888-624-4752. For the Immigrant Defenders Law Center, call (213) 833-8283, and to contact CHIRLA’s Immigrant Assistance Line, call 1-888-624-4752.

text:
Bob Boulé’s second act is hard to beat. After his business went belly-up and his marriage ended, Bob bought a house a spit away from Canada and turned it into a bed-and-breakfast. Drugs and people of varying legalities crossed the border in both directions while Bob — the former owner of the Smuggler’s Inn — played both sides as a government informant and humanitarian activist.

Smuggler: Drugs, Gangs, and Refugees at America’s Northern Border, written by border scholar Reece Jones and immigration attorney Greg Boos, tells the story of life on the northern border with plenty of historical and political context through the central figure of Bob Boulé.

Bob is the most interesting man you’ve never heard of. Or at least I hadn’t heard of him until Reece Jones sent me his latest book with immigration attorney Greg Boos, about this longtime Republican whose years of colorful living on our often-overlooked northern border eventually got him assaulted by a Border Patrol officer, Erik Egbert.

The case went to the Supreme Court, which handed down a ruling that says, in short, the public has no real remedy against federal agents who violate their rights, because the civil rights laws that allow redress against state and local officers don’t apply to federal officers.

At a time when ICE and Border Patrol officers are under scrutiny for roughing up and even killing U.S. citizens, this story — entertaining as it is — comes with a warning: we are not protected.

Reece was way ahead of the curve on this warning. In 2022, when book events were still all virtual, I had the great fortune to join Reece and Politics & Prose for the book launch of his previous book Nobody Is Protected about the expansive and unchecked power of Border Patrol. (Come to think of it, I believe it was Reece’s book launch that initially gave me the idea to host book discussions — yet another thing I owe to Reece.)

Smuggler is a terrific read and it’s a story that is about so much more than just a major lawsuit. At a time when we are digging in our ideological heels, Smuggler shows you that people can change and do change when they encounter migrants and the border for themselves in reality rather than through abstractions.

My conversation with Reece and Greg, like their book, is un-summarize-able, so have a listen for yourself and let me know what you think!

WORTH COUNTY, Ga. (WALB) — More than a dozen people were arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents during a road check operation in Worth County.

According to Sheriff Donald Whitaker, on Oct. 20, his office helped four to six ICE agents with road checks on the east side of the county from noon to 5:00 p.m.

He said the agents were searching for people wanted by ICE under the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

A total of 14 people were taken into ICE custody.

The sheriff says he doesn’t know where they are being held or the specific charges they’re facing.

Whitaker also addressed the community after he says a number of people posted warnings on social media urging locals to avoid the area or take different routes.

“People don’t understand what they could possibly do by doing that. They may be allowing this person that we are looking for to have the information and evade capture. And they don’t know who they are warning, they don’t know what kind of crime they are wanted for,” he said. ”You’re warning somebody, somebody that my end up harming your family or a friend of your family. Don’t do that. That’s not right.”

The sheriff added that he considers these warnings an interruption to law enforcement operations.

“Don’t obstruct law enforcement. When they’re road checking or out patrolling somewhere, they’re there for a reason and it’s for the reason of protecting the citizens of this county and the state,” he said. ”As far as I’m concerned, that is obstructing law enforcement by warning people. Let us do our jobs and protect everybody as we are supposed to do.”

WALB has reached out to ICE and DHS for more information on the arrests and is waiting for their response.

text:
WOODLAND, Calif. —

A Woodland man, 37-year-old Antonio Moreida, said he was struck by a federal immigration SUV on Tuesday morning while documenting ICE activity, sparking outrage among local leaders and calls for accountability.

Meanwhile, DHS denies the allegations, stating “an agitator jumped onto the hood of an ICE vehicle.”

The incident has drawn attention from elected officials, including Congressman Mike Thompson, who spoke Wednesday afternoon in downtown Woodland alongside half a dozen other local leaders.

Many of them expressed support for a full investigation by local law enforcement and demanded ICE’s full cooperation.

“The bottom line is no one is above the law. Our community trust and our community being united is incredibly important, and ICE’s actions have contributed to that growing distrust and a fear within our communities and other communities across the country. And that makes accountability all the more important. I've contacted the acting director of ICE and directly demanded that we have answers to our questions,” Thompson said.

Assemblymember Cecilia Aguiar-Curry said, "ICE is trying to terrorize our communities and create fear and mistrust."

Woodland Mayor Richard Stallard added, "I'm at the point of outrage, to the point where I couldn't even sleep last night thinking about this, realizing the people in our community are living in fear because of this effort by ICE to do whatever objective they're trying to do, but doing it in the most hateful, mean, incomprehensible method."

KCRA 3 reached out to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security for comment multiple times on Tuesday.

On Wednesday, DHS shared this statement: "This is false. ICE did NOT hit a pedestrian. An agitator jumped onto the hood of an ICE vehicle and the officer driving applied the brakes. The agitator slid off the hood. ICE immediately contacted EMS and the Woodland Police Department. Flopping for the camera is dangerous, especially when it interferes with a federal law enforcement operation."

Woodland police said Wednesday claims made in the DHS statement are "inconsistent with the video evidence obtained and reviewed" by the department's investigators.

Police said investigators established the following based on video evidence:

The pedestrian was struck by a vehicle driven by an ICE agent

The pedestrian did not jump onto the hood of the vehicle

The pedestrian did not slide off the hood of the vehicle

The driver applied the brakes before the collision

The driver remained near the scene, contacted Woodland police and cooperated with officers during the initial investigation

When asked about the statement from DHS, Thompson responded, "What I have to say about that I can't really repeat in a crowd. It's just nonsense and you know it and I know it. The local police know it, our community knows it, and they're not going to get away with lying to our community. They're not going to get away with lying to the American people."

Moreida also addressed the statement, saying, "I would say the footage speaks for itself, especially the new house camera angle that clearly shows clearly what happened. And I'll leave it at that."

Moreida expressed frustration over what he called a lack of accountability. He also said he has not been contacted by ICE since the incident but showed a photo of a federal law enforcement vehicle parked outside his house while he was at the hospital.

Woodland Police confirmed they are investigating and that the driver of the SUV is cooperating.

text:
A Venezuelan man who was shot by an ICE agent in North Austin last month has now been federally indicted in connection with the encounter.

According to court documents filed Tuesday, Oct. 20, Wilber Garces Perez was indicted on one charge of assaulting, resisting, impeding, and obstructing a federal officer. The indictment comes three weeks after Perez appeared in court in Austin for his criminal case.

The indictment alleges Perez "used a motor vehicle as a deadly and dangerous weapon", but it does not lay out details of what happened Sept. 20. It also accuses Garces Perez of forcibly interfering with a federal officer who was carrying out official duties.

MORE| APD Chief: Local investigators still waiting for federal evidence from ICE shooting

During Perez’s criminal hearing last month, a federal judge found prosecutors have probable cause to support the charge against him. Prosecutors played ICE body camera footage in court and said it shows the moment Perez allegedly struck an ICE agent with his driver’s side mirror. The footage then shows officers on an eight-minute pursuit of Perez through North Austin neighborhoods.

The pursuit ended near Research Boulevard and Anderson Square, where an ICE agent shot Perez.

Perez admitted to disregarding orders from officers to park and exit his car during an interview with investigators. However, Perez’s defense team argues the video does not make it clear whether the car mirror made contact with the ICE agent.

Austin police released dash-camera video from an off-duty detective and body-camera video from a responding officer, but neither shows the shooting.

Earlier this month, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said the department was still waiting on federal evidence, though the department’s own investigation was continuing.

“We have a lot of the evidence that we need. We have made several attempts or several calls to our federal partners. We’ve not received anything at this point, but I am still hopeful that we will,” Davis said.

A request was sent to the U.S. attorney’s office to confirm whether Austin police have received the evidence for their investigation, and a response is pending.

Perez remains in federal custody as the criminal case moves forward after a judge denied his bond. His immigration and criminal defense team was asked where he is being held, but they said they need to meet first before releasing that information.

text:
Mennonite Church USA and its 26 co-plaintiffs won an important ruling on Oct. 20, 2026, putting them on the path toward injunctive relief in the “sensitive locations” lawsuit, Mennonite Church USA et al., v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, et al.

In a 2-1 decision, a three-judge panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, Washington, D.C., agreed that MC USA and its co-plaintiffs face a real and immediate risk of immigration enforcement at or near their places of worship as a result of the January 2025 Department of Homeland Security (DHS) memo rescinding the sensitive locations policy.

In her Opinion for the Court, Circuit Judge Florence Y. Pan wrote, “Plaintiffs’ members likely face imminent harm from increased enforcement at their houses of worship; that harm is traceable to the new enforcement policy; and the relief requested will likely redress their injury, at least in part.” She also pointed out that the “plaintiffs have direct evidence that the government intends to increase immigration enforcement at sensitive locations – that is the whole point of the Recission Memo.”

This ruling overturned an April 2025 decision by a lower federal district court in Washington, D.C., which found that the risk was not clear enough to justify court action.

What this ruling means

The case will return to the lower court, where MC USA and its co-plaintiffs can again ask for a preliminary injunction, a temporary court order that would protect their congregations while the lawsuit continues. This ruling does not guarantee that outcome, and it does not decide the lawsuit itself. However, it moves MC USA closer to protecting its churches and may also set a precedent for other similar cases.

Why did MC USA file a lawsuit?

MC USA and other faith Christian and Jewish denominations and associations filed the lawsuit on February 11, 2025, after the Trump Administration’s rescission of the DHS “sensitive locations” policy. Since the 1990s, a series of federal “sensitive locations” policies have largely kept immigration agents, including those of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), from making arrests, conducting raids or taking other enforcement actions at houses of worship.

Without it, congregations and the people who attend worship can be targeted as part of the Administration’s mass deportation efforts.

“We’re asking the government to not interfere with our right to practice our faith freely, which is protected by the Constitution … [The lawsuit] is asking [the government] to enforce laws in ways that don’t stop us from following Jesus’ command to love our neighbors,” wrote Associate Executive Director of Church Vitality Michael Danner in his blog, “The free exercise of our faith.”

What can your congregation do?

If your congregation or ministry observes ICE or CBP activity in or around your place of worship, please contact Iris de León-Hartshorn (irisdh@mennoniteusa.org) immediately and copy your conference minister so that we can document any encroachment into sacred spaces with the court.

The plaintiffs in Mennonite Church USA et al., v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, et al. are represented by the Institute for Constitutional Advocacy and Protection, a strategic legal advocacy arm of Georgetown University Law Center that is committed to defending constitutional rights and values while working to restore confidence in the integrity of governmental institutions.

text:
Washington — The Trump administration on Wednesday asked the Supreme Court to allow it to resume for now construction of a border wall and other infrastructure through a remote area of West Texas that includes Big Bend National Park.

The Justice Department urged the high court to lift a lower court injunction that temporarily bars the Department of Homeland Security from building the barrier or related infrastructure in the Big Bend Sector, which covers more than 500 miles of the U.S.-Mexico border and 77 counties in Texas.

"The district court's injunction significantly frustrates the government's ability to stop the flow of illegal aliens and drugs across the southern border," Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in the request for emergency relief. "The Secretary identified the Big Bend project areas at issue because of the high rates of illegal-alien crossings and drug smuggling in the region over the past several years."

President Trump's promise to build a wall along the southern border has been a hallmark of his immigration agenda for the last decade. But earlier this year, the president's plans were met with significant pushback from lawmakers in both parties, cattle ranchers and local law enforcement officials in Texas when photos and videos shared to social media showed bulldozers arriving at Big Bend National Park.

In response to the backlash, Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott paused construction inside the park until the end of September. The agency has said that the proposed border wall will not cut through Big Bend National Park, but other infrastructure would, including patrol roads, detection technology and roughly 17 miles of vehicle barriers.

Construction of a 47-mile-long stretch of wall in the Big Bend region began last month, according to CBP. The government has awarded contracts for five border-barrier projects in that area along the U.S.-Mexico border, the Justice Department said.

The Trump administration announced in February that the Department of Homeland Security would build barriers and roads in the Big Bend Sector. The project includes the construction of 30-foot-tall bollard walls stretching from Fort Quitman, Texas, to Closed Canyon, which is located in Big Bend Ranch State Park. Border walls and roads would span more than 300 miles, according to the government.

Because of the project's impact on cultural, recreational, wildlife and environmental resources, the federal government would typically have to ensure compliance with federal environmental protection and historical preservation laws before moving forward.

But when then-Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem announced the project earlier this year, she invoked a 1996 federal immigration law that gives the secretary the authority to waive all legal requirements deemed necessary to ensure quick construction of physical barriers and roads in the vicinity of the southern border to "deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry." Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who succeeded Noem after her firing, issued two more waivers allowing CBP to construct barrier systems.

In response to the move, an environmental nonprofit, a professional riverboat guide and a religious organization dedicated to preserving the Sacred Heart of the Church of Jesus along the Rio Grande filed a lawsuit in April seeking to stop the Trump administration from implementing the project.

The Trump administration argued that the stretch of land at issue in the case is an area of "high illegal entry" given the rates of illegal crossings and drug smuggling. The government said more than 89,000 people were apprehended trying to cross into the U.S. illegally in the Big Bend Sector between 2021 and 2025.

But the plaintiffs said that the Big Bend Sector ranks last for apprehensions compared to the other six sectors along the southern border. While the area covers more than 25% of the U.S.-Mexico border, annual apprehensions in the Big Bend Sector ranged between 0.3% and 2.2% of total border-wide apprehensions, according to court filings.

Earlier this month, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone granted the challengers' request for a preliminary injunction and barred the Department of Homeland Security from building border barriers or related infrastructure, or engaging in "any construction or ground disturbing activities" in the Big Bend Sector.

Cardone found that Noem and Mullin exceeded their authorities when issuing the waivers between February and July that allowed construction to proceed.

Just before the Justice Department sought the Supreme Court's intervention, Cardone rejected the Trump administration's request to pause her decision.

text:
SALT LAKE CITY — The site of what was to have been a federal immigrant detention center in Salt Lake City has been listed for sale, along with six other sites around the country that had also been proposed as Immigration and Customs Enforcement facilities.

Cushman and Wakefield, a national commercial real estate company, lists the Salt Lake City warehouse site at 6020 W. 300 South as available for purchase along with a site in Michigan, two locations in Georgia, two locations in Pennsylvania and a site in Texas. Cushman calls the package of locations — all former proposed immigration detention center sites — its Federal Warehouse Portfolio.

"Given the tenant demand for modern, high-quality bulk distribution buildings, the portfolio offers investors the rare opportunity to capture substantial value creation through the lease-up and stabilization of the properties," reads the Cushman website listing the seven sites. "The properties will be delivered free and clear of existing financing."

News of the listing of the Salt Lake City location comes in one of the latest filings in the pending federal lawsuit Salt Lake City and Salt Lake County filed against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to halt the detention center plans here. News that federal officials had abandoned plans to convert the Salt Lake City warehouse building into a detention center first emerged in June, and the development was confirmed by federal officials in a filing in the lawsuit in August.

In the latest filing in the Utah case, U.S. Magistrate Judge Dustin Pead on Monday extended the deadline for submission of a status report on efforts to sell the 6020 W. 300 South building for 90 days, until Jan. 18. Monday had been the original deadline.

"Defendants shall not take any action to convert the Salt Lake facility into an immigration detention center during the stay," Pead wrote in the short filing. In suing the DHS, Salt Lake City and county officials had charged that federal officials didn't follow proper federal procedures in designating the proposed site at 6020 W. 300 South as a detention center.

The Salt Lake City location remains in federal hands, according to a joint filing in the lawsuit on Sunday by city, county and federal officials. But they didn't offer many other details.

"Defendants still intend to dispose of this property and do not intend to proceed with plans to convert it into a detention center. Since the stay was entered, defendants have taken necessary steps toward selling the property and the property is now listed on the Cushman and Wakefield website as soon being available for purchase," reads the filing.

ICE purchased the empty 883,000-square-foot warehouse on 300 South for $145.44 million in March for conversion into an immigrant detention center, part of President Donald Trump's crackdown on illegal immigration. The plans sparked an uproar among immigrant advocates and protesting, as did similar proposals around the country, many since stalled.

The seven properties Cushman is selling contain 5.3 million square feet of space between them, and six were built since 2018. The other sites listed for sale, along with the Salt Lake City location, are:

A warehouse in Romulus, Michigan, in the Detroit area. Acquisition of the site by ICE in February prompted a lawsuit by the city of Romulus against federal authorities, according to WDIV in Detroit.

A warehouse in Social Circle, Georgia, southeast of Atlanta. City officials filed suit against the federal authorities over their plans last May, according to WXIA in Atlanta.

A warehouse in Flowery Branch, Georgia, northeast of Atlanta, that the DHS bought for $68.16 million earlier this year, according to the news website, Access North Georgia.

title: Bay Area immigration attorneys warn of uptick in violent ICE arrests - Mission Local
authors: Clara-Sophia Daly, Sarah Hopkins, Sarah Hopkins Staff
description:
His arrest, five immigration attorneys say, is the latest of several across the Bay Area that reflect increasingly aggressive immigration enforcement.
Bay Area “rapid response” hotlines monitoring immigration arrests have seen an uptick in reports since this weekend, said Lisa Knox, co-executive director at California Collaborative for Immigrant Justice.
Mission Local verified six immigration arrests across the Bay Area in the past week.
Regional uptick in arrests Immigration arrests across major Bay Area cities rose 81 percent between July 2025 and July 2026, according to a Mission Local analysis of federal data released by U.C.
Violent tactics Some recent ICE arrests in the Bay Area have resulted in hospitalizations.
text:
When masked immigration agents arrested Luz’s son in SoMa in San Francisco on Monday, they slammed him against a window. One plainclothes agent ran across the street with his gun drawn, according to an eyewitness and widely viewed surveillance footage. The agents pushed him to the concrete, breaking his glasses, Luz said.

Luz’s son has lived in the United States since he was six years old, working on farms in Monterey County. He has a son of his own.

His arrest, five immigration attorneys say, is the latest of several across the Bay Area that reflect increasingly aggressive immigration enforcement.

Bay Area “rapid response” hotlines monitoring immigration arrests have seen an uptick in reports since this weekend, said Lisa Knox, co-executive director at California Collaborative for Immigrant Justice. Knox is in contact with eight regional hotlines that field calls of reported arrests.

The increased activity has extended to the San Francisco jail, where public defenders on Tuesday spotted two Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in the lobby, said Deputy Public Defender Francisco Ugarte. But their presence raises questions about potential violations of city and state Sanctuary City policies.

Ugarte called the recent enforcement a “surge,” and compared it to ICE operations in 2007 and 2008 when agents from around the country came to the Bay Area, identified targets, and then “snatched people up.”

Not everyone agrees there is a surge, but over the past couple of weeks, Bay Area immigration attorneys say they’ve not only seen more arrests but also ICE agents using more violence during arrests, and arrests without valid warrants.

“We are definitely seeing an increase in violence used in ICE arrests, and also an increase in ICE,” said Nikolas De Bremaeker, an attorney with Centro Legal de La Raza in Oakland.

Mission Local verified six immigration arrests across the Bay Area in the past week. Four involved violent tactics like physically forcing individuals out of their cars, slamming them on the ground, and handcuffing them so tightly they experienced pain.

Two arrests led to immigrants being hospitalized, according to De Bremaeker and court filings.

Regional uptick in arrests

Immigration arrests across major Bay Area cities rose 81 percent between July 2025 and July 2026, according to a Mission Local analysis of federal data released by U.C. Berkeley. Attorneys expect those arrests have continued to climb since, though the latest available federal data ends in July, making it difficult to determine exactly how the recent arrests compare with previous weeks.

Most arrests in San Francisco and the region have occurred at immigration courthouses and ICE appointments — controlled locations where immigrants showing up for check-ins come to the officers.

But attorney Jonathan Abel, who directs the Habeas Institute at U.C. Law San Francisco, said that in the past week, “It appears that ICE is going out more into the communities, and arresting people at their homes, car stops, or place of work.”

There, he said, ICE is more likely to “bring more agents,” and there is “more potential for violent tactics than ICE check-ins or asylum office interviews.”

Those aggressive tactics, attorneys say, are driven at least in part by pressure on agents – introduced earlier this month – to meet a reported nationwide target of 3,000 arrests a day.

Violent tactics

Some recent ICE arrests in the Bay Area have resulted in hospitalizations.

On Saturday, ICE agents pursued an Oakland resident from Mexico who works as a truck driver, eventually boxing him in his car, about a block from his home, according to court filings on behalf of the man.

According to those court records, six agents emerged from vehicles and surrounded him. When the man asked to see a warrant, the agents showed him a photograph of what appeared to be a warrant that was “seemingly blank and had only Petitioner’s name typed into it,” the court records stated.

The records go on to describe agents who broke his car window with a hammer, “used a baton to try to pry his leg out of the car,” and “slammed” him “onto the pavement.”

By the time he arrived at ICE’s processing facility in San Francisco, he could not walk, according to the records, and was subsequently taken to San Francisco General Hospital.

He remained hospitalized at SF General and in immigration custody on Monday, according to his attorney and court filings. A federal judge ordered his release on Tuesday morning.

In Sonoma County, a U.S. citizen was driving to work when she was surrounded by immigration vehicles, according to court records filed on behalf of her boyfriend. The agents drew their guns and aimed at her, the filings said.

“I thought they were going to shoot me; I was terrified and shaking,” the documents detail. The agents were seeking her boyfriend, the filings said, who sometimes drives the same car.

Later that morning, the boyfriend sat in his car in a Santa Rosa parking lot when about a half-dozen masked officers drew their guns, pulled the man from his car, and handcuffed him, the documents state. Although he was not physically injured, he had a panic attack.

De Bremaeker, of Centro Legal de la Raza, said he is representing another Oakland resident who was hospitalized at Highland Hospital after he was “violently tackled by ICE” and then had six of his ribs fractured by a 280-pound agent who sat on his chest.

The violence, De Bremaeker said, “shows an escalation in tactics and violence.”

Mili Atkinson, head of the San Francisco Immigrant Legal Defense Collaborative, said her advice to the public is to call their county’s Rapid Response Hotline if they have news of an alleged ICE spotting.

But the arrests have left many in the Bay Area shaken.

Juan Carlos, who witnessed the arrest of Luz’s son outside his Sixth Street apartment in SoMa, said he worries about the children who pass through the neighborhood each morning on their way to Bessie Carmichael Elementary School.

“If I saw someone running with a gun, it would be very upsetting,” he said. “I’ve lived in L.A., Phoenix, Orange County – but I’ve never seen anything like this. Out of all the places it could happen, I never expected this to happen here.”

Additional reporting by Bailey Zitko.

title: ICE pickups spike at Ventura County jail, officials say
description:
The number of individuals picked up by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement spiked at the Ventura County jail last year.
Of the around 169 notifications in 2025, the Ventura County Sheriff's Office reported federal agents picked up two-thirds or 114.
Those same years, ICE picked up fewer than a third of the individuals, or 43 and 45 respectively.
ICE detains others being released Even without the notifications, ICE shows up and takes people into custody when they get released from jail.
At the Ventura County Government Center, the jail's lobby is located not far from the superior court building.
text:
The number of individuals picked up by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement spiked at the Ventura County jail last year.

In California, state law prohibits most cooperation with federal immigration agencies but gives the Ventura County Sheriff's Office and other jurisdictions the option to notify ICE when some individuals are released from jail. That is, if those people meet specific criteria such as having convictions, or being held to answer after a preliminary hearing, for offenses such as robbery, residential burglary or rape.

Of the around 169 notifications in 2025, the Ventura County Sheriff's Office reported federal agents picked up two-thirds or 114. That was more than double the number picked up in either of the previous two years.

Sheriff Jim Fryhoff described the decision to continue notifying ICE in those cases as a difficult one but one he does "to keep the community safe from people who have chosen to violate the law."

"As the chief law enforcement official in the county, my job is to protect the public, and I do so by weighing decisions such as whether or not I'm going to communicate with immigration where I'm allowed," the sheriff said, speaking in front of the county's Board of Supervisors at an Oct. 20 forum.

The Transparent Review of Unjust Transfers and Holds, or TRUTH Act, requires the public forums about such communication. Dozens of community members spoke, urging the county to stop the voluntary notifications and to make other changes. Other counties have opted not to provide the release dates, they said.

Willie Lubka, executive director of Buen Vecino, said the voluntary cooperation with immigration authorities results in separation of local families and long-lasting trauma. The practice itself is known to cause distrust in the community, said Lubka, on the steering committee of ICE Out Ventura County, a coalition of more than two dozen organizations.

"The community is safer when there is trust between all residents and county agencies," he said.

"We're hoping this is our last TRUTH Act forum ever," Lubka said. "But until the policy changes, we intend to keep coming back."

ICE picks up scores at local jail

Fryhoff explained the process, saying the immigration agency makes a request, and sheriff's office personnel then check to see if the individual meets the criteria. When an individual meets the requirements, the sheriff's office notifies ICE of the release date.

If ICE shows up, the person is then released to agents in a controlled environment, Fryhoff said. When agents aren't there, the individual is released and able to leave the facility.

In the last few years, the number of requests steadily increased while notifications initially dropped from a high of 181 in 2023 to 133 in 2024. Those same years, ICE picked up fewer than a third of the individuals, or 43 and 45 respectively.

Last year, ICE made 1,329 requests to the sheriff's office. Of those, local authorities determined that around 169 met the requirements for notifications. ICE picked up 114, according to the sheriff's presentation.

The notifications represent a small fraction of the people booked in the jail — nearly 22,000 last year, officials said. But the pickups, too, accounted for only a portion of those detained by ICE at or outside the jail.

ICE detains others being released

Even without the notifications, ICE shows up and takes people into custody when they get released from jail.

Some in the audience questioned the timing, saying they had seen situations that seemed like ICE knew when the person would be released. Fryhoff, however, said his agency does not cooperate or communicate with immigration about individuals who don't meet the criteria.

"It doesn't take very long to figure out how that process goes, and ICE has figured out that process in ways for people that they want to take into custody," Fryhoff said of the releases.

Supervisor Vianey Lopez asked the sheriff a series of questions, including about how a law prohibiting ICE from courthouses could affect federal agents at the jail facility or in nearby parking lots. At the Ventura County Government Center, the jail's lobby is located not far from the superior court building.

After the public comments, Fryhoff spoke again and responded to questions. He heard the comments, he said, and would research some of the questions. That would include looking at what the law allows his agency to do without interfering with federal agents and having deputies or himself arrested, he said.

"I'm not happy with how ICE conducts their operations. I've made that very clear," Fryhoff said.

Earlier in the forum, Jamie Sanchez, a Simi Valley resident, Navy veteran and volunteer with groups, including 805 Undocufund, told county supervisors she had witnessed the aftermath of what happens when ICE takes a family member and saw the fear that spreads through communities.

"This is not just about immigration policy. This is about children, families and the human consequences of what is happening in our communities," Sanchez said.

title: Investigation finds hundreds of U.S. citizens detained by ICE | PBS News
authors: William Brangham, Molly Mazilu, Bridget Craig

William Brangham has the latest on the growing number of Americans who are being caught up in the administration's enforcement action.
Video shows the moment Ricardo Gonzalez, a U.S. citizen, is riding an e-bike and then is stopped alongside an unmarked ICE vehicle.

text:
Geoff Bennett:

Officials in California are calling for an investigation into the actions of federal immigration officers after they allegedly injured and detained a U.S. citizen this past weekend.

William Brangham has the latest on the growing number of Americans who are being caught up in the administration's enforcement action.

William Brangham:

The incident in question took place on Saturday in Long Beach, California. Video shows the moment Ricardo Gonzalez, a U.S. citizen, is riding an e-bike and then is stopped alongside an unmarked ICE vehicle. It's unclear whether the vehicle hit him or not. He's later seen being held face down in handcuffs screaming.

Ricardo Gonzalez, Detained By ICE:

My arm is broken. Help me. Help me. My arm is (EXPLETIVE DELETED) broken. My arm is (EXPLETIVE DELETED) broken. My arm is broken. It (EXPLETIVE DELETED) hurts!

William Brangham:

Gonzalez was later taken to the hospital and treated for serious injuries. ICE says Gonzalez was arrested because he was rioting and damaged a government vehicle.

Details of Gonzalez's detainment come as a new investigation by ProPublica has found more than 500 U.S. citizens have been caught up in the ongoing immigration dragnet.

For more on this, we are joined by ProPublica's Nicole Foy, who was one of the reporters on this series.

Nicole, thank you so much for being here.

Is this incident that we saw reported in California this weekend, does this align with the kinds of cases that you document in your reporting?

Nicole Foy, ProPublica:

It absolutely does, mostly because we found citizens getting detained by immigration officials for a variety of reasons around the country and sometimes in very similar situations like this, where maybe there was a protest nearby or maybe there was just an unexpected encounter between a U.S. citizen in their neighborhood where they lived with immigration officials, who have really expanded their dragnet and the number of people that they're trying to detain.

And, sometimes, those two people co collide, quite literally in this case. And there are many, many citizens that we have documented of the more than 500 that we found were detained so far who were also really seriously injured after their encounters as well.

William Brangham:

I mean, DHS, as you reported in your series, repeatedly says that they do not detain or arrest U.S. citizens, despite what your reporting shows.

When you say that U.S. citizens are being detained, as you documented, who are the people that are being detained and what are the other circumstances around their cases?

Nicole Foy:

Yes, it's a mix of folks.

Sometimes, it is folks that immigration officials have accused of assaulting or interfering with immigration operations. Sometimes, that seems to be the case. And, other times, there is witness -- witness testimony or footage that really contradicts that narrative.

But there's also been many, many people who have been detained because of questions about their citizenship, whether they were on a construction site and didn't speak English very well, or they were -- there were questions about whether they also were here in the United States without papers. We have seen people detained in a variety of ways.

William Brangham:

What happens after these people are detained? I mean, are formal charges filed? It seems that if ICE then realizes you have an American citizen in custody, you would think that would be the end of it.

Nicole Foy:

Yes, some people who have been charged with -- who have been arrested on allegations of assault were charged with assault, but we found many who still to this day have not been charged with assault, even if officials release statements accusing them of that.

We also found dozens of people who were held for several days, including at least 24 hours without being able to access their phone or their lawyer or to contact their family and let them know where they were. So it's -- some people really had a very brief detention, where it was maybe 15 minutes, 20 minutes where they're in handcuffs on the side of the road.

But other people disappeared into a system that was actually very difficult for their loved ones and their lawyers to find them, and at the same time they sometimes were seriously injured as well.

William Brangham:

You shared a lot of your reporting, including the videos that you compiled, with former immigration officials to gauge their reaction. What was it that they told you about what you had uncovered?

Nicole Foy:

They were really shocked by what they saw. These are folks who -- two particular officials that I'm thinking of retired fairly recently.

And they said that, first of all, they had never seen this many U.S. citizen encounters at all, let alone this level of detention, and that the -- they really characterized much of the use of force, the apparent reason or probable cause for stops, as really troubling, because it did not -- it did not seem that officers were following what they believe that they should have been trained to do.

William Brangham:

Are there constitutional protections for Americans in these kinds of circumstances? And, if so, have there been any sort of enforcement actions against officers who might have been accused of or found committing wrongdoing?

Nicole Foy:

Yes, I mean, everyone in the U.S. has constitutional protections, whether you are an immigrant or you are a U.S. citizen.

But what our reporting found was just, particularly when you're just looking at these detentions and arrests of U.S. citizens, really some very troubling examples of possible violations of folks' Fourth Amendment, the right to be free from unreasonable searches and seizures, whether that's accusations of racial profiling or accusations of really excessive force use during the arrest.

But we also found hundreds of people who were arrested because they were participating in a protest. We found many people who were also film -- were simply filming when they were arrested, and they believe that that is the reason why they are arrested. The government may disagree, but they believe their First Amendment rights were violated in that way as well.

William Brangham:

Nicole Foy of ProPublica, thank you so much for sharing your reporting with us.

Nicole Foy:

Thank you for having me.

name: Litigation
title: Top Justice Department official asks Minnesota judges to step aside from immigration cases
description:
Both of the requests were made by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, the third-highest-ranking official at the Justice Department.
Reyes rejected the Justice Department's effort Sunday and accused the Justice Department of weaponizing "selective quotations to bring a baseless recusal motion."
In the case overseen by Schiltz, the Trump administration is seeking to strip a Minnesota man of his U.S. citizenship.
The Justice Department sued all 15 of the federal judges in Maryland over a standing order that temporarily blocks the immediate removal of immigrants challenging their deportations.
A judge in Virginia dismissed the lawsuit, and the Justice Department has appealed that decision.
text:
Washington — A top official at the Justice Department is attempting to disqualify two Minnesota federal judges from a pair of cases, claiming comments they made to the New York Times about the Trump administration's handling of immigration cases in the state call their impartiality into question.

The motions, filed against Judges Patrick Schiltz and John Tunheim, are an escalation of the Justice Department's ongoing campaign against judges who it claims have treated the Trump administration unfairly. Both of the requests were made by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, the third-highest-ranking official at the Justice Department.

Woodward also moved over the weekend to disqualify U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, who sits on the trial court in Washington, D.C., from overseeing a case involving President Trump's efforts to overhaul a historic public golf course in the nation's capital. Reyes rejected the Justice Department's effort Sunday and accused the Justice Department of weaponizing "selective quotations to bring a baseless recusal motion."

The requests seeking the recusals of Schiltz and Tunheim came in two separate immigration cases and were each filed by Woodward on Tuesday. In the case overseen by Schiltz, the Trump administration is seeking to strip a Minnesota man of his U.S. citizenship. In the second case, assigned to Tunheim, a South African national faces two charges of illegally voting in the 2024 election. She has pleaded not guilty.

Schiltz has scheduled a hearing on the motion against him for Nov. 23. Under ethics rules, judges cannot publicly discuss cases pending before them.

At the center of both requests are comments Tunheim and Schiltz made to the New York Times for an article published last month. The judges each raised concerns about the Trump administration's handling of cases stemming from its immigration crackdown in Minnesota earlier this year, called Operation Metro Surge.

Woodward claimed in each of the filings that the judges' comments raised questions about their ability to remain impartial in the cases.

"A judge who has publicly taken sides on the political issue of immigration enforcement cannot then preside over a case concerning one of the Justice Department's key immigration initiatives: pursuing the largest denaturalization effort in Department history to restore trust and integrity in U.S. citizenship," he wrote in the motion to disqualify Schiltz. "Absent recusal, the American people will reasonably question whether Judge Schiltz can be impartial regarding this important matter defending the integrity of American citizenship."

Woodward separately claimed that Tunheim's remarks to the Times suggest that he may view the charges against the South African national as unwarranted.

"To Judge Tunheim, the 'rule of law' apparently means ignoring the law when it comes to illegal aliens who have broken the law," he wrote.

The associate attorney general said Schiltz and Tunheim's statements and participation in the Times article "give rise to the appearance of bias in immigration-related cases," warranting their recusals. Woodward is the only government lawyer who signed the motions.

What comes next

Experts on judicial ethics expect the Trump administration will likely fail in its efforts to sideline Schiltz and Tunheim from the cases. Still, these motions to disqualify are rare, and yet even more rare when they are made by the government.

"They're looking to essentially antagonize the judges and to square off against them in some manner," said Charles Geyh, a law professor at Indiana University Bloomington who focuses on ethics and judicial conduct.

In the rare instances where the Justice Department believes a judge should step aside from a case, government lawyers might write to the judge privately and lay out the reasons why they think recusal is warranted, said Stephen Gillers, a law professor at New York University who has written on judicial ethics.

But with the efforts involving Schiltz and Tunheim, not only did the Justice Department file their motions on the public dockets, it also promoted them on social media.

"It's obvious DOJ has decided that its game plan is to challenge the fairness of the judges as a way of undermining judicial authority in the eyes of the public," Gillers said.

He called the filings "performative" and said the Justice Department "wants to publicize them to discourage public confidence in what the courts are doing when they rule against the administration."

The disqualification motions are the latest in a line of actions taken by the Trump administration that target judges who have ruled against it. The Justice Department filed a judicial misconduct complaint against all but one of the federal judges in Minnesota, including Schiltz and Tunheim, last month because of the Times article. It also submitted ethics complaints against Reyes and U.S. District Judge James Boasberg, the latter of which was dismissed.

The Justice Department sued all 15 of the federal judges in Maryland over a standing order that temporarily blocks the immediate removal of immigrants challenging their deportations. A judge in Virginia dismissed the lawsuit, and the Justice Department has appealed that decision.

Mr. Trump and senior members of his administration have also publicly insulted judges, including Supreme Court justices, by name and called for their impeachments.

"This is just a perpetuation of the project," Geyh said. "It's part of the network of efforts to delegitimize the judges involved, make them look partisan, make them look biased as a way to quiet them and diminish the check from the judiciary."

Amid rising tensions between the federal judiciary and Trump administration, Schiltz and Tunheim are not the only federal judges who have raised concerns about what they say is the government's disregard of court orders. Others have pushed back against the harsh rhetoric from the president and top administration officials.

The Judicial Conference, the policy-making body for the federal courts, issued an advisory opinion in February stating that ethics principles "permit judges to speak or write about the independence of the judiciary, or advocate for the rule of law in general, including why both values are crucial to our system of government."

Additionally, the Judicial Conference said its Committee on Codes of Conduct believes there is "room, in at least some circumstances, for the measured defense of judicial colleagues from illegitimate forms of criticism and attacks that risk undermining judicial independence or the rule of law, whether or not they rise to the level of persecution."

"If you're talking generally about the concerns with the rule of law as a consequence of the general pattern of conduct the Department of Justice is exhibiting, it's the opposite of bias," Geyh said. "It is them really doing what they need to do to protect the rule of law."

title: ICE Denies Hitting Man With Vehicle as Lawmakers Demand Answers - Newsweek
description:
“ICE did NOT hit a pedestrian.” Video footage shared on social media shows a black SUV striking a man, later identified as Antonio Moreida.
Lawmakers Push for Answers After Incident After the incident, lawmakers have called for answers.
Federal immigration laws must be enforced, but how that happens matters.
ICE Faces Questions Over Incidents The incident in California is the latest in a run of incidents for which ICE has been questioned.
A Newsweek analysis found that as of June of this year, 51 deaths had occurred in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody since Trump returned to office.
text:
A video showing an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) vehicle appearing to strike a pedestrian has sparked condemnation from lawmakers who are seeking answers about the incident, but the Department of Homeland Security denied it in a statement shared with Newsweek. “This is false,” a spokesperson said. “ICE did NOT hit a pedestrian.”

Video footage shared on social media shows a black SUV striking a man, later identified as Antonio Moreida.

The video footage shows him flipping over and falling to the ground.

Read More on News

The spokesperson said that an “agitator” had “jumped onto the hood of an ICE vehicle and the officer driving applied the brakes,” and the person then “slid off the hood.”

The incident is currently being investigated.

Why It Matters

A common thread has emerged in several controversial ICE shootings: claims that a motorist was attempting to use a vehicle as a weapon against federal agents. Immigration authorities have relied on that explanation in cases involving U.S. citizens, including Renee Good and Ruben Ray Martinez, whose deaths drew renewed scrutiny after records revealed ICE's involvement had not been publicly disclosed for months.

Supporters of the agency say the incidents demonstrate the dangers agents face in the field, while critics argue the repeated reliance on vehicle-threat allegations highlights the need for independent investigations and greater transparency whenever immigration operations end in civilian deaths.

What to Know

Moreida spoke at the City of Woodland, California, City Council after the incident. “I’m Antonio, I’m the one that got hit earlier by ICE,” he said.

Moreida was trying to document suspected ICE activity in the area, according to KXTV-TV Sacramento. “We started blowing our whistles and honking our horns that ICE was here,” he said, per the outlet.

“I was there to document and run information to keep track and make sure that they are not hurting our neighbors in our community. It was not my intent to get hit,” he said, per KXTV-TV Sacramento.

The Yolo County District Attorney said in a social media statement that they are “aware of today’s events involving ICE agents,” but because of an “active investigation,” they cannot comment.

The Woodland Police Department said in a statement that it is “actively investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.”

Police Chief Ryan Kinnan said, “I’ve seen the video myself, and I find it very troubling. I understand why people in our community are upset and worried.”

The Woodland Police Department added that they did not participate in the federal operation and that their role is “to investigate this collision independently and establish the facts.”

“The federal agency has been notified, and we have requested its full cooperation,” they added.

Newsweek has contacted the Woodland Police Department via email for further comment.

Lawmakers Push for Answers After Incident

After the incident, lawmakers have called for answers.

Representative Mike Thompson, a California Democrat whose district includes Yolo County, said in a statement that “ICE cannot continue to terrorize our communities.

“I am in communication with local law enforcement, who have informed me that ICE was operating the vehicle in question and that an investigation is underway,” Thompson said, adding, “No one is above the law.”

Senator Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, shared video footage of the incident on X and said, “ICE and CBP are OUT OF CONTROL. Democrats WILL investigate their abuses when we win back Congress.”

The incident comes amid reports of increased enforcement activity in California as of early October.

Padilla, alongside Democratic Senator Adam Schiff and Republican Representative Adam Gray, demanded answers from ICE in response to increased activity in the area of Mendota earlier this month.

“Mendota is a hardworking agricultural community, and families should not have to fear going to work or taking their kids to school. Federal immigration laws must be enforced, but how that happens matters. We need answers about what’s taking place, who is being targeted and whether people’s rights are being protected,” the lawmakers said in a joint statement.

Moreida also pushed for answers while speaking at the city council meeting.

“It’s not about me,” he said, as per video footage of the meeting reviewed by Newsweek. “Really, I guess I just wanted to follow up with ensuring, you know, some of the community's calls for action hopefully do come through. As far as hopefully, the city taking any sort of legal action or the investigation,” he said.

He alleged that ICE was “not concerned whatsoever,” following the incident, and said that he didn’t know “where this investigation is at.”

“I’m really annoyed to say the least,” he said.

ICE Faces Questions Over Incidents

The incident in California is the latest in a run of incidents for which ICE has been questioned.

Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson in California has called for ICE to be investigated after a video showed federal agents restraining and handcuffing a man who local officials say was injured during the incident.

The video appeared to show a man named Ricardo Gonzalez pinned down in a gutter as he yells that his arm is broken.

The Los Angeles Times reported that Gonzalez told Richardson he is a U.S. citizen.

DHS defended ICE’s actions and said its officers used the “minimum amount of force” and followed their training.

Separately, in a recent incident in Texas, a federal officer slammed a vehicle into a Houston construction worker, breaking his leg, while in pursuit of a man who had apparently died years ago, the Associated Press reported, citing a family statement.

Concerns over the conduct of ICE have surged throughout President Donald Trump’s second term in office, amid the enforcement of the Trump administration's hardline immigration policies.

A Newsweek analysis found that as of June of this year, 51 deaths had occurred in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody since Trump returned to office.

In 2025, at least 33 people died in ICE custody, the highest annual total since 2004.

In the first half of 2026, 18 deaths have been reported, which means this year is on track to surpass last year's figure.

A DHS spokesperson told Newsweek, “We have seen a highly coordinated campaign of violence against our law enforcement.”

“This violence must end. Anybody who lays a hand on our officers or tries to obstruct them is committing a felony and a federal crime,” the spokesperson added.

What Happens Next

The investigation is ongoing, and police are appealing for information.

Anyone with information or video is asked to contact Woodland Police Department Dispatch at 530-666-2411.

Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.
