title: Minnesota Human Rights Department Finds Two Businesses Discriminated Against Native ...
description:
The findings highlight ongoing concerns about the recognition of Tribal identification cards and the treatment of Native Americans seeking everyday services, including banking and dining.
Tribal identification cards are official documents issued by sovereign Tribal governments and reflect Tribal citizenship and self-governance.
Under Minnesota law, Tribal identification cards are recognized as acceptable identification in circumstances where a Minnesota identification card is accepted.
Refusing Tribal identification or requiring additional documentation from Tribal citizens may constitute discrimination under the Minnesota Human Rights Act.
The Minnesota Department of Human Rights is Minnesota’s civil rights enforcement agency and investigates discrimination and enforces protections under the Minnesota Human Rights Act.
text:
ST. PAUL, Minn. — The Minnesota Department of Human Rights (MDHR) announced on Friday, October 16th that two Minnesota businesses discriminated against Native American customers by refusing to recognize identification cards issued by their Tribal Nations.

The department found probable cause that Wings Financial Credit Union in Coon Rapids and The Office Pub and Grill in Minneapolis violated state civil rights protections after denying services to customers who presented valid Tribal identification cards issued by the Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate and Red Lake Nation.

The findings highlight ongoing concerns about the recognition of Tribal identification cards and the treatment of Native Americans seeking everyday services, including banking and dining.

“Tribal identification is an integral part of a Tribe’s sovereignty, right to self-determination, and self-governance,” said MDHR Commissioner Rebecca Lucero in the department’s announcement.

“Schools, businesses, and law enforcement cannot refuse Tribal identification or require additional burdens on Tribal members who use their Tribal ID.”

Two Investigations Find Probable Cause of Discrimination

According to MDHR, the two cases involved separate complaints filed by Native American customers who were denied services after presenting identification issued by their respective Tribal Nations.

In the first case, investigators found that Wings Financial Credit Union in Coon Rapids repeatedly denied a customer access to her bank account when she presented a valid identification card issued by the Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate.

The department found that the credit union required the customer to provide additional documentation not required of other customers, treated her with hostility, and prevented her from fully accessing banking services.

In the second case, MDHR found that The Office Pub and Grill, a Minneapolis sports bar, refused to serve a customer on three separate occasions after he presented a valid Red Lake Nation identification card as proof of age.

Despite the identification confirming that the customer was of legal age, the establishment continued to deny him service.

After its investigation, MDHR found probable cause to believe discrimination occurred in both cases.

Tribal Identification and Sovereignty

Minnesota shares geography with 11 sovereign Tribal Nations, including seven Anishinaabe reservations and four Dakota communities. Each Tribal Nation maintains its own government and authority to issue identification to its citizens.

Tribal identification cards are official documents issued by sovereign Tribal governments and reflect Tribal citizenship and self-governance.

Under Minnesota law, Tribal identification cards are recognized as acceptable identification in circumstances where a Minnesota identification card is accepted.

Minnesota Statute § 171.072(a) states:

“If a Minnesota identification card is deemed an acceptable form of identification in Minnesota Statutes or Rules, a Tribal identification card is also an acceptable form of identification.”

The department emphasized that businesses cannot impose additional requirements on Tribal members simply because they present Tribal identification instead of a state-issued ID.

Refusing Tribal identification or requiring additional documentation from Tribal citizens may constitute discrimination under the Minnesota Human Rights Act.

The announcement also comes amid broader concerns about the treatment of Native Americans by federal immigration enforcement officers.

According to MDHR, Native American community members were harassed and, in some cases, detained by federal immigration agents during Operation Metro Surge after officers refused to recognize their Tribal identification cards.

Tribal Nations responded by reaffirming that identification cards issued to enrolled citizens are valid forms of identification.

Department Seeking Changes to Prevent Future Discrimination

Following the findings, MDHR said it will work with affected individuals and businesses to seek changes to prevent similar incidents.

The department encourages Minnesota businesses to review their identification policies and provide employee training to ensure they properly recognize Tribal identification cards.

The findings also remind us that Tribal sovereignty and the recognition of Tribal citizenship extend beyond Tribal lands and into everyday interactions with businesses and institutions throughout Minnesota.

MDHR enforces the Minnesota Human Rights Act on non-Tribal lands, including the locations where both incidents occurred.

How to Report Discrimination

Native Americans who believe they have experienced discrimination because of their Tribal identification or other protected characteristics can submit a complaint inquiry to the Minnesota Department of Human Rights.

Individuals can contact the department through its online discrimination inquiry form.

The Minnesota Department of Human Rights is Minnesota’s civil rights enforcement agency and investigates discrimination and enforces protections under the Minnesota Human Rights Act.

title: ICE arrests disrupt daily life in Teton Valley | Local - JHNewsAndGuide.com
authors: Jeannette Boner, Bradly J. Boner, NEWS&GUIDE
description: A recent uptick in immigration arrests has disturbed Teton County, Idaho, reaching businesses, schools and households while suggesting a closer relationship between federal officials, sheriff’s deputies and county probation staff.
text:
A canceled concert in Victor. Children afraid at school. People detained when they arrived for court-ordered drug testing.
A recent uptick in immigration arrests has disrupted daily life in Teton County, Idaho, reaching businesses, schools and households while suggesting a closer relationship between federal officials, sheriff’s deputies and county probation staff.
A mother whose husband was arrested after an Oct. 9 traffic stop is packing to move her family to Mexico. Another woman said her husband arrived for a probation drug test Oct. 13 and was directed to a back room where immigration agents were waiting.
Wildwood
event center in Victor canceled an Oct. 10 concert featuring a Latino band amid concerns about Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s presence.
The Department of Homeland Security confirmed five arrests in Teton Valley on Oct. 9 and 11, including two it said occurred after calls for assistance from the Teton County, Idaho, Sheriff’s Office. Those statements do not account for other arrests by ICE agents at the county’s Law Enforcement Center in Driggs on Oct. 13 and 15.
Teton County, Idaho, Sheriff Clint Lemieux has maintained that his department “does not conduct joint immigration operations” with the Department of Homeland Security but a DHS spokesperson confirmed ICE agents made at least two arrests recently in Teton Valley “during a call for assistance by the Teton County Sheriff’s Office.”
BRADLY J. BONER / NEWS&GUIDE
County officials maintain that deputies do not enforce civil immigration laws and probation staff did not detain anyone on ICE’s behalf. ICE has reached out to work with the probation director, they say.
Teton County Administrator Billie Siddoway said ICE agents in Idaho entered the local law enforcement building simply “to use the restroom,” and agents later arrived independently at a local traffic stop, addressing community questions about immigration activity last week.
“The Sheriff’s Office does not hold a 287(g) agreement, does not enforce federal civil immigration law, and does not conduct joint immigration operations,” Siddoway wrote in a response prepared in consultation with Teton County Sheriff Clint Lemieux.
Lemieux did not directly respond to multiple requests for comment. He instead provided a statement defending deputies’ responses through Siddoway, who works for the Teton County, Idaho, commissioners.
“We do not conduct immigration enforcement or act as federal immigration agents,” Lemieux said. “At the same time, as Sheriff, I will not order my deputies to obstruct or interfere with federal law enforcement officers.”
However, statements from DHS, personal accounts and bystander videos across at least 11 detentions in the last month appear to contradict local officials’ statements.
Elected leaders said they were largely unaware of the recent ICE activity. Teton County Board of Commissioners Chair Brad Wolfe suggested national immigration policy needs to be reviewed. He said he believed Lemieux when the sheriff said he was not working with federal immigration officers.
The probation department is under the jurisdiction of Wolfe’s board.
This is, however, not the first time Idaho law enforcement and the probation office have worked directly with federal agents.
Similar concerns
surfaced in 2025, when ICE arrested two men summoned for probation check-ins.
A man who was detained by ICE earlier this month told his wife a Teton County Sheriff’s deputy pulled him over for a traffic violation near the intersection of Larkspur Lane and Lupine Lane in Victor. The deputy had the driver and his passenger stopped for about 20 minutes before ICE arrived and detained them.
BRADLY J. BONER / NEWS&GUIDE
In July,
residents reported
ICE agents joining deputies during traffic stops. While deputies initiated traffic stops, witnesses described unmarked vehicles arriving moments later, with federal agents joining deputies during vehicle searches and, in some cases, taking custody of individuals after the stops.
On the way to work
Around 7:41 a.m. Oct. 9, a Victor mother received a text from her husband: A Teton County, Idaho, sheriff’s deputy had pulled him over on his way to work.
He was driving his employer’s truck to a nearby construction job, with a co-worker in the passenger seat, when he was pulled over for passing an intersection’s stop line before coming to a stop, she said. There are no painted stop lines at the intersection.
According to the account her husband later gave her, he handed over his Utah driving credential, registration and insurance card. The deputy returned from his patrol vehicle and said the insurance card had expired. Her husband called his employer, who sent an updated copy.
While he waited for that document, she said, her husband told her the deputy began questioning his passenger about his identity.
Then, about 20 minutes later, she received another message.
“Immigration is here,” she recalled her husband texting.
She was preparing to take her daughter to a sports practice. Instead, she drove toward the stop, where a Teton County, Idaho sheriff’s vehicle and three other unmarked law enforcement vehicles were gathered.
Agents asked him and his passenger for proof of legal immigration status, according to the account he gave her. He told them he had already provided his documents to the deputy.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents detain a man after he was stopped by a Teton County, Idaho, Sheriff’s Deputy earlier this month north of Victor. The man told his wife he was stopped by the deputy for a minor traffic violation, and ICE agents arrived 20 minutes later.
Her husband later told her the deputy said his documents checked out and he would receive no citation, but ICE wanted to speak with him. The deputy stepped back as federal agents approached his window, she said. According to her husband, the sheriff’s deputy was the only one to identify the federal agents.
From her vehicle, she watched and recorded officers taking her husband from the truck, telling him to turn around and arresting him.
She considered pulling over. But her daughter was with her, and she feared being detained, too.
“I left him,” she said. “I was kind of like just in a huge shock.”
He was already handcuffed when the passenger climbed across the cab, exited through the driver’s side and ran toward a nearby gym. Federal agents chased and tackled him, her husband told her.
DHS confirmed in a separate email from an unnamed spokesperson that the driver was arrested “during a call for assistance by the Teton County Sheriff’s Office.”
DHS said the driver had prior convictions for driving under the influence and an invalid driver’s license. According to court records, he had one citation in Idaho for driving without a license in 2015, a similar citation in Jackson in 2013 and a Jackson DUI case in 2013, for which he completed counseling while on probation, according to court records.
Teton County, Idaho, officials confirmed that ICE agents took people into custody at the Law Enforcement Center in Driggs last week as they reported for probation-related check-ins. While county officials stated that “probation staff did not detain, isolate, or hold individuals on behalf of federal authorities,” at least one detainee was instructed by a county probation officer to appear at the center for a drug test, according to the man’s wife.
BRADLY J. BONER / NEWS&GUIDE
Arriving for probation
On Oct. 13, a Driggs woman waited outside the Law Enforcement Center while her husband went inside for a randomized drug test around 6:35 a.m. as part of his requirements for probation.
She said in an interview through an interpreter that he was placed on probation following an incident in which police found him intoxicated in a parked vehicle earlier this year.
By 8 a.m., her husband had not returned. She said she noticed that others who had arrived for probation-related drug tests or check-ins had not exited the building, either. When she went inside, a probation officer handed her a business card with a phone number to call about his detention.
The probation officer told her he did not know why he’d been detained, she said.
But the county said ICE first contacted the probation office with a list of six people who had administrative immigration warrants and were on the court’s probation list.
Her husband later told her a probation officer had directed him and others to a back room of the Law Enforcement Center where three immigration agents were waiting. He had not signed in or completed his drug test, she said.
She did not witness those interactions. Her account of what happened inside before she entered comes from her husband, who told her five people in total were detained that morning.
The county confirmed that immigration agents took people into custody at the Law Enforcement Center on Oct. 13 and 15 as they reported for drug testing or check-ins, but distanced itself from implying cooperation.
“Probation staff did not detain, isolate, or hold individuals on behalf of federal authorities,” Siddoway said. “Federal agents initiated and executed the detentions of those individuals under federal authority.”
Officials said probation sentencing orders are publicly accessible through Idaho’s iCourt portal and that ICE determined its own operational timing. The public court portal, however, does not list days or times for random drug test events at the Law Enforcement Office.
Teton County said it has no written policy governing its probation department’s interactions with ICE.
Uncertain futures
Before his detention, the Driggs woman’s husband worked construction during the day and supervised a cleaning crew serving Jackson public schools in the afternoons, she said. For a decade, she said, he had held two jobs.
The tools belonging to a Victor man who was detained by ICE earlier this month sit on the porch of his family's home. The man worked as a carpenter in Teton Valley and in Jackson and volunteered as a referee for the local soccer club.
BRADLY J. BONER / NEWS&GUIDE
The family had moved from Jackson to Teton Valley because of housing costs. Now she faces rent and household bills without his income.
She said the family had a pending family-based immigration petition and hoped he could be released on bond while pursuing that process. If he is returned to Mexico, she said, she plans to move across the border, where she is from.
For the Victor mother, who has lived in the valley for 9 years with three children in public schools, preparations to leave have already begun.
Her husband worked construction, volunteered at their children’s schools and the food pantry, and stepped in to referee youth soccer games, she said.
“We felt like we were ... a part of the community,” she said.
Since his arrest, she said, their children have become frightened of police. Her older son asked to stay home rather than cry at school, she said.
She said her husband, who is currently being detained in El Paso, Texas, had signed paperwork agreeing to return to Mexico.
Now she is packing belongings, arranging passports and working with her remote employer to determine whether she can continue working from Mexico.
Friends and relatives have offered support and helped ensure the family has food and essentials. But she still fears being detained herself and leaving her children without either parent.
“I’m just so scared to be here,” she said.
Concerns about immigration enforcement prompted Wildwood event center operators to cancel an Oct. 10 concert from a Latino band after the band and the evening’s food vendor reported hearing about traffic stops involving ICE agents.
BRADLY J. BONER / NEWS&GUIDE
Canceling a concert
At Wildwood in Victor, concerns about immigration enforcement prompted venue operator Ian Boucher to cancel an Oct. 10 concert by a Latino band, “Sonideros de Noche,” after the band and the evening’s food vendor reported hearing about traffic stops involving federal agents. The band declined to comment for this story.
An earlier event weighed on Boucher’s decision. During an Aug. 14 show, he said, people were pulled over outside the venue amid reports of ICE activity. He did not know whether those individuals were detained.
“I really felt very kind of responsible or guilty for actually gathering people when that stuff was happening,” he said.
The cancellation affected the venue, the musicians and an effort to bring the valley together when Latin music is usually an hour’s drive away in Idaho Falls, he said.
“Obviously, it takes a lot to organize an event and get ready for an event, and then having to pull the plug not just affects us, but also ... the band who slated this time to come play and perform,” he said.
Boucher had begun seeing people who did not speak Spanish attending, too.
For Boucher, the concerns extended beyond economic disruption.
“Just the humanitarian aspect of that, and how upsetting it is to be targeting people to exclude them from the country,” he said.

text:
WASHINGTON — Two weeks from the midterm elections, Democratic Party leaders are suing in federal court to block President Donald Trump's administration from usurping states' authority to administer elections or trying to intimidate state and local election officials into complying with illegal demands.

The lawsuit, filed Tuesday in Washington, seeks a court order barring the administration from purging legally registered voters from statewide voter registration lists or denying ballots to legally registered voters.

The plaintiffs, including Sen. Chuck Schumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, also ask for a ruling that the administration has illegally threatened state election officials with prosecution before the Nov. 3 election.

The lawsuit cites the Justice Department’s recent actions in California, where it sued to block state election officials from counting mail-in ballots cast by people whom the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.

“For over a decade now, President Donald J. Trump has bombarded the American people with lies and misinformation about American elections and voter fraud," the suit says. "While these lies have been debunked at every turn, that has never deterred the President from employing them as a pretext to seize control over elections, even as courts overwhelmingly reject that effort.”

The Justice Department said in a statement that election integrity is a top priority for the administration and the department's actions on that front are grounded in law and under court litigation.

The Democratic leaders' lawsuit was assigned to Chief Judge James Boasberg, who has been vilified by the White House for rulings against the Trump administration since the start of the Republican president’s second term.

The suit's other plaintiffs are the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Governors Association. Its named defendants are Trump, the Justice Department, Attorney General Todd Blanche, the Department of Homeland Security and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

text:
Attorneys with Centro Legal de la Raza have secured the release of an Oakland man who was detained last week by agents from Immigration and Customs Enforcement, according to Nikolas De Bremaeker, the center’s managing attorney for immigrant rights. The man was detained by ICE agents the morning of Friday, Oct. 16, near San Antonio Park in East Oakland.

De Bremaeker told The Oaklandside that the man, whom he would not name over concerns that it could harm his case, reported being followed that day by an unmarked black SUV. When he parked near his home, several unmarked cars surrounded him. According to De Bremaeker, the agents did not show a valid warrant, and one of the agents broke the man’s car window with a hammer, then violently pulled him from the car through the broken window. Another agent, De Bremaeker said, used a baton to hit the man’s leg, “leaving him unable to walk.”

The agents took him to Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital and Trauma Center, De Bremaeker said.

In response to a query from The Oaklandside about the arrest near San Antonio Park, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson confirmed that an undocumented Mexican man was arrested during a targeted enforcement operation there last week. The agency said in a statement that the man had entered the United States in 2012 and was issued a final order of removal in February 2018.

In the statement, the department alleges that the man had a “criminal history” including “multiple arrests for driving under the influence of liquor, driving with a suspended license, and driving without an interlock device.”

In response to those allegations, De Bremaeker said the man has a “nonviolent vehicle infraction from over a decade ago and a related driving violation.”

The Department of Homeland Security did not directly respond to a query about the claim that ICE agents had hit the man with a baton and used excessive force to remove him from his vehicle.

“During his arrest, he repeatedly resisted ICE officers and disobeyed their lawful commands,” the statement read. “Officers relied on their training to control the situation and successfully arrest him.”

According to De Bremaeker, the man remained hospitalized until Tuesday, Oct. 20, when he was discharged. De Bremaeker said an attorney from Centro Legal’s legal team filed an emergency habeas corpus petition in federal court to challenge his detention and seek his release. That petition was granted on Oct. 20, De Bremaeker said, and the man was able to return home.

In the statement to The Oaklandside, the DHS spokesperson emphasized that the man’s removal order was granted by a “a Biden-appointed activist judge.”

When asked for his response to that remark, De Bremaeker said, “The government’s disparaging and insulting comments regarding the judiciary are extremely problematic and threaten our democracy.”

Centro Legal is one of the nonprofit organizations working with the Alameda County Immigration Legal and Education Partnership, known as ACILEP), a county program launched last year in response to the Trump Administration’s escalation of immigration enforcement. ACILEP, where De Bremaeker serves as the managing attorney, connects people with legal aid and helps verify reported ICE sightings in cities across the county.

The two arrests last week coincide with the Trump Administration’s launch of “Operation Safe California,” a 45-day ICE operation across the state to arrest immigrants without legal status.

De Bremaeker told The Oaklandside that this arrest is not the first time ICE agents have used excessive force in the Bay Area.

“This is now the fifth violent ICE incident in the past week here in the Bay Area, and that’s definitely unprecedented,” De Bremaeker said.

One of the incidents took place in San Francisco, he said, and one involved a Honduran man, being represented by Centro Legal, who was arrested last Friday in Emeryville.

De Bremaeker told The Oaklandside that the man arrested in Emeryville remains hospitalized at Highland Hospital. He said Centro Legal’s legal team also filed an emergency habeas corpus petition in his case, but that it is more complex and the petition has not yet been granted.

description:
The Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon, asking the justices to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas.
Trump sought to resume construction efforts when he returned to office in 2025.
In 2026, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her successor, Markwayne Mullin, issued three waivers of various environmental and conservation laws to allow construction of the border wall in the Big Bend region, including areas in Big Bend National Park.
This region comprises almost one-fourth of the U.S.-Mexico border.
The Trump administration came to the Supreme Court on Wednesday, asking the justices to pause the district court’s order and to grant review and summarily reverse it.
text:
The Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon, asking the justices to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer called the order by a federal trial judge in El Paso temporarily halting the construction “baseless” and “unprecedented.”

During President Donald Trump’s first campaign and his first term in office, his efforts to build a wall along the U.S. border with Mexico were a central part of his immigration agenda. President Joe Biden largely stopped construction when he took office in 2021.

Under the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, the Secretary of Homeland Security has the power to “waive all legal requirements” necessary “to ensure expeditious construction” of border walls and roads. Moreover, federal courts can only hear challenges to such waiver decisions if they allege a violation of the Constitution.

Trump sought to resume construction efforts when he returned to office in 2025. In 2026, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her successor, Markwayne Mullin, issued three waivers of various environmental and conservation laws to allow construction of the border wall in the Big Bend region, including areas in Big Bend National Park. This region comprises almost one-fourth of the U.S.-Mexico border. Noem and Mullin determined that additional border barriers are required in the Big Bend area because it “is an area of high illegal entry”: Sauer states that, in the four-year span between 2021 and 2025, U.S. Customs and Border Protection apprehended more than 89,000 immigrants there who were attempting to illegally enter the United States.

An environmental group, a local landowner, and a group formed to preserve a church went to federal court, challenging the legality of the waivers. On Oct. 2, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone temporarily barred the Department of Homeland Security from continuing construction on the border wall in the Big Bend region “until and unless” the government complies with environmental and other applicable laws.

Cardone issued a written opinion detailing her reasoning on Oct. 14. She explained that the challengers were likely to prevail on their claim that, under the major questions doctrine (which is the idea that if Congress intends to give a federal agency the power to make decisions of vast economic or political significance, it must say so explicitly), the DHS secretary did not have the power to issue the waivers. First, she rejected the government’s suggestion that she did not have the authority to consider the challengers’ claims because they involved a statute, rather than the Constitution. The major questions doctrine, she said, is a “constitutional … rule” based on the idea that “courts should expect Congress to speak clearly when it delegates major lawmaking authority to the executive.” Because Congress had only given the DHS secretary the power to waive the otherwise applicable legal requirements “to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry into the United States,” she wrote, and “the evidence shows that the Big Bend Sector has the lowest rate of illegal entry along the entire U.S.-Mexico border,” Congress could not have given clear authorization for the Big Bend waivers.

The Trump administration came to the Supreme Court on Wednesday, asking the justices to pause the district court’s order and to grant review and summarily reverse it. First, Sauer argued, the district court did not have the power to consider the challengers’ claim based on the major questions doctrine because that claim in their complaint alleged that the DHS secretary “lacked ‘clear congressional authorization’ … to issue the waivers” under the IIRIRA. “As this Court has long held,” Sauer continued, “a claim that alleges that an Executive Branch official acted ‘in excess of his statutory authority’ is not a claim alleging a ‘violation of the Constitution,’” and Congress specified in the IIRIRA that waivers are only subject to constitutional challenges.

But, Sauer wrote, “[e]ven assuming that the Secretary’s waiver authority implicates a question of ‘vast economic and political significance,’ Congress did clearly authorize the Secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction.”

text:
This article was also published in REDESCover, DDIA’s weekly newsletter. Click here to subscribeand get the next edition delivered straight to your inbox.

Rep. María Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.), who is seeking reelection, captured the attention of Latino online audiences this week with a striking prediction thatPresident Donald Trump would support her signature immigration reform bill, despite his administration’s aggressive deportation agenda.

Salazar introduced the Dignity Act in July 2025, proposing to combine tougher border security and immigration enforcement with legal protections for certain undocumented immigrants. The legislation would establish a seven-year, renewable program allowing eligible immigrants to remain in the United States if they meet employment or education requirements and satisfy other conditions. It would also create pathways to permanent residency for certain groups, including DACA recipients, and require employers nationwide to electronically verify workers’ eligibility.

More than a year later, however, the bill remains stalled in Congress, without broad legislative support or a public endorsement from Trump. Yet, just over a month after openly criticizing the president’s immigration policies, Salazar revived the proposal with a new message that together with Trump, when reelected, she could be the one to deliver immigration reform.

"Si alguien lo puede hacer es Trump" ("If anyone can do it, it's Trump"), Salazar declared last Thursday (Oct. 15) after a campaign event in Miami.

The remarks quickly gained traction across Spanish-language media. El Nuevo Herald, Univision, Diario Las Américas, and EFE covered her statements, helping the conversation extend beyond the United States.

Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado publicly endorsed Salazar's reelection, praising her defense of human rights and democracy. Colombian president Abelardo de la Espriella also backed the congresswoman, calling her "la mejor amiga de Colombia en el Congreso de los Estados Unidos" ("Colombia's best friend in the U.S. Congress").

Those endorsements also added to Salazar's visibility within South Florida's politically influential Cuban, Venezuelan and Colombian diasporas. Conservative online commentators, including Cuban influencer Alex Otaola, amplified the international support from Corina and De La Espriella for her campaign, extending even further the conversation across Spanish-language social media. Venezuelan Emmanuel Rincón did the same.

But posts and about 50 comments reviewed by DDIA show that visibility did not necessarily translate into support.

Left-leaning influencer Carlos Eduardo Espina, for example, shared a clip of Salazar's remarks with a skeptical caption: "María Elvira Salazar dice que Trump es un hombre sabio que dará una reforma migratoria" ("María Elvira Salazar says Trump is a wise man who will deliver immigration reform").

His posts generated more than 6,700 interactions on TikTok and 5,100 on Instagram in three days, according to data collected through NewsWhip. The comments left by Latinos on his publications were mostly skeptical, with users questioning how a president overseeing deportations could suddenly become a champion of legal protections for undocumented immigrants as Salazar suggested. “Palabras al aire”, wrote one of them.

In other less viral publications about the topic, other Latino social media users noticed that the Republican congresswoman was not announcing an agreement with the White House and that the administration has not said anything new to support her project. Spanish-speakers in different posts made online highlighted that Salazar was just expressing confidence that Trump would eventually support her proposal if she got reelected. This meant turning an unconfirmed political prediction into a campaign message – and Latinos noticed it.

title: Children in San Antonio face immigration court alone as faster deportations loom | TPR
description:
When Allison brought her six-year-old niece, Frida, to immigration court in San Antonio, she was hoping the family could get more time to find a lawyer.
According to an Oct. 15 analysis by the Vera Institute of Justice, 55% of unaccompanied children's immigration court cases completed so far in 2026 had never had an attorney of record.

text:
Sign up for TPR Today, Texas Public Radio's newsletter that brings our top stories to your inbox each morning.

When Allison brought her six-year-old niece, Frida, to immigration court in San Antonio, she was hoping the family could get more time to find a lawyer.

Frida's attorney had withdrawn from the case, leaving the family facing a consequential court hearing without the legal help they had counted on.

For Allison, the stakes were deeply personal. She said the family was frightened about what the court might decide and what it could mean for the young girl’s future.

“Today is the day that they tell us everything, and we're a little scared because this is her life, and we don't want her in danger,” Allison said. “So, we're basically asking the court if we can have more time because her lawyer bailed on her. But this is the fight right now.”

Frida's case comes as immigration courts are handling growing numbers of proceedings involving children without legal representation. Immigration rights advocates say the loss of federally funded legal services, combined with an increasingly fast-paced court system, is leaving vulnerable children and their families with fewer resources to understand their rights and fight deportation.

The challenges extend beyond San Antonio. But local court data illustrates the scale of the issue facing children in the region.

An analysis of immigration court records by data researchers at bklg.org, a service that helps immigration lawyers organize their deportation defense cases, found that, as of Aug. 31, 183 unaccompanied children in the custody of the federal Office of Refugee Resettlement had open immigration court cases assigned to San Antonio.

Nationwide, 1,523 children in federal shelter custody had open cases.

Those figures represent children in federal custody with pending cases assigned to the courts. They do not include every child with an open immigration case in San Antonio.

Children face court without legal representation

The federal government allowed a contract supporting a network of community-based legal service providers for unaccompanied immigrant children to expire July 31.

Advocates say more than 20,000 children lost access to federally funded legal representation, legal orientations and legal screenings as a result.

The legal service providers helped children understand the immigration process, learn about potential forms of legal relief and prepare for proceedings that could determine whether they would be allowed to remain in the United States. The loss of those services comes as more children face immigration courts without an attorney.

According to an Oct. 15 analysis by the Vera Institute of Justice, 55% of unaccompanied children's immigration court cases completed so far in 2026 had never had an attorney of record. That is up from 48% in 2025 and 38% in 2024.

The Vera Institute also found that 84% of unaccompanied children's cases completed in August resulted in outcomes requiring them to leave the United States. That compares with 54% in August 2025 and 33% in August 2024.

Lauren Fisher Flores, legal director of the American Bar Association's South Texas Pro Bono Asylum Representation Project, said children in South Texas are encountering the consequences of these changes firsthand.

She described a recent case in Harlingen involving a child who appeared without an attorney.

“We were there as a 7-year-old appeared alone before an immigration judge in Harlingen, Texas. No attorney, no friend of court. The judge ordered her to leave the United States within 30 days,” Fisher Flores said.

Fisher Flores said the way children's hearings are being conducted adds another layer of difficulty.

“All children's hearings in our area are being held by Webex with judges from all over the country. It's confusing. It's chaotic. For a child appearing without counsel makes what is already extremely difficult to understand even harder,” she said.

The hearings take place remotely, with judges appearing by video rather than being physically present in the courtroom where a child appears. For a young person navigating an unfamiliar legal system, often in a language they are still learning, that arrangement can make an already complicated process more difficult to follow.

Families struggle to afford legal help

For Frida's family, losing an attorney has also meant added financial pressure.

Allison said Frida's mother has been working long hours to cover the costs of navigating the immigration system, leaving her with less time to spend with her daughter.

“Her mother's been paying out of pocket. I know she's been working like every day. Basically, she doesn't even see her daughter that much because she has to work all this time only to pay the fees for the court, fees for the lawyers, lawyers who just bailed on cases,” Allison said.

The federal contract expiration has left families and advocates scrambling to find other sources of legal assistance.

Immigration proceedings can involve complex questions about asylum, eligibility for other forms of relief and the consequences of agreeing to leave the country. Advocates say children should have access to qualified legal help before being asked to make decisions that could affect their ability to remain in the United States.

The federal government has not provided legal representation to every unaccompanied child in immigration proceedings. But advocates say the recently disrupted network offered an important source of assistance to children who otherwise might have had nowhere to turn.

A broader push to accelerate immigration court proceedings

The cases involving children are unfolding amid a broader effort to move immigration cases through the court system more quickly.

Beginning in May 2026, immigration courts around the country began scheduling large blocks of initial hearings known as “mega master” calendar hearings. The practice expanded to additional cities in late May and early June, including San Antonio.

A master calendar hearing is an initial stage of immigration court proceedings. It typically addresses procedural matters, including the charges against an immigrant, the forms of relief they may seek and the scheduling of future hearings.

Under the "mega master" approach, courts schedule dozens and sometimes more than 100 people to appear during the same session. In some cases, hearings previously scheduled months or years into the future have been moved up with relatively little notice.

The administration's broader effort is intended to accelerate immigration court proceedings and address a backlog of millions of cases. But immigration attorneys and advocates have raised concerns about whether people have enough time to prepare, secure legal representation and understand what is happening in court.

People who fail to appear can be ordered removed from the United States in the absence of an attorney. Researchers tracking the hearings have documented a sharp increase in these orders.

Advocates question the role of the federal agency responsible for children

The loss of legal services has also raised questions about the federal government's treatment of unaccompanied children.

The Office of Refugee Resettlement, part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, is responsible for the care and custody of unaccompanied children transferred to its custody. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, part of the Department of Homeland Security, is responsible for immigration enforcement.

Jason Boyd, vice president of U.S. federal policy at the nonprofit Kids in Need of Defense, said he believes the distinction between the agencies' roles is becoming increasingly blurred.

“ORR is facilitating ICE's mass deportation agenda rather than acting in the best interests of the children whose care and custody Congress vested them with,” Boyd said.

Boyd and other advocates argue that children who arrive in the United States without a parent or legal guardian need specialized protections as they navigate the immigration system.

An uncertain future

Policy debates and national statistics underscore concerns raised by immigration attorneys in South Texas. Children can find themselves in court without the legal assistance needed to understand the proceedings, while their families struggle to pay for private representation.

For advocates, restoring access to legal services is a critical step toward ensuring that children understand their rights before a judge decides whether they can remain in the country.

For Allison and Frida’s family, and for thousands of families throughout the country who find themselves in similar situations, the question is more immediate: Will they have enough time and help to make their case?

Editor's note: This story uses Allison and Frida's first names only to respect their privacy.

text:
The Justice Department is seeking to disqualify two Minnesota federal judges from a pair of immigration-related cases. The move comes on the heels of ethics complaints the DOJ filed against Judges Patrick Schiltz, John Tunheim and five of their colleagues after they spoke to the New York Times for a Sept. 17 story about the Trump Administration’s wintertime immigration operation and its effect on the federal courts.

In one of the cases, which is assigned to Schiltz, the government is seeking to revoke the citizenship of Salah Osman Ahmed, a Somali American man who pleaded guilty to a terrorism charge in 2009 and received a three-year prison sentence.

In the other case, over which Tunheim is presiding, prosecutors allege that Hester Sophia Weihmann, a legal permanent U.S. resident from South Africa, voted illegally in the 2024 election. Weihmann is among at least 11 people charged in Minnesota with voting as a non-citizen.

In separate motions, Associate U.S. Attorney General Stanley Woodard Jr. argues neither judge can be impartial because they’re quoted in a story Woodard characterizes as a “partisan critique of the Trump Administration’s immigration enforcement operation in Minneapolis.”

Tunheim told the newspaper immigration agents were not “arresting, in my view, people who were dangerous criminals on the street.”

Schiltz, who was Minnesota’s chief federal judge during Metro Surge, is quoted more extensively. He said ICE’s violation of hundreds of court orders threatened the rule of law.

“If you don’t have it, you have either anarchy or you have authoritarianism. You have Russia or you have China or you have North Korea,” Schiltz told the New York Times.

In a Sept. 30 statement to MPR News, Schiltz said that he was acting “well within the ethical rules that apply to federal judges in speaking to the New York Times. Indeed, in February of this year, the Committee on Codes of Conduct issued an advisory opinion to emphasize that federal judges may 'speak[] and writ[e] on core judiciary matters such as advocacy for the rule of law and judicial independence.’ That is exactly what I did."

Later that day, a court spokesperson sent a similar statement on behalf of Minnesota’s federal bench.

In an email Tuesday, Schiltz told MPR News that he is unable to comment on the status of the ethics complaint because the proceedings at the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals are confidential.

However, Schiltz is continuing to speak out about threats to the rule of law during Operation Metro Surge.

Two days after the DOJ filed the ethics complaint, he appeared at a University of St. Thomas School of Law symposium on Metro Surge and repeated many of the same things he told the Times.

Schiltz told the gathering he was unable to set aside work because he had to make time-sensitive decisions on many of the hundreds of lawsuits that ICE detainees had filed challenging their detention.

“The difference between me going to a movie and turning my phone off for two hours and me checking my phone regularly either at the movie — that makes you popular in the theater — or not going to the movie, could literally be someone being sent to New Mexico or someone being sent to Texas.

The DOJ cited Schiltz’s comments from the symposium in its recusal motion.

Schiltz and Tunheim will decide on the motions themselves, St. Thomas law professor Greg Sisk said in an interview with MPR News on Wednesday. If the judges don’t recuse themselves, the Justice Department could ask other district judges to rule.

Beyond that, Sisk said, the law makes it difficult to get an appeals court to force the judges off the cases.

“I would imagine that they’re doing it in large part to send a message to every other federal judge,” Sisk said. “If you make public statements about the rule of law in a manner that’s critical of this administration’s Department of Justice, then we will be filing similar motions to recuse against you and questioning your impartiality as well.”

Minneapolis attorney Daniel Gerdts, who represents Ahmed in the denaturalization case, said in an email to MPR News on Wednesday that he has occasionally disagreed with Schiltz’s decisions but has never questioned his impartiality. Gerdts called the Justice Department’s arguments for recusal “contrived and baseless.”

“And who precisely do they think would be a better choice for them on such a weak case? Judge Schiltz is the epitome of a principled, call-it-like-he-sees-it judge who knows the rules of evidence and applies them equally to both sides,” Gerdts said.

text:
23

PHILADELPHIA (OSV News) — Haitian Catholics in Philadelphia are marking a half century of faith and fellowship, amid Trump administration crackdowns on immigration, uncertainty about current deportation protections and ongoing gang violence in Haiti.

“It’s 50 years of determination, 50 years of challenge, 50 years of faith,” said Father Eugène Almonor, an Oblate of Mary Immaculate and chaplain of the Archdiocese of Philadelphia’s Haitian Catholic Community.

Father Almonor spoke with OSV News ahead of an Oct. 17 Mass honoring the community’s golden anniversary at St. William Parish in Northeast Philadelphia, home to one of two “branches” — north and west — of the archdiocese’s Haitian Catholics.

Devotion to Our Lady of Perpetual Help

The liturgy, which drew a congregation of some 350 and several concelebrants, took place on the death date of Jean-Jacques Dessalines, one of the key leaders of the Haitian Revolution (1791-1804) and that nation’s first emperor.

During the Mass — with its prayers in French, Haitian Creole and English — an image of Our Lady of Perpetual Help, named patroness of Haiti by Pope Pius XII in 1942, was displayed before the altar.

The Marian devotion holds profound significance for Haitians, who credit Mary’s intercession with the abatement of an 1882 smallpox epidemic. Her protection was also invoked by Pope Benedict XVI following a 2010 earthquake that devastated Haiti. The devotion’s June 27 feast day is prominently celebrated throughout Haiti and among the Haitian diaspora.

The Mass included a liturgical dance honoring Mary’s Magnificat — her song of praise found in Lk 1:46-55 — as well as a post-Communion presentation at her altar of a candle marked “50,” with the flame transferred from similar candles borne by community elders to the youth.

From a home to a community

In its welcome message for the Mass, which was printed in the liturgy’s worship aid, the Philadelphia Haitian Catholic community said the celebration “must awaken” a “sense of fraternal duty” among Haitians living in the U.S.

“We find ourselves in the midst of struggle with ourselves and confronted by an enemy determined to prevail at any cost, disregarding the most basic principles and seeking to strip us of our humanity,” said the committee, urging faith, fraternity and trust in Mary’s intercession.

“We cannot just stay in the dark,” Marie Vidala Moise, a key lay leader in the Philadelphia Haitian Catholic community, told OSV News.

Echoing Father Almonor, she recounted how the community began in 1976 — the same year as the U.S. bicentennial — at a West Philadelphia home owned by a Haitian family surnamed Cantave, with Haitian Catholics gathering for prayer, faith sharing and a sense of family.

Started with idea for prayer group at someone’s house

“We started with a couple of people who talked about having a prayer group at somebody’s house,” said Moise.

“The Catholic faith of Haiti found a home in the Archdiocese of Philadelphia through the charity and love of one Haitian family,” said Sister Gertrude Borres, a member of the Religious of the Assumption and director of the Archdiocese of Philadelphia’s Office for Pastoral Care for Migrants and Refugees.

The growing community was recognized by the Archdiocese of Philadelphia and in 1977 was first housed at the former Most Blessed Sacrament Parish, where it remained until 1986.

Over the years, Philadelphia’s Haitian Catholics have called several parishes home, with the community now based at St. William Parish and St. Barbara Parish, both in Philadelphia and forming, respectively, the “north” and “west” branches owing to their locations in the city.

But, said Father Almonor, the two branches form “one community,” with Haitian Catholics from both joining for various celebrations throughout the year in addition to their regular Sunday Masses at the two churches.

Faith in the face of deportation fears

Now, that faith and unity have become even more critical as the Trump administration seeks to expel hundreds of thousands of Haitians living in the U.S. under Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, as part of a mass deportation and immigration restriction campaign.

Created by Congress as part of the Immigration Act of 1990, TPS provides deportation protections for those from Homeland Security-designated countries experiencing ongoing crises, such as war and environmental disasters.

More than 330,000 Haitians had TPS protection as of 2025 due to Haiti’s multiyear polycrises of gang-driven conflict, political instability, natural disasters and disease.

While the Trump administration granted TPS extensions Oct. 18 for nationals from Ukraine and Sudan, Haitian TPS beneficiaries now face deportation following a Supreme Court decision allowing the end of the designation for Haiti as well as Syria.

Grave warnings from immigration advocates

Those expulsions come despite grave warnings from immigration advocates and Catholic leaders — including Archbishop Thomas G. Wenski of Miami, whose archdiocese is home to an extensive Haitian community — about the dire conditions in Haiti.

The U.S. Department of State has issued a level 4 “do not travel” advisory regarding Haiti, urging U.S. citizens not to travel there “for any reason” due to “crime, terrorism, kidnapping, unrest, and limited health care.”

Previously, Father Almonor — now a U.S. citizen who serves at St. William Parish — told OSV News that asking someone “to return to Haiti is exposing your life” to danger.

He himself has been unable to travel to visit family in Haiti for some time.

Speaking to OSV News Oct. 16, Father Almonor said the Haitian Catholics he serves “continue to come to Mass,” but “continue to be vigilant.”

“It is so difficult for the families here,” he said. “Many of them have no job.”

The community works to ensure its members have food, he said, adding, “We try to accompany them, support them.”

Youth as the new leaders

At such a moment, both the legacy of the community’s elders and the promise of Haitian Catholic youth are equally essential, said concelebrant and homilist Msgr. Pierre André Pierre, parochial vicar at St. Clare and St. Pius X churches in Rosedale, New York.

“We are here today because of the sacrifices our ancestors have made through the years,” he said, addressing the youth in attendance. “But I must tell you, this is still the beginning of the journey.”

He urged the youth to draw on God’s grace and “make your people raise their heads, and make yourself a child of God, serving God’s will everywhere.”

“The 50 years does not stop here,” said Moise, who reflected on the long tradition of her family’s Catholic faith. “The young people have to take over.”

And, said Msgr. Pierre, they will not be alone in that task.

“We know the power of God,” he said in his homily. “Things can change. Even war can be turned into peace. Even enmity can be turned into fraternity.”

title: State sheriffs divided over ICE immigration policies - Wisconsin Law Journal
description:

Survey shows variety of policies among Wisconsin sheriffs Of the 68 sheriffs who shared their immigration enforcement policies or responded to survey questions: The majority said they do not honor immigration detainers, although some departments had inconsistent answers.
Although most sheriffs added immigration enforcement policies since last year, many remain without one.

Some Wisconsin sheriffs have no written immigration policies A few Wisconsin sheriffs say they have no formal immigration policy and don’t care to make one.
text:
In northern Wisconsin’s Rusk County, known for its winding trails through the forested Blue Hills, Sheriff Phillip Grassmann’s deputies are no longer supposed to notify U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement when booking immigrants into jail.

Close to the Illinois border, Walworth County Sheriff Dave Gerber signed onto a formal partnership with ICE to hold undocumented immigrants in jail past their release date, though he says that’s how they’ve always operated.

And in Milwaukee County, Sheriff Denita Ball has added to her office’s immigration policy to make it explicit that deputies will not detain people for ICE unless agents produce a warrant signed by a judge.

These three agencies are among many Wisconsin sheriff’s offices that updated or created immigration policies within the last year.

For the second year in a row, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel and Green Bay Press-Gazette surveyed all 72 Wisconsin sheriffs about their cooperation with ICE.

The results show that many sheriff’s departments have tightened their rules for working with federal immigration authorities since the start of President Donald Trump’s crackdown in January 2025.

Most did so when they adopted a standard immigration policy created in 2020 by Lexipol, a Texas company that designs policies for law enforcement agencies across the country.

However, others have gone in the opposite direction. Since the start of last year, the number of Wisconsin sheriffs that have signed formal agreements with ICE has nearly tripled, bringing the total number now to 20.

Many sheriffs’ departments said the agreements merely codify longstanding practices.

“Nothing the Sheriff’s Office is doing has changed in over 20 years,” Outagamie County Sheriff’s Office Capt. Nathan Borman said in an email. “Immigration enforcement is not part of our daily duties, nor do we want it to be.”

However, it is likely that Wisconsin sheriffs will be asked to play a bigger role in the Trump administration’s next chapter of immigration enforcement.

In his March confirmation hearing, new U.S. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told Congress he would like to see ICE be more of “a transport” from local jails, rather than “the front line” of enforcement.

That would be a shift from the far more public, forceful approach ICE took in its operations in Chicago, Minneapolis and other cities.

In a statement to the Journal Sentinel, ICE echoed the importance of local law enforcement cooperation.

“ICE has supercharged efforts with state and local law enforcement to assist federal immigration officers in our efforts to make America safe again,” a spokesperson said.

Survey shows variety of policies among Wisconsin sheriffs

Of the 68 sheriffs who shared their immigration enforcement policies or responded to survey questions:

The majority said they do not honor immigration detainers, although some departments had inconsistent answers. Detainers are requests from ICE for sheriffs to hold people in jail past their release dates so immigration officers can pick them up.

At least 14 departments signed formal agreements with ICE since the start of last year. One-third of Wisconsin sheriffs now have some kind of contract with ICE.

Six counties permitted deputies to detain people they have “reasonable suspicion” of entering the country illegally. That same policy language prompted a federal lawsuit over racial profiling in Washington state eight years ago.

On the other hand, Milwaukee and Adams counties added language in their policies prohibiting deputies from detaining anyone unless ICE produces a warrant signed by a judge.

Generally, policies and responses varied. Although most sheriffs added immigration enforcement policies since last year, many remain without one. Other sheriffs never responded to the survey.

In addition, policy and practice frequently seemed to clash. Many sheriffs gave answers that conflicted. For example, eight counties that signed formal agreements with ICE to honor detainers either said in the survey or in their written policies that they would not.

On the question of whether they would alert ICE about encountering undocumented immigrants when arresting or booking them into jail, multiple sheriffs said that decision is out of their hands. Once an individual is fingerprinted, that person’s information is automatically uploaded to a national database that is accessible by ICE and other federal agencies, they said.

“What they choose to do from there is up to them,” Dane County Sheriff’s Department spokesperson Elise Shaffer said.

Four sheriffs with policies that say deputies “generally” should not notify ICE about undocumented people they encounter still said in the survey that they would alert ICE in certain instances.

Even if a law enforcement agency has a policy saying that contacting them will not automatically lead to an immigration inquiry, Milwaukee-based immigration attorney Gabriela Parra said she can’t promise her clients that the agency won’t share their information.

According to Parra, Trump’s crackdown has created a rift between immigrants and local law enforcement, which has tried to encourage immigrants to report crimes and cooperate in investigations.

“Unfortunately, that’s really being jeopardized,” Parra said. “I’ve seen a shift among my clients.”

Wisconsin sheriffs face legal scrutiny over ICE detainers

One of the most common ways that ICE asks for local law enforcement cooperation is by asking local jails to hold people until immigration officers can pick them up – also known as a detainer request.

The use of detainers has risen sharply in recent years. In 2025, ICE made 579 arrests using detainers in Wisconsin, according to figures from the Deportation Data Project, compared to just 49 in 2022.

However, the legality of detainers has long been a point of contention.

Forty-eight sheriffs told the Journal Sentinel they do not honor ICE detainers, including those in Milwaukee and Dane counties. Another seven gave conflicting answers.

Many of these departments are using a default policy created by the private company Lexipol. Their policy states that deputies should not honor ICE detainers for civil immigration violations. The company made that change in 2020 in response to scrutiny and litigation around detainers.

The sheriffs of both Jefferson and Grant counties also said they were advised not to honor detainers by legal counsel.

The issue is now in federal court. The ACLU of Wisconsin is suing five local sheriffs on behalf of the immigrant advocacy group Voces de la Frontera, arguing that detainers are illegal because state law prohibits deputies from making civil immigration arrests.

“You can’t just sign a contract and suddenly get the right to make an arrest that the Wisconsin Legislature has never given you that right to before,” said ACLU of Wisconsin senior staff attorney Timothy Muth.

The five counties involved — Brown, Kenosha, Sauk, Walworth and Marathon — all signed formal agreements with ICE promising to honor detainers. None responded to requests for comment.

Muth said holding people past their release date denies them their civil liberties. Unlike those in prison, most people in jail have not been convicted of crimes.

“It’s two days being held in a jail cell,” Muth said. “It is two days of being separated from your family, two days of not being able to return to a job.”

He said ICE is arresting more people directly from local jails because it is focusing more on people who are still awaiting trial or serving sentences for minor offenses, rather than those convicted of serious crimes.

In court filings, U.S. Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate has argued that immigration detainers are legitimate under federal law and that ignoring them endangers Wisconsin residents.

“Crucial law-enforcement, public-safety, and rule-of-law interests will be undermined by the relief that Petitioner seeks,” Shumate wrote.

Sheriffs who joined formal ICE agreements say little will change

Even though most sheriffs are backing away from detainers, many others are signing formal agreements to welcome them.

Fourteen Wisconsin sheriffs have signed onto a program, commonly referred to as 287(g), that gives their deputies the power to perform certain functions on behalf of ICE. Of the 20 sheriffs with such agreements, the vast majority signed up for the version that authorizes jail staff to execute detainers.

Several sheriffs said signing on was a formality.

“We have been honoring ICE detainers back through multiple presidents,” Washington County Sheriff Martin Schulteis said in a statement. “[The agreement] gives us the legal authority to honor ICE detainers while simultaneously protecting taxpayers from any potential liability.”

Others, like Dunn County Sheriff Kevin Bygd, said they joined to stay in the federal government’s good books.

Bygd cited the example of former Milwaukee County Circuit Judge Hannah Dugan, who was convicted on felony obstruction charges last year for steering an undocumented defendant away from immigration agents.

“The flip side to not honoring an ICE detainer, my staff could be charged obstructing federal law enforcement,” Bygd said. “We run a risk of not being eligible for federal funding and grants when they come along.”

Although agencies get reimbursed for the training costs of a 287(g) agreement, Bygd said the money is not enough to cover the expenses needed to enforce it.

Nationwide, 94% of local law enforcement agencies with 287(g) agreements signed up during Trump’s second term.

In addition, since the start of Trump’s second term, at least six sheriff’s departments have joined a program to have the federal government reimburse the cost of incarcerating certain undocumented immigrants in their jails. The program is known as the State Criminal Alien Assistance Program.

Some Wisconsin sheriffs have no written immigration policies

A few Wisconsin sheriffs say they have no formal immigration policy and don’t care to make one.

Sawyer County Sheriff Doug Mrotek said he always checks the immigration status of anyone his deputies arrest, always reports undocumented immigrants to ICE, and will work with the agency when asked. His department has no written immigration policy.

“We’re not dealing with it any more or less than we have for years,” Mrotek said. “I think the media has made more of an issue and surfaced to the public.”

Muth, of the ACLU, said more attention should be paid to sheriff’s departments that cooperate with ICE without formal agreements or policies.

“That’s a harmful practice, but it is hard to track down and isolate,” he said.

In Price County, home to the state’s smallest jail, Sheriff Brian Schmidt said he doesn’t have many policies because he trusts the officers he hires will use proper judgment. In a county of just 14,000 residents, immigration issues don’t come up much, Schmidt said.

Even so, on that very day in February, Schmidt said he was holding someone in his jail on an ICE detainer related to a warrant out of Minnesota. He said he also once alerted ICE about a man from Ukraine in his jail who appeared to be in the country illegally.

Schmidt described other examples of pulling over people from Mexico, South Africa and Nicaragua. In all three instances, he said he let the drivers go without checking their immigration status.

His department has no written immigration enforcement policy. Schmidt said he treats people the same regardless of their citizenship.

“Am I going to contact ICE?” Schmidt asked. “I may, I may not.”

text:
Kennedy Questions ICE Officials and Witnesses State of the Facility and its Detainees Firsthand

BUFFALO, N.Y. - After receiving written confirmation from Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin that ICE is proceeding with a nearly $17 million expansion at their Batavia facility, Congressman Tim Kennedy (NY-26) made an unannounced visit to the Service Processing Center to witness firsthand the wellbeing of detainees, conditions of the facility, and to inspect the expansion. DHS held 653 individuals at Batavia as of July 2026 and has begun construction to create a new detention facility for women. DHS noted that, depending on the need, men may be housed in the new facility as well. More than 70% of the detainees at Batavia have no criminal history.

However, several questions about the expansion, medical care, and the treatment of detainees remained unanswered. Following his visit, Congressman Kennedy, a member of the House Committee on Homeland Security, sent a letter to DHS seeking additional information about the planned expansion, the availability of adequate medical care, the number and circumstances of individuals being detained, and policies impeding access to legal representation. The letter calls for greater transparency and accountability as DHS moves forward with its plans for the facility.

“Conducting oversight of federal agencies is one of my fundamental responsibilities in Congress, and I will not allow a nearly $17 million expansion of a federal detention facility to move forward without demanding answers. I went to Batavia to see the conditions firsthand, ask questions, and get clear answers about the planned expansion, medical care, and the treatment of detainees. When questions about medical care, the treatment of detainees, and access to legal representation remain, DHS has a responsibility to provide clear answers,” said Congressman Kennedy. “I will continue pressing for transparency and accountability to ensure taxpayer dollars are being spent responsibly and the basic needs of those in federal custody are being met.”

Pursuant to Section 527 of the FY2024 DHS Appropriations Act, DHS is legally obligated to allow Members of Congress to inspect detainee facilities without prior notice. This law has been upheld in federal court in the case of Neguse et al v. U.S. ICE et al.

text:
KUT has obtained an audio recording from the ICE traffic stop and car chase that preceded the shooting of Wilber Garces Perez, the Venezuelan DoorDash driver who was shot by an ICE agent in North Austin last month.

The audio comes from the body camera of an ICE agent that the government has identified as “D.F.” He is one of two ICE agents involved in the initial encounter with Garces Perez. The other one, who ultimately shot Garces Perez, is “L.G.”

Federal prosecutors say Garces Perez hit L.G. with his car, and that the alleged assault was captured on D.F.’s body camera. They submitted video footage of the incident as evidence in a criminal case against Garces Perez, and the Department of Homeland Security has pointed to that evidence as justification for his shooting.

The video is sealed from public view. But prosecutors displayed it during a criminal court hearing for Garces Perez on Sept. 30. Court staff also made an audio-recording of the entire hearing, which KUT later requested and obtained.

A federal grand jury formally indicted Garces Perez on assault charges yesterday. He remains in federal custody while the charges are pending.

Below, you can listen to some key moments in the tape along with a description of the body camera footage that KUT reporters watched in court.

Here’s what happened before the video started

At the hearing in which the body camera video was shown, the court heard testimony from Department of Homeland Security Special Agent Rick Bazan.

Bazan was not present for the traffic stop or the chase, but he investigated the incident later and filed the criminal complaint against Garces Perez.

In his testimony, Bazan described the morning leading up to the shooting as a typical one for L.G. and D.F..

“They were doing immigration enforcement on that day, doing random checks on vehicles and at random places,” he said. “They're out there everywhere, you know, running license plates.”

Bazan testified that agents ran the license plate of Garces Perez’s blue Toyota Corolla while he was in a restaurant and determined he had a deportation order against him.

Bazan said the agents decided to pull Garces Perez over rather than detain him at the restaurant because it would be “safer.”

The body camera footage played in court begins at that traffic stop.

Despite earlier statements from one of Garces Perez’s attorneys that he did not know he was being pursued by ICE, the recording captures an exchange between him and the two ICE agents that lasts a little over a minute.

Agent L.G., who Bazan said was not wearing a body camera, can be seen standing at the driver’s side window next to Garces Perez’s car. He is armed and dressed in a bullet proof vest and ski mask.

D.F. is not shown in the video, since the footage is coming from his body camera. He appears to be standing behind Garces Perez’s car.

One of the agents asks Garces Perez, “can you roll down the window, bro?” The conversation then continues in Spanish as L.G. identifies himself as “immigration” and orders Garces Perez to leave his vehicle.

Garces Perez protests, saying he wants to park his car and call someone to pick it up. The agent says they will move his car and tells him to get out.

Gacres Perez appears skeptical. “I know how it is,” he says at one point.

The back and forth continues for about 30 more seconds, with the agent telling Perez, “this is the only option we're going to give you, and I'm not going to repeat it."

Approximately one minute and eleven seconds after first being asked to roll his window down, Garces Perez pulls his car away from the ICE agents, who can be heard shouting and swearing in response.

This is the moment where the government says L.G. was struck by the mirror of Garces Perez’s car. But D.F., the agent wearing the body camera, turns away right as Garces Perez begins driving, so it is not clearly captured in the video. D.F. then gets into his car and activates his siren, which can be heard in the audio recording.

At the preliminary hearing, there was a lot of back and forth over what this video showed.

Under cross examination, Bazan conceded that a still image of the incident submitted as evidence did not conclusively show contact between the car and L.G.

Once agent D.F. is back in his car he begins following his partner, L.G. who is following Garces-Perez. He seems excited and nervous in the audio, at times cursing and nervously laughing. He also appears to use his cell phone to make various calls, and the respondents can be heard talking with him through what sounds like a speakerphone.

In one call, D.F. tells someone, “we’re in the middle of a pursuit right now.”

The man replies with profanity.

“That mother*****r didn’t stop?” he appears to say, though the audio is muddled.

“That’s DPS [Department of Public Safety] chase or what?” the man asks.

“No, that’s us, ICE,” agent D.F. responds with a laugh.

“Are you going to [inaudible] for DPS, bro?” the man asks.

In the next section of the video played in court, agent D.F. makes another call to a friend who works at DPS.

“Hey, bro are you working? Because we’re in the middle of a pursuit right now,” D.F. says.

“I am not, what’s going on?” his friend replies.

“We have a guy not stopping, are you able to get a trooper to us, bro?” agent D.F. asks.

The DPS employee gives D.F. the number to call dispatch, saying it will be “way faster.”

Agent D.F. then places another call to DPS dispatch, still while in pursuit of Garces Perez.

In that call, the DPS dispatcher asks D.F. for the plate number of Garces Perez’s car. After he pulls over to give her the plate number, she asks him what their current location is.

He tells her he has lost the location of the chase but says he is going to call his partner to “see where he’s at.”

Soon after this, he turned off his body camera.

What the recording does not show

The video evidence submitted by the government shows neither the car crash nor the shooting that ended the chase. Nor does it show a crucial phone call that D.F. made to L.G. after turning off his body camera. Bazan described D.F.'s account of that conversation in court.

According to Bazan, L.G. told D.F. he had caught up with Garces Perez, struck his car, and then shot him. D.F. said he shot Garces Perez because he feared he was in danger of being hit by the car himself.

There is no video or audio recording supporting that account, since L.G. was not wearing a body camera.

During the court hearing, Garces Perez’s defense attorney, Shane McMahon, asked Bazan why L.G. did not have a camera.

“We haven’t spoken to him,” Bazan replied.

Bazan said a separate federal investigation that he was not involved in would focus on the shooting incident.

McMahon also asked why agent D.F. turned off his camera before the crucial conversation describing the shooting.

“You would have to ask D.F. I don’t know why he turned it off,” said Bazan.

“Well I haven’t talked to D.F. but I know that you have,” said McMahon. “Did you ask D.F. why he turned it off?”

“No,” said Bazan.

WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump’s administration has revoked over 300,000 U.S. visas during his second term, the State Department said on Tuesday as the federal government continues its sweeping immigration crackdown.

The number showed an acceleration in the pace of visa revocations in recent weeks.

In an update issued on August 10, the State Department had put the number of visa revocations since Trump’s current term began in January 2025 at over 175,000.

Trump says his immigration crackdown and deportation drive aim to improve domestic security. Rights advocates say the crackdown has violated due process and free speech rights and has created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

In announcing the latest number on X, State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said the Trump administration “has revoked more visas at a faster pace than any administration in history.”

Pigott said the administration had “zero tolerance for foreigners here on visas who break the law, commit fraud, or undermine our national security.”

Among visa revocations particularly condemned by rights advocates are those of pro-Palestinian foreign protesters demonstrating against U.S. ally Israel’s attacks on Gaza and of foreigners over their social media comments about conservative commentator Charlie Kirk’s assassination.

In addition to attempts to deport foreign protesters, the Trump administration has enforced tightened social media screening of immigrants and visa applicants.

Rights advocates say the government has deployed national security reasons to target critics and used isolated cases of fraud to broadly target immigrant communities such as the Somali American community in Minnesota.

While Trump campaigned in 2024 on stopping illegal immigration, his administration has also made legal immigration more difficult — for example by imposing expensive fees for certain work visas.
