text:
However, her father, the hypothetical defendant in this case, is deceased. Nur Omar Mohamed, the congresswoman’s father, died from COVID-19 complications in 2020.

Omar says she obtained U.S. citizenship in 2000 at 17 through her father, when he naturalized. Foreign-born minor children automatically become U.S. citizens upon the naturalization of a parent.

ILHAN OMAR IMMIGRATION HISTORY: SCRUTINY SURROUNDS FAMILY’S REFUGEE CLAIMS

Where she may have allegedly provided false information to the federal government, though, would not be found on a traditional citizenship application, but rather whenever Omar or Omar’s father applied for documentary proof of her derivative citizenship.

Children born outside the United States are not automatically issued documents showing that they derived citizenship through their parents because derivative citizenship is granted by a statutory mechanism, explained Andrew Arthur, the resident law and policy fellow at the Center for Immigration Studies.

Arthur, a former immigration judge who has heard thousands of deportation cases and considered asylum applications, said such immigrants seeking physical documentation of their new citizenship status must either file an N-600 to receive a certificate of citizenship or apply for a passport with the U.S. State Department.

“If Rep. Omar fraudulently applied for either a citizenship certificate or a passport after she turned 18, her claimed status — if any — could be revoked, which would return her to green card status,” Arthur told the Washington Examiner. “At that point, the fraud would potentially make her deportable.” There is no public evidence that Omar committed fraud in obtaining citizenship as a teenager.

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services instructions for Form N-600 stipulate that a parent or legal guardian may file the application on behalf of a minor child. Those over the age of 18, however, must file the N-600 themselves.

Children ages 16 and 17 can apply for a U.S. passport provided they have parental permission.

Regardless of who actually submitted the applications in question, the statute of limitations has long expired if Omar’s submissions date back to the early 2000s. The federal statute of limitations for prosecuting immigration crimes is 10 years, or within a decade of the “commission of the offense.” That 10-year prosecution deadline also applies to conspiracy to violate U.S. immigration law.

Lying on a U.S. passport application, including making false statements about one’s age or attaching forged birth certificates, is a crime in itself, generally punishable by up to 10 years in federal prison. The statute of limitations concerning passport fraud is even shorter, set at a prosecutable period of five years.

2019 inquiry determined fraud claims were not worth pursuing

An earlier federal investigation of Omar’s immigration history, which reportedly examined many of the same fraud claims now under review, seemingly found no issues with how she acquired her citizenship.

Former immigration officials in the first Trump administration told the Washington Post that investigators were ordered in 2019 to review her immigration records for signs of fraud.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s investigative arm, Homeland Security Investigations, eventually concluded that there was insufficient evidence of wrongdoing to pursue a case against the newly elected congresswoman.

Investigators determined they could not answer questions concerning Omar’s age, given that refugees often come from countries with little to no birth records on file, making it difficult to determine key facts with certainty.

Birth year discrepancy

Omar’s actual birth year, also at the center of the latest controversy, may be less of a smoking gun than her conservative critics believe.

Her staff had her birth date changed in state and federal records, from 1981 to 1982, after she was elected to Congress, which made the amendment requests seem to critics like attempts to conceal her true age rather than simple corrections of inaccurate information.

However, the record-keeping offices that altered Omar’s biographical details appeared to have relied initially on secondhand information, in which one resource repository sourced unverified information from another, and so forth.

The fraud suspicions stem from the government website for the Minnesota legislature originally listing Omar’s birth year as 1981, which would have made her 18 years old at the time her father naturalized and therefore a legal adult ineligible to acquire derivative U.S. citizenship.

Her birth year on the state legislature’s site has since been corrected to 1982, a note at the bottom of Omar’s government biography now reads.

“It is incorrectly reported as 1981 in other sources,” the site says. “As of May 24, 2019, Rep. Omar’s congressional staff are working with Wikipedia and the U.S. House to correct her birth year in those sources.”

Her office was indeed able to edit the congresswoman’s congressional biography as well as Omar’s personal Wikipedia page, which cited a civic-engagement platform that is no longer operational.

Emails reviewed by the New York Post show that the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library based the initial 1981 birth year on “widely available” information from Wikipedia and the biographical directory of Congress.

In response to a Washington Examiner inquiry, the legislative archives center said its database of state lawmakers sometimes pulls biographical data from third-party sources without independent verification.

David Schmidtke, the reference library’s deputy director, confirmed that Omar’s congressional staff previously contacted the center to correct her birth date but did not provide documentary proof, as the archives center does not require evidence that corroborates “self-reported” information.

“However, we do not have supporting documentation, as the information was ‘self-reported.’ The library does not independently verify birthdates before publishing or updating them,” Schmidtke told the Washington Examiner.

When she first ran for Congress in 2018, Omar’s congressional campaign said that she could not retrieve her birth certificate because the Somali civil war had collapsed the government’s infrastructure.

Omar’s office did not respond to a Washington Examiner request for any corroborating documentation of her birth year.

Contemporaneous records, however, support the congresswoman’s claim that she was still a minor when her father became a naturalized citizen.

According to the fact-checking site Snopes.com, her high school yearbook shows that Omar was a junior in 2000. That year’s Edison High School yearbook identified Omar, appearing in the “Juniors” section, as a member of the graduating class of 2001.

DID ILHAN OMAR MARRY HER OWN BROTHER? THE CLAIMS EXPLAINED

Under state law, Minnesota school districts may request some form of age verification from students applying to enroll in the public school system. Following a Washington Examiner inquiry into Omar’s admissions records, a public information officer for Minneapolis Public Schools said that a student’s date of birth is confidential data excluded from public disclosure.

Omar’s alma mater, North Dakota State University, similarly said that student records containing personally identifiable information are protected by the federal Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act. “Even if such information was in NDSU’s possession,” a school spokesperson said, “NDSU could not release it without the consent of the student.”

text:
Former Columbia University graduate student and anti-Israel protest organizer Mahmoud Khalil asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Oct. 19 to review a federal appeals court ruling that overturned his release from immigration detention.

Khalil, a permanent resident who participated in Columbia’s 2024 pro-Palestinian demonstrations in New York City, is challenging whether federal district courts can intervene in immigration detention cases before immigration proceedings conclude.

[RELATED: 25 state attorneys general urge Columbia University president not to divest from Israel]

The Supreme Court petition follows a January ruling by the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that reversed a federal judge’s decision ordering Khalil’s release from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody.

Federal immigration authorities arrested Khalil in March 2025 after Secretary of State Marco Rubio determined that his presence in the United States could undermine American foreign policy interests.

Rubio’s determination invoked immigration law permitting the removal of noncitizens whose presence could have potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences.

The Trump administration has maintained that Khalil’s activities undermined efforts to combat anti-Semitism, while Khalil argues that federal officials targeted him for constitutionally protected political expression.

A federal judge ordered Khalil’s release in June 2025 after he spent more than three months in immigration detention.

However, the 3rd Circuit subsequently ruled that the district court lacked jurisdiction to intervene before the immigration process concluded.

Khalil’s attorneys argue that the decision prevents detained immigrants from promptly challenging potentially unconstitutional government actions in federal court.

text:
El Paso City Council members are set to consider a push to close Camp East Montana, a migrant detention center located on Fort Bliss, after two representatives placed the issue on an upcoming council agenda.

City Representatives Josh Acevedo and Lily Limón placed an item before City Council calling for the facility’s closure.

The item is expected to be discussed at a City Council meeting next week on Oct. 27 and directs the city manager and city attorney to draft a resolution calling for the facility's closure.

“It is long past time to close this draconian facility that has been proven to bring harm to people housed there,” Acevedo said. “Attorneys, civil rights organizations, and members of Congress have issued alarming concerns about the maltreatment and unlivable conditions at Camp East Montana, raising further concerns after three people have died while in custody.”

He added, “El Paso is a welcoming, binational community that prides itself on being one of the largest border communities on the planet. We are a community that upholds human dignity, human rights, workers’ rights, and civil rights. I urge my colleagues on the City Council to join me in calling for the closure of this inhuman facility.”

Camp East Montana is a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility that has been operated privately since it began operations on Aug. 1, 2025, as part of a broader federal effort to expand immigration detention capacity following increased enforcement actions.

The council item calls for a resolution calling for the closure of Camp East Montana, citing several issues, including detainees having reported being denied legal access, inhumane treatment, excessive force, and medical neglect with no congressional oversight.

According to the council item, the facility has also posed a public health risk after a measles outbreak occurred at the detention center over the summer, impacting nearly 180 detainees

While Camp East Montana is a federal facility and would need federal approval to close the detention center, city leaders hope the item "urges the United States Congress to use its appropriations to close Camp East Montana and to end the contracts that fund its operation."

The public is invited to sign up and speak during the Oct. 27 meeting.

READ THE AGENDA ITEM:

The item placed on next week's agenda comes as allegations and concerns of abuse, inhumane conditions, medical neglect, and use of force have continued to be raised at Camp East Montana.

In June, a federal lawsuit was filed by a coalition of civil rights organizations, including the ACLU and Human Rights Watch, against ICE, alleging widespread abuse, medical neglect, and unconstitutional conditions at Camp East Montana.

Attorneys representing detainees describe Camp East Montana as a humanitarian crisis, citing allegations of severe medical neglect, excessive use of force by guards, arbitrary solitary confinement, unsanitary living conditions, and inadequate food. The lawsuit argues that conditions at the facility violate detainees' Fifth Amendment due process rights and federal administrative law.

RELATED:Quarantine at Camp East Montana affects 178 detainees after possible measles exposure

Meanwhile, this is not the first time city leaders have urged more action against Camp East Montana.

In March, during a City Council meeting, representatives agreed to ask the El Paso City Attorney to move forward with a request for the grand jury to conduct a full investigation into the deaths that occurred at Camp East Montana, the largest immigration detention facility in the country.

Since mid-December, three people have died at Camp East Montana, which was built last year to house thousands of immigrants.

According to ICE, 48-year-old Francisco Gaspar-Andres died from natural causes. An autopsy obtained by KFOX14/CBS4 states that Gaspar-Andres died from complications of liver disease. He was the first migrant who died at Camp East Montana.

WASHINGTON– Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., says that one of his priorities in the next Congress, should Democrats win majorities, will be to give immigrants with temporary protected status the right to apply for a green card and permanent residency.

The Safe Environment from Countries Under Repression and Emergency Act would open a path for immigrants who fled conflict or other unsafe conditions to apply for permanent residency. When the bill was reintroduced, in June 2025, Van Hollen’s office cited estimates of about 860,000 TPS holders nationwide.

“It’s definitely in my top list of priorities because of the urgency of the matter,” Van Hollen told Capital News Service in an interview. “Right now we are facing this situation where the Trump administration is actively attacking the program.”

However, the bill, cosponsored by 35 senators, currently lacks any Republican support.

“The challenge, as you can see from the cosponsors on this bill, has been that Republicans have not joined us,” Van Hollen said. “A lot of them talk about the importance of the TPS program back home in their states, but then they don’t join this effort, and so that’s why these upcoming elections are so important.”

“One thing that should be understood is that we need to change the Senate filibuster rule in order to pass this, unless we get Republican support,” he added.

Since President Donald Trump returned to the White House, his administration has moved to end temporary protected status for immigrants from at least 13 countries.

In June, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in a case involving Haitian and Syrian TPS holders that federal courts cannot hear nonconstitutional challenges to TPS terminations, citing a provision of the TPS law that says the Department of Homeland Security’s decisions on TPS designations are not subject to judicial review.

Van Hollen, who disagreed with the majority decision, said the ruling removed the remaining protections against the White House actions, leaving Congress as the last path for TPS holders.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Wednesday to let it resume building a border wall project through the Big Bend region of Texas.

The government filed an emergency appeal asking the justices to lift a lower court decision halting construction. That ruling marked a setback for one of President Donald Trump’s signature projects.

The administration has been racing forward with construction on a border wall and other infrastructure from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico.

But in the Big Bend region, the administration has run into opposition from ranchers, residents, business owners and environmentalists who argue the projects are a waste of money in an area of historically low illegal immigration and that construction could harm the region’s scenic landscapes.

Opponents have filed numerous lawsuits seeking to stop the project, which in the Big Bend comprises a mixture of walls, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology.

Ruling in one of those cases, Judge Kathleen Cardone on Oct. 2 ordered the government to stop construction across the roughly 500-mile project area while the case plays out in the courts. It was a major victory for the bipartisan opposition.

The case hinges on sweeping waivers signed by the secretary of Homeland Security that allow U.S. Customs and Border Protection to bypass environmental and other regulations that would otherwise slow down construction of such a major project.

The government argued that the Big Bend sector is an area of high illegal entry and said legislation dating back to 1996 explicitly gives the secretary these far-reaching powers as necessary to build physical barriers or roads near the border to stop people from crossing illegally.

Opponents disagreed, arguing that Congress gave that power to waive regulations specifically in areas of “high illegal entry.” They said Big Bend, a remote and rugged region, doesn’t fit that description.

Cardone sided with the opponents.

“The Court finds that Plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits of their major questions doctrine claim that the Big Bend Waivers were issued in excess of the Secretary’s authority,” she wrote.

Trump has long vowed to build a border wall along the roughly 2,000-mile length of the southwest border. Last summer, Republicans in Congress allocated Homeland Security $46 billion to finish the project, which will be a mixture of 30-foot-tall steel bollard walls, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology.

The opposition in Texas’s Big Bend region had been brewing for months, but it escalated in August when bulldozers were spotted clearing land in Big Bend National Park.

The preliminary injunction filed by Cardone stops construction there as well as land up and downriver from the park that is owned by private landowners or the state.

The government has argued that if this region is one of the few areas left without a wall or other border infrastructure, illegal immigration could end up funneling to the Big Bend. But opponents have argued that other forms of infrastructure such as drones or surveillance towers are just as effective and a lot less expensive than the wall plans.

text:
Olga Rivera Galati, a deputy director at We Are Casa, an immigrant-advocacy organization, was starting her car in the parking lot outside her office, in York, Pennsylvania, when a white S.U.V. pulled into the spot next to her. It was just after five o’clock, on August 18th. Rivera Galati, who is fifty-five and was born and raised in Lancaster County, was seven months into the job. Her work included providing social services such as access to employment counselling and health care to low-income, minority residents in central Pennsylvania. She reversed a few feet out of the parking space, then stopped. The S.U.V. backed out beside her. In a panic, she pulled forward and parked. The S.U.V. did the same.

Rivera Galati, whose parents moved to Pennsylvania from Puerto Rico, was carrying her passport and birth certificate. “I’m a U.S. citizen, but I didn’t feel that way that day,” she told me. “I thought, I’m Hispanic.” There were now six S.U.V.s parked on the street outside her office. Another one rolled up slowly behind her. Rivera Galati believes the agents, who drove off when she got out of her car to confront them, were taking down her license-plate number. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been an unavoidable presence in the area during Donald Trump’s second term. But, lately, the unmarked S.U.V.s, widely recognized as the kind used by the agency, seemed to be multiplying. “As we got closer to the election, in the summer, is when it picked up,” Rivera Galati said. “They’re literally everywhere.” (“None of this ever happened,” a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told me, when asked for comment. “ICE doesn’t even have any white S.U.V.s in York, Pennsylvania.”)

In early June, Homeland Security Investigations, an arm of ICE, issued an internal report on noncitizen voting. The phenomenon is virtually nonexistent—research has repeatedly shown that isolated votes cast by noncitizens have never affected the outcome of an election—but the President has turned it into a pretext to involve the Department of Homeland Security in the midterms. The June report stated that there were efforts at multiple branches of the Department to identify organizations that “may be predatory in nature, particularly those suspected of illegal alien registration and voter encouragement.” Groups in several states, including Michigan, Minnesota, and Ohio, were being investigated, but two locations were sources of special interest: Pennsylvania and New Jersey. The Department reviewed eighty-two N.G.O.s in Pennsylvania alone. We Are Casa is almost certainly one of them.

D.H.S.’s role in elections has, until recently, been limited to technical issues like monitoring cyberattacks and defending critical infrastructure. Its prominent place in this election cycle is without precedent. In the lead-up to the midterms, the Trump Administration has sued thirty states, along with the District of Columbia, which have refused to turn over complete voter records; D.H.S. wants to cross-check them with its own databases. Federal courts have mostly rebuffed these lawsuits. But hundreds of Department officials have been assigned to search for unlawful voters. Agents from H.S.I., together with personnel from the fraud division of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, have been routinely contacting county boards of elections to request voter files.

At the same time, according to a government whistle-blower, D.H.S. officials have been impersonating voters and entering their personal information into state voter databases, which is likely a violation of privacy laws. (The D.H.S. spokesperson denied that it was doing anything controversial and described these practices as “commonplace law enforcement.”) Between August and mid-September, leadership at U.S.C.I.S. imposed quotas: staff were required to investigate forty names per day, at a rate of roughly twelve minutes per subject. To conduct these searches, D.H.S. seems to have purchased commercially available voter data and run it through agency databases to turn up the names of noncitizens; the process is notoriously error-prone, generating frequent false positives. The fixation on illegal voting has also meant that other work was being neglected. At H.S.I., between ten and fifteen per cent of agents are investigating voter fraud. Jason Houser, a former high-ranking ICE official, told me, “Agents should be focussed on dismantling fentanyl-trafficking networks, combating child exploitation, and taking violent criminals off our streets.”

These efforts are being directed by political appointees at the top of the Department and at the White House. “They’re zealots,” a former H.S.I. official told me. “They won’t believe anything that doesn’t prove their point.” Anthony Salisbury, the current head of H.S.I., personally reports to Stephen Miller, the President’s deputy chief of staff. “It’s all directed by Miller,” the former official said. Elsewhere within the government, conspiracists with discredited views about voter fraud now have prominent roles overseeing elections. One of them is Heather Honey, a conservative researcher from Pennsylvania whose skewed data on the 2020 results was cited by Trump as grounds for contesting the outcome. Last year, she was appointed to a job that didn’t exist during the Presidency of Joe Biden: Deputy Assistant Secretary for Election Integrity at D.H.S.

Earlier this summer, Markwayne Mullin, the Secretary of Homeland Security, said that the Department had found more than two hundred and fifty thousand potential noncitizens registered to vote in California, Nevada, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania. The Trump Administration has provided no evidence to back up Mullin’s claim. D.H.S. said it had found sixteen thousand potential noncitizen voters in Nevada, but, by late September, the Department had submitted the names of only a hundred and eight-five to the state for review. A subsequent investigation by Nevada election officials revealed that each person on the D.H.S. list was a citizen. (“Since then,” the D.H.S. spokesperson told me, Department officials have “manually confirmed about two thousand more aliens from the same list.”)

Pennsylvania, for its part, was told in July that some fifteen thousand people should be investigated. Votebeat, a nonprofit newsroom focussed on covering elections, obtained e-mails between D.H.S. and the state. According to the Secretary of the Commonwealth, D.H.S. representatives said at a virtual meeting held with state officials, in August, that “they did not have high confidence” that the people identified by Mullin “were, in fact, noncitizens who had improperly registered to vote.” (D.H.S. called the Secretary’s letter a “blatant mischaracterization.”)

Predictably, the few cases in which legal permanent residents, who cannot legally vote, were found to have actually done so have received outsized attention. On Monday, the Department of Justice announced that it was charging twenty-eight green-card holders in California with election-related crimes. Twenty-one of them, officials said, had voted illegally. The others appear to have never actually voted, or they registered more than twenty years ago. The government has accused some of them of making false statements about whether they had ever been registered to vote when they later applied to become naturalized citizens. These names came from a list of twenty thousand people who the Trump Administration claims are on the California voter rolls despite likely being noncitizens. In a letter sent last week, the acting Deputy Attorney General warned California officials that they could be prosecuted for knowingly processing votes “cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens.” On Truth Social, Trump wrote, “They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!”

To date, the Department of Justice has accused a hundred and fifty-six people of violating election laws nationwide, and in the past two months, the government’s attempts to find further instances of fraud have intensified. Armed D.H.S. agents, in uniforms and flak jackets, have been knocking on doors in multiple states to ask residents about their immigration status and whether they were registered to vote, CBS News reported. “It seems that they’re trying to manufacture a narrative any way they can,” Claire Trickler-McNulty, another former senior ICE official, told me. “They can now arrest green-card holders without convictions who are accused of voting.”

Inside D.H.S. there may be at least a tacit acknowledgment that the campaign to uncover voter fraud hasn’t generated results. On August 26th, ICE officers were instructed to fill out an additional field in the “Biographics Section” for those it detained: “Have you voted in a federal election?” About a month later, the agency added another prompt: “If you answer ‘Yes’ to ‘Have you ever voted in a federal election,’ you must now specify how the subject voted: Mail-in Ballot [or] In Person.” The purpose of these questions, Houser told me, is “to create an investigative paper trail.” “You question enough people, particularly individuals who may be intimidated or confused by federal agents, and you’re going to get inconsistent statements,” he said. “That doesn’t establish voter fraud, but it can generate investigative reports, referrals, and individual cases that the Administration could later point to as evidence of a broader problem.”

York County falls partly in Pennsylvania’s Tenth Congressional District, which is currently represented by the Republican Scott Perry, a Trump ally who, in 2020, had attempted to overturn the state’s election results and later disregarded a congressional subpoena over his involvement in the January 6th riots at the Capitol. In 2024, Trump carried the county with sixty-two per cent of the vote; that year, Perry, who is running for his eighth consecutive term, beat his Democratic opponent, Janelle Stelson, a former newscaster, by five thousand votes. This year, Stelson has a significant funding advantage, and polls show her with a slight lead.

On October 7th, Charles Wall, the deputy director of ICE, issued a press release: “It’s unbelievable that Janelle Stelson would employ an illegal alien to work on a Congressional campaign, let alone a pervert who exposed himself in public.” This was a reference to a Nigerian immigrant who was arrested in East Pennsboro Township on September 27th after police investigated a report of a suspicious vehicle parked in a residential neighborhood. According to the incident report, which was obtained by the Associated Press, when the man opened his car door, the officer noticed that his “genitals were exposed.” The man was booked for indecent exposure, and eventually handed over to ICE. (He pleaded guilty to one count of disorderly conduct; the indecent exposure charge was dropped.) There were flyers for Stelson in his car, the report noted. But D.H.S. has refused to substantiate its claim that the man was employed by Stelson’s campaign. She has denied that he worked for her, which campaign-finance reports confirm. The ICE press release cited a news report that quoted a conservative activist who made the allegation. According to e-mails viewed by Axios, the Office of Special Counsel, a federal agency that monitors the behavior of government employees, is looking into whether Wall violated the Hatch Act, which limits partisan activities by executive-branch officials.

The police departments of several towns in and around York County, meanwhile, have signed partnerships—known as 287(g) agreements—with the Trump Administration to receive federal funding in exchange for collaborating with ICE. Routine traffic stops enable police officers to detain someone and then transfer them directly to ICE. More than five hundred immigrants have been arrested by local law enforcement in the county since 2025, according to data analyzed by the Philadelphia Inquirer. During that time, some thirty-one per cent of all 287(g) arrests made in Pennsylvania occurred in York County, despite it comprising less than four per cent of the state’s population. This year, canvassers with We Are Casa stopped working in Spring Garden and West York borough, two independent municipalities in the county, because of the 287(g) agreements.

On September 4th, a Haitian pastor named Molis Augustave was stopped by the West Manchester Township police for a broken headlight. Augustave, who is married to a U.S. citizen and had been living in York with his two-year-old son and nine-year-old stepdaughter, lost his legal status weeks earlier, when the Trump Administration cancelled Temporary Protected Status for three hundred and thirty thousand Haitians in the U.S. Augustave had a pending application for a green card—as a result of his marriage—and a previous petition for asylum. The officers transferred him to ICE custody. On September 24th, he was deported. Augustave had worked as an organizer for We Are Casa; when I visited the group’s office, banners and signs with his photograph still adorned the walls.

That afternoon, I joined a group of We Are Casa canvassers as they offered to register voters outside of a grocery store in the city of York. The team consisted of four women, two of whom were legal permanent residents. They couldn’t vote themselves, but seemed to take pride in registering those who could. Their work was not without risk. Several weeks earlier, someone spotted an ICE patrol vehicle in the store’s parking lot, and the canvassers decided to leave. On another occasion, one of them realized she’d left her green card at home, and rushed off to get it. “ICE has been going after people who are U.S. citizens, just for your accent,” Lymari, a Puerto Rican canvasser, told me. “It’s a huge stress for everyone.”

text:
In at least the second death this year in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody in Laredo, Texas, a 56-year-old Mexican man was found dead in his cell Saturday morning. According to a statement released by ICE, Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias was found unresponsive by facility staff at the Rio Grande Processing Center during a security check at around 10:00 a.m. and was not able to be resuscitated when staff performed CPR and contacted emergency services. He was declared dead approximately 20 minutes later.

Andrade-Covarrubias’ daughter, Estefani Andrade, informed the Texas Tribune that he had been in custody since June, and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) never informed her or any relatives of her father’s death. Instead, she was only notified by the Webb County Medical Examiner’s Office, which is performing Andrade-Covarrubias’ autopsy.

In a statement released Monday, ICE denied any culpability in the death of Andrade-Covarrubias, who was a lawful legal resident. The cause of his death remains unknown, but the agency said he received proper medical care and attention while at the facility, something belied by the record of inhumane conditions at immigration detention facilities and his daughter’s own testimony.

Andrade told the Tribune her father said medical staff would regularly ignore his pleas for aid. He was ill with chronic conditions, including high blood pressure, diabetes and a heart condition. His daughter said that her father had medicine with him when he was detained but added that staff at the center would not give him his medication. She said she witnessed the deterioration of his health in video calls between them.

In addition to losing a noticeable amount of weight, Andrade-Covarrubias developed a cough while in custody. The persistent cough worried Andrade since her father was hospitalized for COVID-19 in 2021, which took a toll on his overall health. She said her father told her that medical staff at the center brushed off his concerns, even when he told them he was having trouble breathing and felt tightness in his chest.

Andrade-Covarrubias was a resident of Dallas for decades and had three adult children, who were all born in the US. Like Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, an immigrant murdered by ICE in Houston in July, Andrade-Covarrubias worked in construction, helping to build homes for families in Texas. His daughter says he worked as a contractor painting apartments and townhomes. He planned on returning to Mexico eventually and had actually been traveling between the US and Mexico to build a house of his own in his native country.

In its Monday statement, ICE said Andrade-Covarrubias was arrested while returning to Texas from Mexico on June 26 because immigration officers believed that he fraudulently obtained his legal status by failing to disclose a 2004 arrest for theft during his review process. His daughter maintains that her father disclosed the 2004 arrest during the review process and was granted a green card.

His arrest came three days after the Supreme Court’s June 23 ruling in Blanche v. Muk Choi Lau, which weakened protections for lawful permanent residents returning from abroad. In a 6–3 decision written by Justice Clarence Thomas, the court held that border officers need not have “clear and convincing evidence” that a returning resident committed a qualifying offense before treating that person as an applicant for admission. This means a working-class immigrant could be torn away from the life they have built over decades for a minor non-violent incident they may, or may not, have committed.

Indeed, DHS officials were seeking to deport him, saying that he was in removal proceedings before an immigration judge. According to court records, Andrade-Covarrubias was due to appear at an immigration court hearing on November 2.

Andrade-Covarrubias is at least the seventh person confirmed to have died while detained by ICE in Texas this year and the second to die at the detention center in Laredo. Other deaths include:

Luis Gustavo Núñez Cáceres, 42, passed away from a heart-related medical emergency on January 5, 2026, at HCA Houston Healthcare in Conroe, Texas, following his transfer to the ICU from the Joe Corley Processing Center.

Victor Manuel Diaz, 36, died on January 14, 2026 at Camp East Montana in El Paso, Texas. ICE claimed the death was due to suicide, but his family maintains it was medical distress suffered during early-year tent facility surges.

Felix Alcorta-Rodriguez, 63, died of cardiovascular failure on June 19, 2026, after being found unresponsive in his cell at the Webb County Detention Center in Laredo, Texas (the same facility Andrade-Covarrubias died in) and rushed to a local hospital.

Adrian Andreas Florian, 85, died on June 24, 2026, from medical complications at Valley Baptist Medical Center in Harlingen, Texas, after being transferred there from the Port Isabel Detention Center in Los Fresnos.

Geraldo Lunas Campos, 55, died on January 3, 2026, at Camp East Montana in El Paso, Texas, from homicide via asphyxia, according to the El Paso County Medical Examiner. Witnesses described seeing guards choking him before he died.

After learning of the tragedy, US Representative Henry Cuellar, a Democrat from Laredo, told the Tribune that he visited the detention center to investigate the quality of the facility’s medical care. Cuellar said he could not get any details about Andrade-Covarrubias’ case because it was still under investigation. In a statement, he said that he has written to DHS officials to demand more transparency.

“Any death in federal custody is a serious matter, and we need to know what happened,” Cuellar said on Monday.

It must be stated, however, that the Democratic Party offers no progressive solution to the escalating war against immigrants and the broader working class. In fact, workers and immigrants have not forgotten that Joe Biden continued the immigration policies of Barack Obama, who was dubbed the “deporter-in-chief.”

Why did the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires lose out on a government security contract to an American firm over a measly $80,000?

Despite the Elbows Up rhetoric of the Carney government and the Buy Canadian policy officially adopted last December, the Commissionaires lost out on a contract for the Canada Revenue Agency to Allied Universal. That firm, which makes hundreds of millions of dollars from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, including ICE — Immigration and Customs Enforcement — underbid the Commissionaires by just over $80,000 on a $12-million multi-year contract.

Hypocrisy on the Hill

Several Conservative MPs raised the question in the House of Commons, pointing to the hypocrisy.

Article content

Story continues below

Article content

“It is the height of hypocrisy that after all the buy-Canadian, support-Canadian and defend-Canadian sovereignty lectures that have gone on with the Liberals that the Prime Minister would allow an American security company with ties to Donald Trump’s ICE, the very agency that has been central to Trump’s mass deportation efforts, to replace a hundred-year-old Canadian institution like the Commissionaires for security services at the CRA over an $80,000 difference in bids,” Conservative MP John Brassard said during question period.

Brassard asked why the Carney Liberals were undermining instead of supporting the Commissionaires.

Liberal MP Wayne Long, secretary of state for the Canada Revenue Agency, defended the move time and again.

“The CRA had an independent decision. The decision was clear. It is a Canadian company employing 8,000 Canadians,” Long said in response.

As the Conservatives pushed with question after question, Long stated that Allied Universal met the criteria of the contract. He also said several times that the company is a Canadian company and disputed the idea that the contract went stateside.

Advertisement 4

Story continues below

Article content

Made in Canada? Hardly

Calling Allied Universal a Canadian company is a bit of a stretch.

The company lists two headquarters, Conshohocken, Pa., and Irvine, Calif. It has a Canadian head office in Mississauga, but the company is American-based and American-controlled.

Employing Canadians doesn’t make you Canadian. The profits, the decisions and the ICE contracts all run through Pennsylvania and California.

So far in 2026, Allied Universal has received contracts worth more than US$290 million through the American Department of Homeland Security. Its subsidiary, G4S Security has received contracts worth US$83 million from ICE.

That’s not the type of company that Liberal voters, or most Canadian taxpayers, would be comfortable doing business with.

Yet Allied Universal was awarded the contract, and despite spending the last 18 months lecturing everyone about buying Canadian, the Carney government is defending this move.

Article content

Vets left out in the cold

The Commissionaires is a non-profit Canadian organization founded in 1925 to provide employment to veterans. The Carney Liberals keep saying they stand with veterans and with Canadians, but they keep making moves that show the opposite.

Before awarding the CRA contract to Allied Universal, the Carney government announced it was ending the decades-old practice of giving the Commissionaires the first right of refusal on providing security to federal government buildings. That move came after extensive lobbying from global security giant GardaWorld, which also makes a ton of money providing security for ICE and other parts of Trump’s mass deportation apparatus.

Garda hired well-connected Liberal lobbyists who held meeting after meeting pleading with the Carney government to end the practice. Despite years of successive governments saying no, Garda got the yes it was looking for earlier this year.

First the Liberals took away the Commissionaires’ right of first refusal. Now they’ve handed a contract to an ICE contractor. We are watching a century of standing with veterans, undone by $80,000 and a few well-placed lobbyists.

title: What's new in Homeland Security's updated AI policy | FedScoop
description:
The Department of Homeland Security quietly released an updated policy governing internal artificial intelligence use earlier this month.
“Use of Super Intelligence by ICE is subject to applicable governance, use-case documentation, and reporting requirements,” an ICE spokesperson said, referring to the Trump administration’s self-styled terminology for artificial intelligence.
The new policy includes language around AI asset sharing and reuse, aligning with the Office of Management and Budget’s memorandum on accelerating federal use of AI that was published in April 2025.

Under the new directive, DHS is also tasked with releasing and maintaining AI code as open-source software in a public repository.
text:
The Department of Homeland Security quietly released an updated policy governing internal artificial intelligence use earlier this month.

The directive, which took effect in September, is mostly in line with the 2025 version in terms of scope and overall content. DHS, for example, kept in a prohibition with minimal changes that barred the agency from using AI for improper “systemic or large-scale monitoring, surveillance, or tracking of individuals, or predictions of emotional state or future behavior.”

It’s a notable inclusion given that Immigration and Customs Enforcement awarded a $125 million contract to Thomson Reuters Special Services in September to provide services that would enable monitoring of 1 million individuals and identifying potentially criminal and fraudulent behavior before it happens.

DHS had been working on the surveillance system with CACI since at least 2020, per documents obtained via a public records request by Democracy Forward and shared exclusively with FedScoop.

“Use of Super Intelligence by ICE is subject to applicable governance, use-case documentation, and reporting requirements,” an ICE spokesperson said, referring to the Trump administration’s self-styled terminology for artificial intelligence. “To the extent that Thomson Reuters Special Services uses SI in support of this contract, ICE OCIO will assess the specific role and intended use of the SI capabilities for consistency with DHS Directive 139-08, Revision 01, Artificial Intelligence Use and Acquisition.”

Some sources, however, questioned whether ICE would even need to follow its own rules, given the latest AI policy includes a provision allowing the agency’s chief AI officer to waive any requirement outlined in the directive, including prohibited use cases.

“A rule that comes with its own off switch is not a rule,” said Tom Bowman, policy counsel for the Center for Democracy & Technology’s Security and Surveillance Project. The CAIO “can turn the prohibition off, with no independent review from the privacy or civil rights offices, no notice to Congress or the public, and no expiration date.”

Rachel Levinson-Waldman, director of the Brennan Center’s Liberty and National Security program, said the CAIO’s ability to waive requirements was one of her biggest concerns, too.

“While the directive says the waiver must be ‘consistent with law, regulation, and government-wide policy,’ it’s still a loophole big enough to drive a truck through,” Levinson-Waldman said. “Any CAIO worth his salt will be able to assemble a justification for a waiver that explains away any tension with other policies, especially given the sweeping authority granted by this directive.”

Some of the other changes to the AI policy were expected and reflect the Trump administration’s priorities, such as the removal or editing of previously included language around promoting equity and references to underserved communities, environmental efficiency and sustainability.

The chief privacy officer is also no longer responsible for ensuring AI “does not erode” privacy protections and now just needs to make sure it “complies” with the established guardrails.

The new policy includes language around AI asset sharing and reuse, aligning with the Office of Management and Budget’s memorandum on accelerating federal use of AI that was published in April 2025. The addition instructs DHS to proactively share its custom-developed code, AI models, use cases and related data across the agency and governmentwide. Under the new directive, DHS is also tasked with releasing and maintaining AI code as open-source software in a public repository.

“This preference for open-source could be a real transparency gain if DHS follows through,” Bowman said. “But the civil liberties problem is purpose limitation. A model built, tested, and reviewed for one mission will be picked up by another component for a different mission, but the privacy and civil rights analysis that justified it the first time might be entirely different.”

text:
Haitians in white detention sweatsuits shuffle off deportation flights in shackles and into the unknown in Haiti’s second-largest city, Cap-Haitien.

Some arrive with small sacks of belongings. Others without their phones, money or identification. They’re given a hot meal, 25,000 Haitian Gourds (about $191), and spend one night in a hotel after being screened by police.

Then they are on their own – back amid the gang violence, displacement and hunger that led many to flee.

It has become a weekly ritual.

“It’s a kind of a nightmare situation for people,” said Yael Schacher, director for the Americas and Europe at Refugees International, who observed an Oct. 8 deportation flight arrival, interviewed deportees and described the scene to USA TODAY.

It has been two months since an Aug. 20 deportation flight marked the first to arrive in Haiti after President Donald Trump revoked Temporary Protected Status for Haitians in the United States. To date, 766 people have been deported to the Caribbean island nation, according to Human Rights First, a U.S. organization that tracks deportations. Flights have accelerated from monthly to weekly.

They return to a raft of steep challenges: Finding jobs and housing in an overcrowded Cap-Haitien, traveling to meet distant relatives without being extorted or killed by gangs on the road, and restarting their lives in a country bereft of government assistance.

TPS, used to prevent deportation to countries facing dangerous conditions, was first granted after Haiti’s earthquake in 2010 and renewed over the years as the nation struggled. In 2021, President Jovenel Moïse was assassinated, leaving a vacuum where a functioning government should be. Gangs now control much of the capital of Port-au-Prince.

Violence has left 5,700 people dead or wounded this year, through September, according to the United Nations, while more than 1,000 women and girls have been raped and at least 230 kidnapped. More than half the population does not have enough to eat, the International Rescue Committee said recently.

For some of those returning, the Haiti they find is in worse shape than the one they left.

Humanitarian aid is scarce. Deportees from the United States may find relatives who have “lost everything,” said Stenley Orbruth Doriscar, a spokesman for GARR, a Haitian group supporting repatriated Haitians.

“The country is not prepared to receive these individuals repatriated from the United States with dignity,” he wrote to USA TODAY on WhatsApp.

From US detention to Cap-Haitien

Deportees on one recent flight arrived stunned and unprepared.

Some lacked documents or the means to access their money in the United States, said Schacher, who interviewed many of the arrivals from Oct. 8.

Others struggle with having left behind family members. One man from Maryland was detained after he’d taken his daughter to a hospital and gone back to his car to retrieve something, she said.

“Almost everybody I spoke to was separated from family in the United States,” she said.

Some had left Haiti as little as two years ago or been gone for more than a decade, they told Human Rights Watch when it interviewed 44 deportees on two flights in August. Most had been detained before the official end of TPS.

Among them were those who had established lives in Massachusetts, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Florida and Ohio, the group’s report said. They had jobs – nursing assistants, farm hands and construction workers.

A 36-year-old factory worker in Indiana said he was detained in early August during his lunch break, three years after he fled Haiti because criminal groups killed his parents, the HRW researcher wrote. One 38-year-old man who worked in a Florida hotel said he left behind a wife and their 5-year-old U.S. citizen son, who had just started school.

“I was working so he could grow up without experiencing the fear, violence, and uncertainty I had known in Haiti, ” he was quoted in the report as saying.

The Department of Homeland Security wrote in an unsigned email to USA TODAY that in the last month, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement flights to Haiti have deported some of the “worst of the worst,” citing 15 people with criminal convictions, including for violent and drug crimes.

These flights often contain a mix of people: Haitians who lost TPS or another status, detainees who agreed to be deported to get out of detention and some convicted of crimes, said Michelle Karshan, a former press liaison for two Haitian presidents, who directs a support program for deportees with criminal histories.

The flights typically leave from Louisiana, sometimes making a stop in Miami to pick up deportees. The HRW report noted that some people were told their documents and belongings would arrive with them but never did.

A few hundred Haitians have instead been deported to Mexico or third countries, said Savi Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First. How those decisions were made, she said, are unclear.

DHS wrote in a statement that third-country removals are “an essential public safety tool that remove(s) the most dangerous” immigrants.

Those who arrived in Haiti since August have all landed at Cap-Haitien – far away, on the north coast, from the capital of Port-au-Prince from which many came. The FAA halted flights there in November 2024 after three U.S. ​commercial jetliners were struck by gunfire.

Haiti's National Office of Migration said it offers help, including medical and other assistance in conjunction with the Haitian Red Cross and the Ministry of Public Health.

But there is no sustainable shelter, health care, transportation, protection or reintegration support, according to HRW.

Now what? Deportees to Haiti face difficult choices

In Cap-Haitien, many first scramble for immediate needs.

Among those: finding a place to stay, obtaining medicine, including for conditions that may have worsened during detention, and replacing prison garb that could make them a target for criminals. Some needed new identification before they could receive money wired from family.

On Oct. 8, following processing, a few arrivals were picked up by waiting relatives who lived nearby, Schacher said. Many had to figure out if they could reach relatives in other parts of the country, including Port-au-Prince, about 125 miles away.

Buses and taxis may mean using major roads controlled by gangs, who often set up roadblocks. Traveling risks extortion, kidnapping or worse.

Staying in Cap-Haitien, a city bursting with people, brings its own challenges.

Nationwide, nearly 1.5 million residents have been displaced by violence, according to the International Organization for Migration, pushing many into the countryside or cities like Cap-Haitien where it is stretching limited services, housing and employment opportunities.

In addition, some of the Haitians returning from other countries, including between 26,000 and 35,000 Haitians deported each month from the neighboring Dominican Republic, seek out relative safety in the city. That has strained housing and employment options.

“The city is completely saturated,” said Angie Bell, who served as mayor of Cap-Haitien until earlier this year.

Some U.S. deportees seek work at call centers or restaurants in Haiti, Karshon said. But opportunities are limited. In 2025, Royal Caribbean cruise line paused visits to a private beach destination in nearby Labadee, which added to employment struggles.

Sledge Seide, who was deported in June, told USA TODAY in September that he was staying in a friend’s building that’s under construction. With jobs scarce, he was scraping by with help from friends in the United States, while helping new arrivals find their footing.

“If you just come back, you don't know nobody,” he said. “To find a place to stay, for people to try to find a job, it's hard.”

Bell said that in her city, some locals are discussing ways to better assist arrivals in finding work and reintegrating into society. Churches may help some individuals, but there isn't a broader program. She said housing is the biggest need right now.

Some stayed in town only a few days before setting out to other parts of Haiti or trying to cross the border into the Dominican Republic. From there, some seek to emigrate to countries such as Mexico or Brazil in which they may have lived or traveled through.

What’s ahead for Haiti

Outside of Cap-Haitien, Haiti is still in shambles.

Food and fuel shortages, limited access to health care and gangs ruling much of the capital city and roads in between have kept the country mired in crisis.

Gangs tax everything that moves through the Port-au-Prince port, from food to fuel, said Allie Pasieka, International Rescue Committee’s deputy director for programs in Haiti.

“The whole country is under crisis, and it's not a safe place,” Pasieka said.

That reality hovers over Haitian communities in the United States, where advocates say many of the estimated 330,000 Haitians who lost TPS protection, along with work authorization, constantly fear arrest.

The Haitian community in Springfield, Ohio, that Trump derided as eating dogs and cats has recently seen less visible ICE activity, but many feel “very much still under attack and struggling” amid the pressure, said Theresa Hice-Fromille, a board member of the Ohio-based Haitian Community Help and Support Center.

Some have called on Congress to restore protections given Haiti’s dangers. A bill that would require DHS to designate Haiti as eligible for TPS passed the House in April but stalled in the Senate.

Whether deportations will increase isn’t known. Haitian officials were told the United States intended to send two deportation flights a week, each carrying about 200 people according to the Human Rights Watch report.

DHS declined to answer whether it plans to boost deportations to Haiti, citing security and safety concerns. DHS has previously defended ending TPS as a “de facto amnesty program despite Congress never intending it to be permanent.”

Compounding the crisis in Haiti is a shortage of humanitarian aid, the majority of which had been provided by the United States since 2024. But in 2025, the Trump administration’s cuts to foreign aid and USAID halted nearly 80% of U.S.-funded programs, according to the U.N.

The effect is being seen across a wide range of programs, including access to hospitals and health care, Pasieka said, with international aid donation reaching just 28% of the need.

Haiti still has had no elected president since the 2021 assassination. Recently, the Haitian electoral council postponed the first elections since 2016, scheduled to start in December, as violence continued to disrupt preparations, AFP reported. Criminal groups have expanded from Port-au-Prince into at least five of ten Haitian departments.

​​Whether security can be stabilized hinges in part on the U.N. Gang Suppression Force, which took over from the under-equipped Kenya-led Multinational Security Support mission. Up to 5,500 personnel from various nations are set to work alongside Haitian police to target gangs, reopen roads and stabilize the capital.

In August, at least 47 people were killed and more than 50 others kidnapped when armed men attacked Kenscoff, a town located in the hills above Port-au-Prince.

Meanwhile, deportees continue to arrive. On Oct. 8, a man arrived from Ohio only to realize he couldn’t safely reach his family in Haiti from Cap-Hatien. He broke down crying, Schacher said.

With no other options, he hoped to stay in Cap-Haitien and try to start again, she said, despite the impossible odds.

Chris Kenning is a national correspondent for USA TODAY. He can be reached at ckenning@usatoday.com

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested four people during a targeted enforcement operation on Oct. 19, according to the Department of Homeland Security.

Witnesses say they saw some of the arrests as they happened at Margarita's restaurant on Walton Street in Armory Square.

Video of the arrests was taken from the sidewalk outside the restaurant by Eri Solomon. Homeland Security would not confirm the location of the arrests, and it is not clear if all four individuals were arrested at the restaurant or if some were captured elsewhere.

The four people arrested are identified as Ismael Espejo Sarmiento, Jonnathan Castro-Alay, Hector Velsai Vasquez Perez and Natividad Tania Ramirez Vasquez.

According to ICE, Sarmiento is from Mexico whose criminal history includes simple assault and aggravated assault. The agency said he entered the U.S. illegally at an unknown time and location. He will remain in custody pending removal proceedings.

Castro-Alay is from Ecuador and also allegedly entered the country illegally at an unknown time and location, according to ICE. He will remain in custody pending removal proceedings.

Vasquez Perez is from Guatemala and allegedly entered the U.S. illegally at an unknown time and location. ICE said he will remain in custody pending his voluntary departure.

The documents show that a Boeing 767 operated by ICE charter Eastern Airlines will leave the United States on Thursday and make stops in Senegal, Equatorial Guinea, Burundi, and the Central African Republic.
One flight, also operated by Eastern Airlines, passed within about 15 miles of Malabo on October 13, flight data shows.
Soliman came to the United States with his family as a young child and was raised in Arizona.
At least 63 third-country nationals have been sent to Equatorial Guinea since last November via at least six ICE-chartered flights, where they have reported being beaten, threatened, held at gunpoint, and deprived of food, water, hygiene products, and medical care.
text:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) charter flight is heading to Equatorial Guinea Thursday, two weeks after a federal judge ordered the return of a man expelled there under the Trump administration’s third-country removal program, according to documents obtained by the Prospect. It is unclear whether the plane is being sent to expel more immigrants to the authoritarian country, to retrieve the man—31-year-old Egyptian national Ahmed Soliman—or both.

The documents show that a Boeing 767 operated by ICE charter Eastern Airlines will leave the United States on Thursday and make stops in Senegal, Equatorial Guinea, Burundi, and the Central African Republic. Senegal is often used by ICE-chartered aircraft to refuel and make crew changes; the other three countries are all known “host” countries in the Trump administration’s third-country removal network.

“We are deeply concerned for Ahmed’s welfare. There is no doubt as to his location, and the government has the ability to bring him back to the United States, as they have been ordered to do,” one of his attorneys, Dana Camilleri, told the Prospect. “The government making a planned stop in Equatorial Guinea demonstrates that it can bring Ahmed home, and should do so immediately.”

ICE, the Department of Homeland Security, and the State Department did not immediately reply to questions about the flight and whether Soliman will be put on it. It also did not respond to questions about the legality of potentially sending more people to a country that has subjected third-country nationals to severe abuse, as has been widely reported.

Soliman was hospitalized in the island city of Malabo over the weekend after becoming seriously ill, according to his attorneys in a Tuesday court filing. The filing also said he was now back at the Hotel Bamy, where dozens of other third-country nationals are being imprisoned, despite his medical condition not improving. Soliman also has untreated injuries from a car accident that occurred when he was being transported from a local jail to the hotel several weeks ago, the filing said.

“The government no longer has any plausible deniability as the human rights abuses are already well-documented. It is disturbing to consider that the government, as it hopefully picks up Ahmed, may also be removing others in his place who will be indefinitely detained at the Hotel Bamy, or worse, sent under duress to their home countries,” Camilleri said.

Arizona District Court Judge John C. Hinderaker, a Trump appointee, ordered the government to facilitate Soliman’s return to the United States earlier this month after ruling Soliman’s right to due process had been violated when he was forced onto an ICE charter flight in April and expelled to Equatorial Guinea.

Late on Monday, Justice Department attorneys said the government intended to appeal, after dragging its heels on complying with the judge’s orders, blowing past at least one deadline for a status report, and providing minimal documentation about the steps it had taken to facilitate Soliman’s return.

In a brief Monday filing, the government said for the second time that it was still trying “to confirm [Soliman]’s exact location.” Soliman’s attorneys responded by saying it had repeatedly sent the government updates whenever Soliman’s location changed but had never received a response, and that their repeated messages to the U.S. ambassador to Equatorial Guinea had also gone unanswered.

The filing did say that the government is “coordinating return efforts with both the State

Department and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS),” adding that U.S. Attorney for Arizona Timothy Courchaine is “working to streamline communication” with Soliman’s attorneys and ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations.

Even before the scheduled flight this week, flight data shows at least four ICE-chartered aircraft flying within a few hundred miles of Equatorial Guinea a total of eight times since October 8, any of which could have conceivably been directed by ICE to retrieve Soliman. One flight, also operated by Eastern Airlines, passed within about 15 miles of Malabo on October 13, flight data shows.

Eastern Airlines is not related to the historic Eastern Air Lines, which ceased operations in 1991, other than that the new entity bought the unused trademark.

Soliman came to the United States with his family as a young child and was raised in Arizona. He lost his lawful permanent resident status after a conviction relating to an accident he caused while driving under the influence of drugs in 2021. An immigration judge had previously ruled Soliman could not be deported to Egypt because he was likely to face harm due to his family’s political affiliation and because he is gay.

Soliman has previously told media, including the Prospect, that he turned to drugs as a young man to deal with feelings of shame about being gay, but that he has since recovered from his addiction issues and accepted his identity.

At least 63 third-country nationals have been sent to Equatorial Guinea since last November via at least six ICE-chartered flights, where they have reported being beaten, threatened, held at gunpoint, and deprived of food, water, hygiene products, and medical care. All are believed to have had legal protections barring deportation to their countries of origin due to harms they faced there, yet about half have been forced back to those countries anyway—a maneuver called chain refoulement that is barred under U.S. and international law.

description:
Brad Lander, the Democratic nominee for New York’s 10th Congressional District, said Wednesday he was released from Israeli military custody after being detained while participating in an olive harvest in the West Bank.
The volunteers said they were accompanying Palestinian farmers to harvest olives near Bethlehem.
The group was participating in an event organized by the “Protect the Harvest” coalition, which Lander said supports Palestinian farmers and promotes human rights and safety for Palestinians and Israelis.
He said the harvest was also a protest over the treatment of Palestinian farmers.
The detentions come as the West Bank olive harvest has drawn international attention over reports of violence.
text:
Brad Lander, the Democratic nominee for New York’s 10th Congressional District, said Wednesday he was released from Israeli military custody after being detained while participating in an olive harvest in the West Bank.

The volunteers said they were accompanying Palestinian farmers to harvest olives near Bethlehem. Rabbis for Human Rights said the farmers had been unable to reach their groves for three years.

About two hours after the volunteers began working, the Israel Defense Forces declared the field a closed military zone, according to activists. Activists said they agreed to leave but were detained anyway. The supplied reports did not include an IDF explanation for the detentions.

Lander said he was held for about three hours and released with a warning. He suggested his public profile may have influenced the decision, writing on social media that he told authorities he was a congressional nominee, not a member of Congress.

“Several dozen rabbis & participants harvesting olives with me are still in detention,” he wrote.

Lander later said about 60 people, including American rabbis, international volunteers, Israelis and Palestinians, remained in custody eight hours after the group was detained.

The group was participating in an event organized by the “Protect the Harvest” coalition, which Lander said supports Palestinian farmers and promotes human rights and safety for Palestinians and Israelis. He said the harvest was also a protest over the treatment of Palestinian farmers.

Israel Police said the harvest had not been properly coordinated with military authorities and was not authorized without that coordination. Lander disputed the explanation, saying the group was on private Palestinian land and had not crossed a checkpoint or barrier.

He said the farmer had welcomed the volunteers and had been unable to harvest the field for three years because of fears of attacks by settlers from a nearby settlement.

As an American Jew, Lander said, he believes in “the vision of a Jewish and democratic Israel,” but argued that the occupation makes it impossible for Palestinians to live peacefully and harvest their own olives.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani condemned Lander’s detention and expressed support for him on social media.

The detentions come as the West Bank olive harvest has drawn international attention over reports of violence. A Washington Post photographer was injured in a settler attack on Oct. 16, and the State Department condemned criminal violence and said it offered consular assistance.

Lander won the Democratic primary and is running in the Nov. 3 election. He has criticized Israel’s military campaign in Gaza and called for an end to U.S. military aid to Israel.

text:
An Alaska Superior Court judge has allowed a lawsuit challenging election officials’ decision to hand over the state’s voter rolls to the Department of Justice (DOJ) to go forward, saying the Division of Elections may have violated voters’ right to privacy.

In December, after the DOJ demanded each state’s unredacted voter rolls, Alaska signed a memorandum of understanding with the department and turned over the data. In the document, the state also committed to “clean” its voter rolls within 45 days of any DOJ notification.

But that violates the Alaska Constitution’s right to privacy and state voter registration laws, the League of Women Voters of Alaska, the Alaska Black Caucus and the Alaska Public Interest Research Group alleged in a lawsuit filed in April.

The defendants — Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom, who supervises the Division of Elections, and elections director Carol Beecher — asked the court to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing the privacy harms were still hypothetical.

After a hearing in September, Judge Adolf Zeman ruled Friday that the lawsuit could continue, saying the Division of Elections could have negotiated the terms of the memorandum to ensure Alaska laws were followed.

“Instead, the state has given DOJ carte blanche to submit whenever it pleases, a list of whosoever names it decides, for whatever reason DOJ determines, for any number of eligible voters,” Zeman wrote.

Zeman held that the risk of harm was high, noting that the DOJ memorandum’s 45-day provision meant that “Alaskan voters could be removed from the [voter registration list] in violation of the law right before the upcoming general election in November.”

The lawsuit also points to statements from current and former DOJ officials suggesting that the agency will use the voter data for purposes beyond routine list maintenance, like the kind of immigration investigations the administration is now pursuing in California. Zeman refused to dismiss those concerns as too outlandish to consider as a matter of law.

“[G]iven the fundamental nature of the rights at stake, the seriousness of the allegations, and the existence of similar litigation in other states,” Zeman wrote, the lawsuit may now proceed to discovery, where the plaintiffs can ask for relevant records related to the DOJ’s demands and the Division of Elections’ decision to comply with them.

text:
SAN ANTONIO (KTSA News) — The Trump administration has revoked more than 300,000 U.S. visas since President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025, as the White House intensifies its crackdown on immigration.

The State Department announced the latest figures Tuesday, showing a sharp increase from the more than 175,000 visa revocations reported in August. State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said the administration has revoked visas at a faster pace than any administration in history, emphasizing its zero-tolerance policy toward foreign nationals who break the law, commit fraud or threaten national security.

Trump has defended his immigration enforcement campaign as necessary to protect Americans and strengthen national security.

However, civil rights advocates have criticized some of the administration’s actions, arguing that visa revocations and deportation efforts have raised concerns about due process, free speech and potential racial profiling.

The controversy includes cases involving foreign nationals who participated in pro-Palestinian demonstrations against Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, as well as individuals whose social media comments about conservative activist Charlie Kirk’s assassination drew scrutiny.

The administration has also tightened social media screening for immigrants and visa applicants while pursuing deportation cases involving foreign protesters.

Advocates contend that national security concerns have been used to target critics and that individual fraud cases have prompted broader scrutiny of immigrant communities, including Somali Americans in Minnesota.

While Trump campaigned in 2024 on stopping illegal immigration, his administration has also introduced measures affecting legal immigration, including higher fees for certain work visas.

text:
For two decades, Aleksander Nilaj has served the Bronx, making sure no one in the community goes hungry. Now, the Albanian immigrant is locked up in Delaney Hall in New Jersey after being detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement last week.

Nilaj is just one of many immigrants whose sole crime is residing in the U.S. for an extended amount of time, who have been detained by ICE, which claims to only be targeting “the worst of the worst.”

Significance. Nilaj is known in the Bronx community for serving about 8,000 people a month through his Open Hands Association Food Pantry. He spent the last 20 years ensuring residents in the Bronx can receive fresh food and other kitchen staples every Thursday and Saturday.

He has even used his own money to feed people in need.

Meanwhile, says he has spent years pursuing legal pathways to remain in the U.S. despite losing his visa in 2008, according to Eyewitness News, the local ABC station.

Nilaj was detained by ICE last Monday when attending his immigration hearing at 26 Federal Plaza in New York City, according to multiple local news outlets.

He is currently being held at Delaney Hall, a widely controversial detention center in Newark, New Jersey, for its detention conditions and practices that many immigrants inside report violate human rights laws.

The Emancipator has reached out to ICE for a response.

Overlooked angle. The Trump administration and ICE officials have continuously pledged to arrest and deport criminals and “the worst of the worst.” However, many immigrants like Nilaj, who have not committed serious crimes, have been targeted, detained, and deported by ICE agents amid the recent immigration crackdowns across the country.

Power structure. As of July, 70.6% of the immigrants detained in ICE facilities have no criminal convictions, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, whose mission is to provide “comprehensive information about staffing, spending, and enforcement activities of the federal government.”

Rep. Richie Torres, D-N.Y., said many immigrants detained at Delaney Hall also have no criminal records in an interview with Eyewitness News.

“Delaney has about a thousand inmates. None of them are serious offenders or violent offenders. None of them. As far as I’m concerned, Delaney Hall should not even exist,” Torres said.

What experts say. “Donald Trump’s cruel policy of mass deportation is tearing communities and families apart,” Torres said in a video.

“Detaining a man who has dedicated his life to feeding those in need is not justice… It’s cruelty,” Torres said. “The people of the Bronx are demanding the immediate release of Aleks because he is one of our own. Aleks has always stood up for the Bronx; now we in the Bronx must stand up for him.”
