text:
In a new lawsuit, Democrats are asking a federal court to block President Donald Trump and his administration from threatening state and local election officials with criminal prosecution and from pressuring states to remove voters from the rolls.

Those threats “intimidate and coerce election officials who aid and urge registered voters to cast ballots, as well as lawful voters—particularly naturalized citizens—who seek to exercise their most fundamental right,” they allege.

The suit comes just a week after Trump’s Department of Justice (DOJ) sued California and Los Angeles County when election officials refused to set aside 20,000 voters’ ballots based on unverified claims they were noncitizens.

The plaintiffs — three national Democratic organizations, the Nevada Democratic Party, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.), House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) and a California voter who is a naturalized citizen — filed suit Tuesday in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia against Trump, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, the DOJ and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

States have traditionally been responsible for running elections, but the Democrats note that Trump has called on Republicans to “nationalize the voting” and advocated for federal legislation that would impose more control over state elections.

The Democrats’ suit cites Trump’s recent threat that California election officials would “go to jail for a long period of time” as an example of a “pattern of intimidation” that is “meant to frighten officials into complying with the administration’s demands to unlawfully remove voters from the rolls.”

It also emphasizes that the administration has repeatedly made unsubstantiated allegations that state voters are illegally registered, claiming, for example, that 16,000 Nevada voters were noncitizens. DHS later narrowed that claim to 185 voters it said it had confirmed were noncitizens, but Nevada officials said their records showed all 185 were citizens and that DHS had provided “nothing of substance to suggest otherwise.”

All those actions violate Section 11(b) of the Voting Rights Act, which bans voter intimidation, the complaint argues. The Democrats specifically contend that threatening election officials who help registered voters cast and count ballots constitutes prohibited intimidation or coercion under the law.

With the midterms fast approaching, the Trump administration has rapidly ramped up its voter-suppression efforts.

In addition to its lawsuits against states, the White House has transformed the federal Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) database, which traditionally has been used to verify the immigration status of people applying for government benefits, into a highly inaccurate tool for purging alleged noncitizens from voter rolls.

When Texas used the SAVE database to identify 2,724 potential noncitizen voters last year, over 20% were later confirmed to be citizens.

The Democratic plaintiffs point to federal courts’ repeated repudiations of the White House’s actions and Congress’ refusal to enact Trump’s agenda as evidence that the president is acting illegally.

“Thwarted in Congress and the courts, the administration has now simply disregarded the tools Congress provided it and fashioned its own cudgels instead,” the complaint reads. “It once more falls to the judiciary to staunch the resulting lawlessness.”

*The Elias Law Group (ELG) represents the Democrats in this case. ELG Firm Chair Marc Elias is the founder of Democracy Docket.

title: Man who died in ICE custody in Texas was lawful permanent resident - USA Today
description:

Family of man who died in ICE custody disputes account Andrade-Covarrubias' daughter, Estefani Andrade, has disputed ICE's claims that her father concealed his criminal history when applying for permanent residency, according to The Texas Tribune.
Latest ICE custody death in Texas Andrade-Covarrubias is the seventh person to die in ICE detention in Texas this year and the second detainee death reported in Laredo, according to agency records.

text:
A man who died while in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody in South Texas over the weekend was a lawful permanent resident who had lived in the state for decades, according to federal authorities and family members.

Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias, a 56-year-old from Mexico, was found unresponsive in his bed at the Rio Grande Processing Center in Laredo, Texas, on Oct. 17. Security personnel "declared a medical emergency and immediately began lifesaving measures," ICE said in a statement released on Oct. 20.

Paramedics with the Laredo Fire Department responded, but Andrade-Covarrubias was pronounced dead at 10:10 a.m. local time, according to ICE. The agency said he had documented medical conditions including diabetes, hypertension and anxiety and received medical care while in custody.

The cause of death remains unknown pending an autopsy, ICE said. The Texas Tribune first reported Andrade-Covarrubias' death on Oct. 18, citing confirmation from his daughter and Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar.

ICE said Andrade-Covarrubias had been in custody since late June. U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers detained him at the Juárez-Lincoln International Bridge, a port of entry in Laredo, as he was returning from Mexico.

"Andrade, a lawful permanent resident, was determined to have obtained status through fraudulent means by failing to disclose his previous arrest during the review process," the agency said in the statement. "He was processed and transferred to ICE custody pending removal proceedings before an immigration judge. He was receiving due process."

Texas lawmaker seeks answers from ICE

Cuellar, whose district represents Laredo, said he inspected the Rio Grande Processing Center on Oct. 18 and spoke with staff about medical procedures at the facility. Because the death of Andrade-Covarrubias remains under investigation, facility personnel were unable to provide details specific to his case, he said.

Following the visit, Cuellar said he submitted seven written questions to ICE seeking additional information. Among other issues, he asked whether Andrade-Covarrubias requested medical attention during the 72 hours before his death, what treatment and medications he received while in custody, and whether detention staff followed medical and emergency response protocols.

Cuellar also requested information about medical staffing levels at the facility, detention standards and Andrade-Covarrubias' immigration status, including whether he was a lawful permanent resident of the United States. The congressman said he plans to continue following up with the agency as the investigation proceeds.

"My condolences go out to the family of Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias," Cuellar said in a statement on social media on Oct. 19. "Any death in federal custody is a serious matter, and we need to know what happened."

Family of man who died in ICE custody disputes account

Andrade-Covarrubias' daughter, Estefani Andrade, has disputed ICE's claims that her father concealed his criminal history when applying for permanent residency, according to The Texas Tribune. She told the newspaper that her father disclosed his arrest in 2004 for theft during the immigration process and that federal officials approved his green card application.

Andrade-Covarrubias had lived in Dallas for decades, raising three U.S.-born children while working as a painter for apartments and townhomes, the newspaper reported. He frequently traveled to Mexico and was building a home there, according to his daughter.

The Tribune also reported that Andrade-Covarrubias suffered from a heart condition, diabetes, and high blood pressure. He had medication with him when he was detained but his daughter told the newspaper that staff at the Rio Grande Processing Center would not "give him his medications."

She said her father sought medical help after developing a cough, breathing difficulties, and chest tightness but believed his concerns were ignored, according to the Tribune.

Latest ICE custody death in Texas

Andrade-Covarrubias is the seventh person to die in ICE detention in Texas this year and the second detainee death reported in Laredo, according to agency records.

The first ICE detainee death reported in Texas in 2026 was that of Geraldo Lunas Campos, a 55-year-old Cuban migrant. Lunas Campos died on Jan. 3 at Camp East Montana, a detention center in East El Paso near the U.S.-Mexico border.

At the time of his death, Lunas Campos had been held at the facility for nearly four months. His death was later ruled a homicide, according to an autopsy report by the El Paso County Office of the Medical Examiner.

In June, Felix Alcorta-Rodriguez, a 63-year-old man from Mexico, died after being found unresponsive at the Webb County Detention Center in Laredo, according to ICE. Agency records show that medical staff identified a blood clot extending from the right atrium into the inferior vena cava during resuscitation efforts.

Andrade-Covarrubias' death comes amid heightened scrutiny of conditions in immigration detention facilities nationwide. At least 58 people have died in ICE detention facilities since President Donald Trump's second term began in January 2025, according to USA TODAY's immigration enforcement tracker.

Immigrant and civil rights groups, including the American Civil Liberties Union, have raised concerns about conditions in detention facilities and increasing deaths in custody. ICE has disputed allegations of poor conditions, saying it is committed to the health and safety of people in its custody.

text:
Washington Attorney General Nick Brown has joined a multistate coalition backing a legal challenge to what they describe as unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

Brown joined 22 attorneys general in filing an amicus brief Monday in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in support of litigation challenging DHS’s policy and practice of conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests.

SEE ALSO | DHS denies reports of increased ICE arrest goals

Under federal law, immigration officers making warrantless civil immigration arrests must have probable cause to believe a person is unlawfully present in the United States and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained.

The brief argues DHS officers “routinely carry out warrantless arrests without determining if the individual is an escape risk.”

“The Bill of Rights protects the public from unlawful search and seizure, but the administration treats our constitutional protections as optional rather than bedrock requirements,” Brown said. “Checks and balances are essential if we want a country that is both governed and policed fairly.”

The brief also outlines what it calls widespread harms from immigration enforcement practices, including in Washington.

It says escalated enforcement has disrupted communities and undermined public health, safety, education, and local economies. title: The right to enforce civil rights is under attack in the US - Al Jazeera
description:
This autumn, the Supreme Court will consider a question with potentially far-reaching consequences for civil rights in the United States: Who gets to enforce them?
A private right of action allows individuals, or groups acting on their behalf, to file lawsuits to enforce rights protected by law.
Republican-led states have increasingly challenged the doctrine of implied private rights of action, arguing that courts should reject private suits to enforce various types of rights.
One of the most consequential implications of restricting private rights of action is the threat to voting rights.
But even then, the erosion of private rights of action would leave the enforcement of civil and political rights increasingly dependent on a federal agency with limited resources and subject to political direction.
text:
This autumn, the Supreme Court will consider a question with potentially far-reaching consequences for civil rights in the United States: Who gets to enforce them? On November 30, the justices will hear a case over whether employees of federally funded universities can sue under Title IX over alleged workplace sex discrimination. The Trump administration has urged the court to rule that they cannot, arguing that Congress never gave university employees a private right to bring such claims.

The dispute is the latest front in a broader legal push to restrict the ability of individuals and advocacy groups to take rights violations to court themselves. In June, the Supreme Court declined to hear a challenge to a federal appeals court ruling that barred Arkansas United, an immigrant advocacy organisation, from suing to enforce protections for voters who need assistance at the polls. Across a growing number of cases, Republican-led states and the Trump administration are advancing the same basic principle: Unless Congress has clearly authorised private citizens to sue, enforcement should largely be left to the government.

That may sound like an arcane legal argument, but its implications are anything but. If individuals and civil rights groups cannot go to court when laws protecting them are violated, the power to decide which rights are actually enforced increasingly rests with the very government that may be violating, ignoring or choosing not to enforce them.

A private right of action allows individuals, or groups acting on their behalf, to file lawsuits to enforce rights protected by law. These lawsuits can seek compliance with the law or compensation for past violations. Private rights of action are not automatic under US federal and state law. Congress and state legislatures sometimes explicitly authorise private lawsuits. Where they have not, courts have had to determine whether a law implicitly allows individuals or groups to sue, or whether enforcement rests solely with government authorities.

In practice, private litigation has been an essential part of enforcing rights throughout much of US history. As University of Virginia School of Law Professor George Rutherglen writes in a 2015 law review article (PDF):

“The long history of civil rights, dating back to Reconstruction, makes them quintessentially private rights, whose exercise and enforcement should depend primarily on the initiative of the individuals who bear those rights. Public enforcement no doubt remains necessary, and it has an equally long and distinguished pedigree in civil rights law, but it cannot entirely displace individual control over individual rights.”

Proponents of private rights of action, such as AARP, consider them an effective tool for vulnerable individuals and groups to protect their rights when government agencies are unwilling or unable to act. Critics, such as the US Chamber of Commerce Institute for Legal Reform, however, argue that private lawsuits can encourage frivolous litigation.

These critics, often from the political right, have attempted to restrict private litigation through legal arguments against private causes of action. An example is the 2001 Alexander v Sandoval decision, in which a Supreme Court majority led by Justice Antonin Scalia ruled that Title VI did not provide a private right of action to enforce regulations prohibiting policies or practices with a disparate impact on protected groups – discrimination that can occur without clear evidence of intent.

The legal push against private rights of action has intensified in recent years. Republican-led states have increasingly challenged the doctrine of implied private rights of action, arguing that courts should reject private suits to enforce various types of rights. The Trump administration has also adopted this stance. When the court decided a 2021 voting rights case, Justice Neil Gorsuch submitted a one-paragraph concurrence, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas, questioning whether “the Voting Rights Act of 1965 furnishes an implied cause of action,” despite that issue not being raised in the case itself.

The conservative push to restrict private rights of action has extended to a variety of areas. In June, the Supreme Court ruled against Falun Gong practitioners who accused Cisco Systems of helping the Chinese government develop surveillance technology used to facilitate their persecution, concluding that they could not pursue those aiding-and-abetting claims under the federal laws they had invoked.

One of the most consequential implications of restricting private rights of action is the threat to voting rights. In the Arkansas United case, the Eighth Circuit ruled that the immigrant advocacy organisation did not have the right to sue on behalf of non-native English speakers over the right to have language assistance in the voting booth. The ruling concerned Section 208 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. But it extended a much broader argument already adopted by the Eighth Circuit: that private individuals and advocacy organisations cannot sue to enforce key provisions of the Voting Rights Act. The Supreme Court’s refusal in June to hear Arkansas United left that ruling in place.

This argument has also been pushed by Republican-led governments in two redistricting and vote-dilution cases: Board of Election Commissioners v NAACP in Mississippi and Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians v Howe in North Dakota. In May, the Supreme Court vacated judgments in both cases and sent them back for reconsideration in light of its ruling in Louisiana v Callais, without resolving the private-enforcement question. That decision sharply raised the bar for some racial vote-dilution claims, endangering the voting power of Black, Hispanic and Native American communities across the US. At the same time, conservative-controlled governments are attempting to deny members and advocates for these communities the right to even bring some of these cases before the courts, arguing that only the Department of Justice can initiate action over such voting rights violations.

The broader danger is that, as private rights of action are curtailed, enforcement of federal law increasingly depends on decisions made by the executive branch.

The Trump administration is now pursuing a different means of restricting private enforcement. The Clean Air Act explicitly gives private citizens the right to bring certain lawsuits, yet the Justice Department has sought to intervene and dismiss a case brought against xAI over allegations that gas turbines at its power facility in Southaven, Mississippi, are violating federal environmental law and polluting surrounding communities. The facility powers xAI’s Colossus 2 data centre in nearby Memphis. In September, the Justice Department appealed to the Fifth Circuit and sought to halt the case. The department has argued that allowing the suit to proceed would threaten national security and the US pursuit of global leadership in AI. Here, the issue is not whether Congress created a private right to sue – it did – but whether the executive branch can nevertheless step in to stop such a case when it conflicts with its priorities.

Relying solely on the Justice Department to pursue such cases at the federal level is a particularly dubious proposition under the current administration. The department has also been weaponised to target political foes of President Trump. Its Civil Rights Division has been steered away from defending the rights of racial and ethnic minorities and refocused on cases brought by white plaintiffs alleging so-called “reverse discrimination”.

The Justice Department’s current politicisation may be reversed under a future administration. But even then, the erosion of private rights of action would leave the enforcement of civil and political rights increasingly dependent on a federal agency with limited resources and subject to political direction. For example, as Democracy Docket noted in 2024, of the 216 active voting rights and redistricting cases it was tracking at the time, only five were cases brought by the Justice Department. As Professor Rutherglen noted in his article, to rely primarily on government actors to enforce rights “is to transform the nature of those rights: from private to public, from individuals to groups, from legal control by plaintiffs to political control by administrators.”

Private rights of action are now being eroded, case by case. Politicians, civil liberties advocates and organisations must challenge this trend before more avenues for enforcement are closed off. Otherwise, protections won over decades may become increasingly dependent on the willingness of government authorities to uphold them, leaving those whose rights are violated with fewer ways to seek redress.

text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, sent a letter to the Government Accountability Office (GAO) urging them to investigate the Trump Administration’s decision to rapidly establish new, hidden immigration courts. In the Homeland Security Act, Congress preserved the separation of Department of Homeland Security (DHS) immigration enforcement functions from immigration courts’ adjudicatory role. Yet the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) is establishing new courts in DHS facilities where they are managed by DHS personnel.

“DOJ regulations require that members of the public, including family members and loved ones, have access to immigration courts—but my staff documented DHS officials, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) personnel, regularly prohibiting public access to immigration courtrooms at DHS facilities. Worse still, the Administration has established new court locations—where judges are appearing virtually—without providing formal notice to the public and in apparent violation of regulations and policies intended to ensure transparency and due process in immigration court proceedings,” Durbin wrote.

Immigrants are expected to appear for their immigration court hearings unless a judge has waived their appearance, or they may be ordered removed in absentia. In the letter to GAO, Durbin noted that these new courtrooms seem deliberately designed to increase the number of missed hearings to accelerate removals. For example, EOIR does not make these locations publicly available, despite EOIR policy stating a complete list of immigration courts is available on its website.

In the letter, Durbin also noted that EOIR appears to be targeting individuals who do not have legal representation. The Administration’s unprecedented decision to open courts in DHS buildings worsens these due process concerns, given that DHS is the party seeking the removal of immigrants in immigration court proceedings, serving as the prosecutor in these matters. According to recent reports, over the summer, the White House directed DHS to find space for additional courts, and DHS components such as ICE, FEMA, the Coast Guard, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services volunteered.

Durbin wrote, “My staff have observed that these new courtrooms are not just housed within DHS facilities, but DHS is controlling access to the facilities. Immigration court proceedings are open to the public with few exceptions, yet DHS personnel—not EOIR personnel—barred my staff from entering the court in the FEMA building on three separate occasions. During these attempted visits, my staff observed that the doors to the courtroom were locked, and the courtroom lacked any signage, a violation of EOIR policy. During one of the visits, a person who identified herself as a DHS contractor stated that my staff would have to contact FEMA personnel and DHS to gain access because the courtroom was located in a ‘secure’ federal building and was ‘not open to the public.’”

Durbin continued, “My staff also observed DHS agents and contractors prevent the family of unrepresented respondents from entering the courtroom. There was no evidence EOIR personnel were physically present at the court in the FEMA building, and no DHS personnel or contractors would acknowledge that EOIR, not DHS, oversaw immigration court operations. The placement of courts within DHS buildings seems to have no other purpose than to intimidate unrepresented respondents and increase the likelihood that individuals will fail to appear at hearings and be ordered removed in absentia.”

GAO previously has reported that problems with notices, changes in hearing dates, lack of understanding of court processes, and confusion regarding the differences between immigration courts and DHS can affect respondents’ ability to appear for hearings and lead to in absentia removal orders, even when respondents intended to participate in their proceedings. The new courts raise many of these issues, in addition to unprecedented concerns regarding DHS’s direct participation in running our immigration court system.

In the letter, Durbin requested GAO address a number of questions about these new, hidden immigration courts.

Durbin concluded, “It is vital to understand the threats to due process and judicial independence posed by this Administration’s restructuring of the immigration court system. Although Congress separated immigration enforcement functions from the immigration courts, DHS-managed immigration courts should end any illusion that courts are operating independently of this Administration’s mass deportation machine.”

Full text of the letter is available here.

description:

Under federal law, immigration officers conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests must have probable cause to believe that an individual is unlawfully present in the United States and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained.

text:
Attorney General Nick Brown joined a coalition of 22 attorneys general in filing an amicus brief Monday in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in support of litigation challenging the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests.

Under federal law, immigration officers conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests must have probable cause to believe that an individual is unlawfully present in the United States and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. However, DHS officers routinely carry out warrantless arrests without determining if the individual is an escape risk. The brief highlights the widespread harms that unlawful immigration enforcement practices have inflicted on communities across the country, including in Washington.

“The Bill of Rights protects the public from unlawful search and seizure, but the administration treats our constitutional protections as optional rather than bedrock requirements,” Brown said. “Checks and balances are essential if we want a country that is both governed and policed fairly.”

Across the country, federal immigration agents have escalated their enforcement activities, disrupting communities and undermining public health, safety, education, and local economies. Washington has seen these harms firsthand, as aggressive immigration enforcement tactics have kept students out of school, disrupted agricultural work, discouraged people from seeking medical care, blocked access to courts, prevented kids from using the library, impeded shoppers from getting groceries, undermined families’ financial stability, and weakened the relationship between immigrant communities and local law enforcement. Federal agents’ use of ski masks, dark sunglasses, plainclothes, and unmarked vehicles, and refusals to identify themselves while carrying out operations have further contributed to fear and uncertainty in affected communities.

The brief was filed in Escobar-Molina v. DHS, a case challenging DHS’s policy and practice of conducting unlawful warrantless civil immigration arrests in the District of Columbia. On December 2, 2025, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted in part a motion for a preliminary injunction.

In filing the brief, Brown joins the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, and Virginia.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to allow the Trump administration to immediately enforce new medical restrictions for transgender people in prison.

The decision leaves in place a lower-court block on the policy. It was adopted after an executive order from President Donald Trump, a Republican who has taken several steps to roll back transgender rights during his second term.

WATCH: Supreme Court upholds Tennessee law banning gender-affirming care for transgender minors

The brief order did not detail its legal reasoning. Justice Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas would have allowed the policy to be enforced as the lawsuit played out in lower courts.

The Supreme Court has previously allowed other policies for transgender people to move ahead for now, including restrictions on military service and passport sex markers.

Trump's order called on the Bureau of Prisons to revise its medical care policies so that federal funds aren't spent "for the purpose of conforming an inmate's appearance to that of the opposite sex."

WATCH: Where trans advocates are focusing efforts after recent court defeats

The new policy would halt surgeries, taper off hormones and end social accommodations like makeup and wigs. Prisons would continue to offer mental health services.

Attorneys for transgender inmates challenged the policy in court and U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth ordered treatments to continue. Lamberth, who was nominated to the bench by Republican President Ronald Reagan, pointed out that untreated gender dysphoria can cause severe side effects like depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts.

The Trump administration appealed, arguing that treatments raised security concerns and "could no longer be justified." A divided appeals court panel left the order in place.

About 600 inmates were receiving hormone therapy in 2025, the agency said in court records. Withdrawing care would have significant effects on their bodies and mental health, their lawyers said. The government has not detailed evidence of security problems linked to hormone therapy for transgender inmates over the 30 years it has been provided, they wrote.

The conservative-majority Supreme Court has previously upheld state laws banning certain medical treatments for transgender youth, and restricting sports participation by transgender athletes in women's sports.

title: Lawsuit: Tennessee to impose immigration checks in HIV/AIDS safety-net program
description:
Nashville CARES is represented by the Tennessee Justice Center.
But, in its place, the Department of Health has imposed an even broader immigration verification mandate on agencies serving low-income Tennesseans living with HIV/AIDS.
On Monday, Nashville CARES filed suit in Davidson County Chancery Court seeking to declare the contract changes invalid.
A spokesperson for the Department of Health did not respond to a request for comment about the lawsuit on Monday.
Monday's lawsuit is the second this year to challenge efforts by the health department to impose immigration status verification requirements in public safety-net health programs for low-income patients.
text:
In August, Tennessee organizations that aid low-income individuals living with HIV received a surprise memo from the state's health department:

"Effective immediately," the memo said, "no patients without documentation of citizenship or legal residency may be newly enrolled" in many of the services provided through the federal Ryan White HIV/AIDS program or a companion program known as HOPWA, or Housing Opportunities for People with AIDS.

The federal government does not require immigration status checks as a condition of receiving services through HOPWA or Ryan White, a program that has served as the cornerstone of the U.S. government's response to HIV/AIDS for more than 30 years. Even as the Trump administration has sought to exclude immigrants from an array of public benefits, federal law explicitly exempts immigration status checks in federal programs for the treatment of communicable disease.

Attorneys for Nashville CARES, one of the state's largest providers of Ryan White services, immediately filed an administrative challenge to the new rules laid out in the memo, and the Department of Health rescinded it days later. Nashville CARES is represented by the Tennessee Justice Center.

But, in its place, the Department of Health has imposed an even broader immigration verification mandate on agencies serving low-income Tennesseans living with HIV/AIDS.

In a memo dated Oct. 1, the department is now requiring all agencies that serve patients via the Ryan White program to amend their existing contracts to require "eligibility verification for each potential beneficiary/recipient."

The memo cites Tennessee law that requires verifying anyone seeking federal, state or local benefits is lawfully present in the United States; an amendment to the law this year imposes criminal penalties on healthcare and other public benefit providers who fail to report immigrants without legal status to the Tennessee Department of Safety.

On Monday, Nashville CARES filed suit in Davidson County Chancery Court seeking to declare the contract changes invalid.

Nashville CARES argues the state rules violate federal law and is seeking an immediate injunction barring the new contract language from taking effect while its legal challenge is ongoing.

Ryan White covers the cost of medical care, drug assistance, home health care, case management, financial assistance for health insurance premiums and hospice care for low-income individuals living with HIV.

The new contract language "threatens access to medically necessary HIV-related services for otherwise eligible low-income individuals, frustrates (Nashville CARES) organizational mission, disrupts continuity of HIV treatment and support services, and places burdensome verification" requirements that have never before been required and are not supported by federal or state law, the lawsuit said.

"Individuals who lose access to those services face increased risk of worsening HIV disease, transmission of HIV, progression to AIDS and other serious health consequences," it said.

The contract amendment could directly impact hundreds of Nashville CARES' patients and clients. Among then are at least 129 patients with HIV who receive financial help to cover health insurance costs, 150-160 individuals whose mental health and medication management care is paid for by Nashville CARES and 80-100 individuals who receive healthcare at Nashville CARES clinics, according to figures cited in the lawsuit.

Additionally, patients who are U.S. citizens but unable to provide documentation could also be impacted, the lawsuit said.

Lawyers for the nonprofit have sought further clarity from the department about the new contract requirements, but received none, the legal petition said. In legal filings, the lawyers noted that the new contract language may or may not extend to core Ryan White services, including medical treatment and medications; the Tennessee law cited by the department references federal exclusions for these services.

But, the lawyers noted, even if that is the case, one critical component of Ryan White funding is financial assistance that enables individuals to purchase private insurance that gives them to access healthcare, a benefit the amended contract language puts at risk for those who cannot provide proof of citizenship or legal immigration status.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health did not respond to a request for comment about the lawsuit on Monday. The department, earlier this month, provided the Lookout copies of the memos sent to Ryan White providers, but has not responded to a subsequent request for details about impacted recipients of the contract changes.

Monday's lawsuit is the second this year to challenge efforts by the health department to impose immigration status verification requirements in public safety-net health programs for low-income patients.

In July, the department agreed to temporarily halt a new policy requiring the reporting of sick and disabled children to a state immigration enforcement office while a legal challenge brought by three doctors to the policy remains ongoing. About 400 children with chronic and, in some instances terminal illnesses, have remained enrolled in the state's Children's Special Services program as a result.

title: Conditional cautions for people subject to immigration control
description:
What this information is about This blog is about the expansion of the use of conditional cautions as they relate to immigration status.
What is a conditional caution?
A conditional caution can be given for any minor criminal offence that carries a sentence of two years in prison or less.
Previously, people classed as “foreign national offenders”, who could be issued with this kind of conditional caution, were people with no immigration status.
The policy also says: If the foreign national offender raises any issues that may prevent removal within the time period specified in the foreign national offender conditional caution, this may be a breach of the caution.
text:
What this information is about

This blog is about the expansion of the use of conditional cautions as they relate to immigration status. A recent change means people with limited leave to remain (LLR) will now be treated as “foreign national offenders” and may be given cautions which include a condition to leave the UK.

This is a further encroachment of the hostile environment and expansion of the unjust system of double punishment faced by non-British people accused of crimes.

Who is this information for?

The recent change means that anyone with LLR, insecure or no immigration status could be impacted if they come into contact with the criminal justice system.

This blog is for the whole community, particularly for those supporting or working with people in the criminal justice system. We hope people will help us spread awareness. There has been very little publicity around this change and we are concerned that people will face these measures without knowing their rights.

What is a conditional caution?

A conditional caution can be given for any minor criminal offence that carries a sentence of two years in prison or less.

When the police suspect someone of a minor criminal offence, and that person admits the crime, this can be recorded as a formal “caution” without further action being taken. This is instead of the person being charged with the crime or prosecuted.

Accepting a caution means admitting the criminal offence. You can refuse a caution, which may mean being charged and prosecuted for the offence.

Certain conditions can be attached to a caution which must be met, otherwise formal prosecution will follow. This could include things like tackling addiction issues or paying a fine.

One of those conditions, for people classed by the Home Office as “foreign national offenders”, might be to leave the UK.

What has changed?

Previously, people classed as “foreign national offenders”, who could be issued with this kind of conditional caution, were people with no immigration status. This changed with the Crime and Policing Act 2026, which meant that people with limited leave to remain – anyone with temporary immigration status or a visa in the UK – could also be classed as a “foreign national offender”.

What can you do about it?

It is very important for people to know their rights and to get immigration advice if they are in a situation where they may be given this kind of caution. Criminal solicitors may not be familiar enough with immigration law to help.

There are in reality a lot of reasons why it may not be possible for someone on a visa to be given this kind of caution. If there are barriers to removal, this caution cannot be imposed.

According to the policy these barriers to removal are if:

there is an outstanding asylum or human rights claim or related appeal and the person does not withdraw that claim or appeal

there are medical conditions impacting on the foreign national offender’s fitness to travel

the foreign national offender claims their family circumstances in the UK preclude them from accepting a caution

a valid travel document cannot be obtained within the time period for the foreign national offender to leave the UK

We know that in a situation where someone is threatened with prosecution for a minor offence, accepting a caution may instead feel like the better option. Instead, we advise people get immigration advice as well as criminal legal advice.

text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, sent a letter to the Government Accountability Office (GAO) urging them to investigate the Trump Administration’s decision to rapidly establish new, hidden immigration courts. In the Homeland Security Act, Congress preserved the separation of Department of Homeland Security (DHS) immigration enforcement functions from immigration courts’ adjudicatory role. Yet the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) is establishing new courts in DHS facilities where they are managed by DHS personnel.

“DOJ regulations require that members of the public, including family members and loved ones, have access to immigration courts—but my staff documented DHS officials, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) personnel, regularly prohibiting public access to immigration courtrooms at DHS facilities. Worse still, the Administration has established new court locations—where judges are appearing virtually—without providing formal notice to the public and in apparent violation of regulations and policies intended to ensure transparency and due process in immigration court proceedings,” Durbin wrote.

Immigrants are expected to appear for their immigration court hearings unless a judge has waived their appearance, or they may be ordered removed in absentia. In the letter to GAO, Durbin noted that these new courtrooms seem deliberately designed to increase the number of missed hearings to accelerate removals. For example, EOIR does not make these locations publicly available, despite EOIR policy stating a complete list of immigration courts is available on its website.

In the letter, Durbin also noted that EOIR appears to be targeting individuals who do not have legal representation. The Administration’s unprecedented decision to open courts in DHS buildings worsens these due process concerns, given that DHS is the party seeking the removal of immigrants in immigration court proceedings, serving as the prosecutor in these matters. According to recent reports, over the summer, the White House directed DHS to find space for additional courts, and DHS components such as ICE, FEMA, the Coast Guard, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services volunteered.

Durbin wrote, “My staff have observed that these new courtrooms are not just housed within DHS facilities, but DHS is controlling access to the facilities. Immigration court proceedings are open to the public with few exceptions, yet DHS personnel—not EOIR personnel—barred my staff from entering the court in the FEMA building on three separate occasions. During these attempted visits, my staff observed that the doors to the courtroom were locked, and the courtroom lacked any signage, a violation of EOIR policy. During one of the visits, a person who identified herself as a DHS contractor stated that my staff would have to contact FEMA personnel and DHS to gain access because the courtroom was located in a ‘secure’ federal building and was ‘not open to the public.’”

Durbin continued, “My staff also observed DHS agents and contractors prevent the family of unrepresented respondents from entering the courtroom. There was no evidence EOIR personnel were physically present at the court in the FEMA building, and no DHS personnel or contractors would acknowledge that EOIR, not DHS, oversaw immigration court operations. The placement of courts within DHS buildings seems to have no other purpose than to intimidate unrepresented respondents and increase the likelihood that individuals will fail to appear at hearings and be ordered removed in absentia.”

GAO previously has reported that problems with notices, changes in hearing dates, lack of understanding of court processes, and confusion regarding the differences between immigration courts and DHS can affect respondents’ ability to appear for hearings and lead to in absentia removal orders, even when respondents intended to participate in their proceedings. The new courts raise many of these issues, in addition to unprecedented concerns regarding DHS’s direct participation in running our immigration court system.

In the letter, Durbin requested GAO address a number of questions about these new, hidden immigration courts.

Durbin concluded, “It is vital to understand the threats to due process and judicial independence posed by this Administration’s restructuring of the immigration court system. Although Congress separated immigration enforcement functions from the immigration courts, DHS-managed immigration courts should end any illusion that courts are operating independently of this Administration’s mass deportation machine.”

Full text of the letter is available here.

text:
Dive Brief:

A federal judge last week dismissed the Trump administration’s 2025 lawsuit seeking to preempt New York City’s “sanctuary” provisions regarding cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

The U.S. Department of Justice’s claims that federal immigration law preempts New York City’s administrative code and a police department operations order aligning with its “sanctuary” policies lack standing, Judge Ramón Reyes Jr. of the U.S. District Court of Eastern New York stated. “A state’s ability to control its officers and employees lies at the heart of state sovereignty,” Reyes wrote, quoting a previous ruling.

The ruling is “a victory for New Yorkers,” New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement. “We will continue to uphold our local laws and use every tool at our disposal to protect New Yorkers from [Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s] abuses.”

Dive Insight:

The Trump administration’s lawsuit sought to preempt sections of the New York City administrative code that prohibit the NYC Department of Correction from honoring civil immigration detainers or notifying federal immigration authorities of individuals’ release unless a federal judge has issued a judicial warrant and the person has been convicted of a violent crime or is flagged in a federal terrorist screening database. The code also restricts the NYPD from sharing certain custody and non-public information with federal immigration agents.

The lawsuit also sought to preempt NYPD Operations Order No. 4, which limits NYPD officers’ assistance with civil immigration enforcement.

The DOJ asserted the provisions violated the Supremacy Clause by preempting federal immigration law and discriminating against the federal government. These claims failed, Reyes wrote, because “when courts are called upon to address preemption questions, ‘the analysis always begins with the assumption that the historic police powers of the States are not to be superseded by the Federal Act unless that was the clear and manifest purpose of Congress.’”

The Tenth Amendment’s anticommandeering doctrine further prevents the federal government from compelling local governments to participate in federal immigration enforcement, Reyes wrote.

“The court made clear that the federal government has no standing to bring this case and cannot commandeer our City workers to do its bidding,” Mamdani said. “The federal government wants to use fear to divide our city. We will not let them.”

The DOJ declined to comment on ongoing litigation.

text:
Key points:

A coalition of faith groups has grounds to sue to curb immigration enforcement activities at houses of worship, a federal appeals court ruled.

The coalition of Jewish and Christian bodies includes three United Methodist conferences and a general agency.

United Methodist churches already have experienced ICE agents targeting their ministries.

A U.S. federal appeals court ruled Oct. 20 that United Methodists and other faith groups can move forward with their lawsuit to stop a Trump administration policy that allows immigration enforcement within houses of worship.

A divided three-judge panel for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit found that the coalition of Christian and Jewish groups has grounds to sue over the enforcement change.

The faith groups have demonstrated under the new policy, “their members face a ‘credible threat’ of enforcement that will likely cause imminent, if not immediate, injury,” Judge Florence Pan wrote for the majority.

Judge Robert Wilkins joined the majority, and Judge Neomi Rao dissented.

The ruling in “Mennonite Church USA, et. al., vs. U.S. Department of Homeland Security,” revives the lawsuit after a lower court in April 2025 denied the organizations’ bid for early relief. The appellate court has reversed that denial of a preliminary injunction and sent the case back to the lower court.

At issue in the suit is the U.S. Department of Homeland Security guidelines that permit federal agents to carry out immigration raids in “sensitive locations,” such as schools, hospitals, synagogues and churches.

Homeland Security instated the new policy in January 2025, soon after President Trump’s second inauguration. The move put an end to the longstanding practice of restraint in such locations.

The faith groups’ suit, filed Feb. 11, 2025, seeks to prevent Immigration and Customs Enforcement from intruding on ministry without a judicial warrant or special circumstances. The suit contends that the new policy violates both the Religious Freedom Restoration Act and the religious freedom protections in the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution.

The United Methodist Commission on Religion and Race as well as the denomination’s New York, North Georgia and Western North Carolina conferences are among the groups bringing the legal action.

More United Methodist ministries wanted to join the case, but the constraints of the lawsuit limited the number of plaintiffs. Each United Methodist body is a separate legal entity under federal law.

United Methodist leaders, meeting at the Leadership Gathering in Calgary, Alberta, cheered the ruling while noting this is only one step in a long legal battle.

“It’s inherent in our Wesleyan DNA to fight for justice for those that are marginalized and those that are oppressed, and this is an accentuated case,” said Bishop Thomas Bickerton, who leads both the New York and New England conferences. “This was the right thing to do because there are people that are suffering great, great injustices.”

The United Methodist Church’s Social Principles, based on multiple passages on Scripture, have long affirmed “the dignity, worth, and rights of migrants, immigrants and refugees, including displaced and stateless people.” United Methodist congregations don’t check to see if people have the right documentation before welcoming them to worship.

Bickerton added that United Methodist churches in New York have a long history of receiving immigrants into their membership. After all, New York City historically has been where multiple waves of immigrant populations first came ashore in the U.S.

“They are our people, and we’re standing with them at all costs.”

A big source of contention in the case is whether the faith groups involved have shown that the new policy endangered their members and whether reinstating the previous sensitive-location policy would provide relief.

The appellate court’s ruling sided with the faith group’s arguments on both counts.

“Plaintiffs point to several specific examples of the government engaging in enforcement activity at or near their members’ houses of worship,” Pan wrote.

In fact, shortly before the appellate court held oral arguments in the case in February, ICE agents arrested a member of North Hills United Methodist Church Hispanic Mission in Los Angeles, while the church was distributing food. United Methodist Carlos Chavez, an undocumented immigrant from Mexico, was deported shortly after — leaving behind his wife and children. He was not accused of any crime.

“The trauma that the church had to go through is incredible,” said California-Pacific Conference Bishop Dottie Escobedo-Frank, whose area includes Los Angeles.

“We’ve seen it happen in several churches that people won’t come to church if ICE is going to come in,” she said. “Why would they? And so, it affects our ability to gather as worshipping communities because people are afraid to go to church.”

Last year, armed ICE agents also staged an operation in the parking lot of a Charlotte, North Carolina, United Methodist church during preschool pickup.

Western North Carolina Conference Bishop Ken Carter, whose area includes Charlotte, said the conference’s cabinet and trustees decided to join the lawsuit precisely to ensure churches could be safe from such intimidation tactics.

“Sanctuaries are set-apart places that protect human dignity and the image of God,” Carter said. He added that sanctuaries are supposed to provide places “that value people, where they can worship God and trust God.”

The 27 plaintiffs also include the Christian denominations of the Mennonite Church USA, the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church, the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), the Episcopal Church, the Friends General Conference (Quakers) and the Presbyterian Church (USA). The Unitarian Universalist Association is another plaintiff.

Also joining the suit are three Jewish branches — Union for Reform Judaism (the largest Jewish movement in the U.S.), Reconstructing Judaism and the United Synagogue of Conservative Judaism.

They all share a common belief that God calls the faithful to welcome the stranger.

text:
Why Should Delaware Care?

A federal agent was seen at a Delaware middle school campus Tuesday before apprehending a man in front of the school. The action followed a surge of immigration arrests nationally over the summer that highlighted the political divide between President Donald Trump and his supporters and many leaders in Delaware.

A federal immigration agent entered the campus at Stanton Middle School on Tuesday morning, then left after school security approached, according to school officials. An agent or agents then arrested a person just off the school grounds.

The incident appears to be the first time an agent with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement entered a Delaware school campus — a “sensitive place” where state officials have sought to restrict their actions.

It also comes just weeks after the Trump administration announced increased immigration enforcement efforts ahead of the November midterm election, including other public arrests around Delaware.

A video circulating on social media shows agents placing a man into a vehicle near the school, as school buses and other vehicles drove past.

A spokesperson for the Red Clay Consolidated School District said the apparent enforcement activity took place off of school grounds after the school’s administration and security personnel approached the agent on campus.

The spokesperson said no students were taken into custody and none were removed from the school.

“We recognize that situations like this can create concern and uncertainty for our school community, and we remain committed to providing a safe, supportive, and compassionate learning environment for all students,” the spokesperson said.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not comment on the incident when reached by Spotlight Delaware. Instead, it requested the name of the detainee in question, the location the incident took place, and photos and videos from the arrest.

What happened?

Stanton Middle School parent Sade Garnica told Spotlight Delaware she received a call Tuesday morning from her sister, who said she witnessed an ICE agent detaining a father who had previously dropped off his daughter at school.

The sister had also just finished dropping off Garnica’s own daughter at the school.

Fearing ICE could return, Garnica picked up her daughter from school later that morning. She said school officials reassured her that federal agents would not enter the school. Still, she was fearful and pushed administrators to tell her the school’s protocol for suspicious cars.

“They were on school grounds,” Garnica said.

Garnica’s sister told her that the agent’s car was in the drop-off line with other parents before the arrest occurred across the street.

Images shared with Spotlight Delaware of the suspected-ICE vehicle show no visible identifiers. The license plate on the car was also tinted to obscure it from plain view.

ICE vehicles commonly have no markings, and sometimes no identifiable license plate, according to a report last year from NPR. Such unidentifiable plates sparked a dispute last spring between four states and the U.S. Department of Justice, the USA Today reported.

Garnica said Tuesday she still plans to drop her child off at school the next morning. But she remains scared, noting her husband is a Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipient — the immigration program for people brought into the country as children.

“These are just parents. They are trying to just get to work,” Garnica said. “Listen, they don’t know if it’s their turn or not. Or you know, like how do I know I’m not gonna get picked up?”

Can ICE agents go onto school grounds?

Last month, Gov. Matt Meyer signed House Bill 94 into law, which prohibits state and local law enforcement from directly participating in ICE arrests at sensitive locations such as schools, medical facilities, and places of worship unless there is a valid court order.

But because ICE agents are federal police, the new law does not restrict their actions.

Still, Meyer expressed defiance when asked about the incident Tuesday. In an emailed statement he said, “ICE, leave Delaware alone. Our schools are not hunting grounds.”

“Parents of every ethnicity and any nationality must be able to drop their kids off at school without worrying that federal agents are watching, waiting, and tearing families apart,” Meyer said in the statement.

As of Tuesday evening, seven school districts told Spotlight Delaware that there have not been federal agents on their schools’ campuses before the Stanton incident.

text:
A 78-year-old Ugandan priest, who spent more than a year in immigration detention, was released from an Aurora facility Tuesday, but he was unable to walk out on his own.

CBS Colorado cameras captured two fellow detainees carrying Edward Nalwamba from the GEO-operated ICE detention facility to his ride after staff reportedly refused to allow him to use a wheelchair beyond the facility's gate.

Nalwamba, who has lived in Colorado for more than two decades, was released after a federal judge granted his petition challenging his continued detention and ordered immigration officials to free him by Tuesday.

His release comes after 13 months in ICE custody, during which his attorney says his health deteriorated dramatically.

"I was walking. I was exercising. I was playing ping pong," Nalwamba said shortly after his release, describing his physical condition before he was detained in September 2025.

Now, he says he cannot walk without assistance. Nalwamba told CBS Colorado that staff initially brought him toward the facility's exit in a wheelchair, but would not allow him to take it the rest of the way to his transportation.

"They get me outside and say we can't go beyond this," Nalwamba explained. "And I'm asking, 'Can't the car come here?' They say, 'No.' I say, 'So how am I going to get the car?'"

Nalwamba said two other detainees stepped in and offered to carry him. He knew one of the men from his housing unit but said he did not know the other.

"Those friends offered to carry me, and, I mean, I'm so grateful to them," he said.

The circumstances of his release have drawn criticism from Colorado U.S. Sen. John Hickenlooper.

In a social media post Tuesday, Hickenlooper said members of his staff visited the detention center earlier in the day and specifically requested that GEO staff allow Nalwamba to call his caretakers before his release and provide a wheelchair to take him to his ride home.

The senator said GEO staff assured his office that both requests would be honored.

"They failed to deliver on either," Hickenlooper wrote. "No phone call. No wheelchair. No human decency."

Hickenlooper called the incident an act of cruelty and pledged to continue holding those responsible accountable.

CBS Colorado has reached out to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security seeking an explanation for the wheelchair restrictions, the circumstances surrounding Nalwamba's release and allegations concerning his medical treatment. DHS had not responded to those questions as of Tuesday evening.

Nalwamba's attorney, Joy Athanasiou, says her client entered into ICE custody in good health but has experienced serious medical problems while detained.

"When he came to the detention center a year ago, he was extremely healthy. He was very fit. He exercised regularly. He could do 15 to 20 push-ups. Now, he is wheelchair-bound. He is extremely weak," Athanasiou said.

Athanasiou said Nalwamba was diagnosed with pneumonia in January, lost more than 30 pounds and collapsed while detained. She also says he has suffered from an ongoing respiratory illness since June, and accuses ICE of failing to provide adequate testing and treatment.

Nalwamba described experiencing chest pain, coughing, dizziness and weakness in his legs.

His attorney says his supporters are working to arrange a medical appointment and hope he can begin physical therapy and rehabilitation.

In a statement provided to CBS Colorado in June, the Department of Homeland Security defended the medical care available to people in ICE custody.

"It is a longstanding practice to provide comprehensive medical care from the moment an alien enters ICE custody," a DHS spokesperson said. According to the agency, that includes access to medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care.

Nalwamba previously served as a priest at Resurrection Anglican Fellowship in Greenwood Village for approximately 15 years. He arrived in the United States from Uganda in 2002 and remained in the country after his tourist visa expired.

Nalwamba and his supporters have said he fears returning to Uganda because of persecution connected to his pro-democracy political activities.

In its June statement, DHS said Nalwamba had overstayed his visa, was granted voluntary departure in 2007 and received a final order of removal in 2010. ICE detained him on Sept. 18, 2025.

Before that arrest, Nalwamba says he had been living under an immigration order of supervision.

His attorneys challenged his prolonged detention through a federal habeas corpus petition, arguing the government could not continue holding him indefinitely.

Athanasiou says she is concerned that ICE could attempt to detain Nalwamba again.

On Monday, a judge granted the petition and ordered Nalwamba released no later than Oct. 20. Despite that ruling, his underlying immigration case remains unresolved.

"I am back to where I was when they first arrested me," Nalwamba said. "So I was asking myself, 'Why did they arrest me in the first place?'"

text:
The YPU hosted former DHS secretary Alejandro Mayorkas to debate Resolved: America Needs Deportation. Student speakers on both sides challenged him.

Mayorkas addresses the YPU in Sterling-Sheffield-Strathcona Hall. (Credit: Michelle Zheng)

Michelle Zheng

Managing Editor, The Buckley Beacon

Former Homeland Security secretary Alejandro Mayorkas told the Yale Political Union that the United States must keep the power to deport, even as he conceded that “there are unjust deportations.”

“To be clear,” Mayorkas told the Union, “today I advocate in support of the proposition that the United States must have the legal authority to deport an individual.”

The resolution before the Union was Resolved: America Needs Deportation. Mayorkas opened in the affirmative by calling it ambiguous. He spent the rest of the night arguing that a country without the power to remove people, in effect, has no border. He then closed by conceding that the system is broken, slow and, at times, unjust.

Born in Havana in 1959, Mayorkas came to the United States as a child the following year. He was U.S attorney in Los Angeles under President Bill Clinton. Under President Obama, he directed U.S citizenship and immigration services, where he oversaw the rollout of DACA, and then served as deputy secretary of Homeland Security.

As secretary from 2021 to 2025, the first immigrant and first Latino to lead the department, he oversaw the border during the largest number of migrant encounters at the U.S Mexico border in 20 years. House Republicans impeached him in February 2024, accusing him of failing to enforce immigration law and misleading Congress. The senate dismissed both articles on April 17, 2024, in party-line votes. He is a resident fellow at Harvard’s Institute of Politics this fall.

His record as DHS secretary shadowed the debate. Students on the right pressed him on the border under his watch, while those on the left challenged the case for deportation itself.

Mayorkas built his case from first principles: sovereignty, territorial borders and the social contract. He quoted President Ronald Reagan’s description of America as a nation of immigrants, then added, “As we are a nation of immigrants, we are also a nation of laws.”

He did not defend the current law as a good law. The limits set by Immigration and Nationality Act “need to be revisited,” he said. “They were last codified 30 years ago. Yet the world has changed over these past three decades.” But, he continued, “the limits now in place need to be obeyed.”

He rejected the idea of open borders as an ideal that “does not comport with or even recognize the reality in which we live.” Housing, hospitals and schools, he argued, cannot absorb unregulated migration. He pointed to New York City between 2022 and 2024, when tens of thousands of migrants arrived, some on buses sent by other states’ governors, in a city already short of housing.

Obedience to the law, he said, “requires the power to enforce the law,” and the main tool is removal. “Without that authority, our borders are virtually erased.”

The floor pressed him on his own record. One student asked how an administration committed to the rule of law had allowed millions of migrants into the country. Mayorkas answered that his administration believed in the right, written into U.S law, to claim asylum on arrival at the border.

Asked whether he backed the Trump administration’s mass deportations, he began with what he called a point of unanimity: “our immigration system is fundamentally broken.” With limited resources, he said, an agency must use discretion the way a prosecutor does. “I will focus the allocation of resources on those individuals who are unlawfully present in the United States and pose a threat to public safety.”

On whether people may resist laws they consider unjust, he drew a line. “It is our responsibility to react appropriately, but within the bounds of the law,” he said, pointing to the courts and the vote.

One student made a remark about enforcement becoming a “paper tiger.” Mayorkas said he doubted most people, whatever their politics, would describe that way today. When part of the room hissed, he stopped. “I am very interested in understanding why my remark just received some hiss,” he said and invited someone to explain.

A student from the Party of The Left answered that enforcement was aggressive against a few heavily publicized targets while thousands of undocumented workers were left in slaughterhouses, farms and factories because their labor benefits large employers. Mayorkas responded that his department had shifted worksite enforcement away from rounding up workers and toward the employers who exploit them.

The students then debated the matter.

Conservative party member Carlos Perez, arguing in the affirmative, made an economic case, citing the 2016 National Academy of Sciences study. Its estimated $54 billion annual gain to native-born Americans, he said, was about three-tenths of one percent of native income, while wage effects shifted roughly $500 billion from competing workers to their employers. Then he turned to the guest. “I’m quite happy to stand on the same side of this debate as former Secretary Mayorkas, and I welcome his conversion. But for millions of Americans, vague platitudes about immigration enforcement aren’t enough.”

Pressed on families with U.S.-citizen children, Perez said he did not want to separate families but that the state has “an obligation” to remove those who entered illegally, with “a few exceptions.” Asked to clarify, he went further: “I do not think it’s necessarily immoral for an illegal immigrant who happens to have U.S. citizen children to be deported.”

Corinne Cowan, also a member of the Conservative party, mentioned Abraham Lincoln’s Lyceum Address and its call for a “political religion” of reverence for the law. Illegal immigration, she argued, “dilutes the power” of that civic faith and of the distinction of citizenship.

Massimo Mejia, Chairman of the Progressive party, responded to Cowan’s remarks in a rebuttal. He asserted that “the American nation was not founded upon a deep-seated respect for law, but the fear of the law,” and that the American mission, grounded in the proposition that all men are created equal, extends universally.

Beatrix Lozach of The Party of The Left opened with the story of Liam Conejo Ramos, the 5-year-old detained with his father in Minnesota on Jan. 20. “Social media virality should not be a prerequisite for due process,” she said. The Fifth and 14th Amendments protect every “person,” she noted, “not citizen,” yet the government does not provide lawyers in removal proceedings. She proposed extradition, which requires a crime recognized in both countries, as the tool for gang members instead of deportation.

Mayorkas used his closing remarks to answer the opposition directly. “I do not consider a deportation in and of itself a threat to due process,” he said. Many people in the system, he argued, have had competent counsel and “an abundance of due process” before their claims were denied.

Then he conceded ground. “We need to be clear. There are unjust deportations,” he said. “There are unjust methods by which immigration laws are enforced. We have seen that,” with “tragic and calamitous” effects in recent months. “Nevertheless, the fact of an unjust deportation does not translate to the fact that we should not have any deportation.”

After the debate, when the Beacon asked, Mayorkas declined to comment on specific immigration policies under the Trump administration.

The resolution passed, 86-27, with four abstentions.

title: Haitian migrants changed this town - Trump's deportation drive is reshaping it again - BBC
